m: an official order or proclamation issued by a person or body in authority
x: Nobody in the household dared to question Grandmother's edict that phones stay off the dinner table.
A company-wide edict from headquarters banned personal travel on business accounts, effective immediately.
The university issued an edict requiring all theses to be submitted electronically by the end of May.
In 1685, a royal edict revoked the religious protections that French Protestants had enjoyed for nearly a century.
She resented her father's edicts about curfews, but years later she admitted they had kept her out of trouble.
tc: Rather than consulting the staff, the new director simply announced his decision by ______, leaving no room for discussion.
'Rather than consulting' and 'no room for discussion' show the decision was imposed as an official order.
se: The emperor's ______ forbade anyone from leaving the city during the plague.
decree
Both 'edict' and 'decree' mean an official order from a ruler, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: strange and frightening in a mysterious way; unsettling
x: There was an eerie silence in the house after the power went out and the fans stopped whirring.
The empty office had an eerie feel on Sunday evening, with half-drunk mugs still sitting on abandoned desks.
Researchers noted an eerie resemblance between the two manuscripts, though they were written centuries apart.
Residents described the eerie glow in the night sky that appeared minutes before the meteor struck.
It was eerie how my sister seemed to know I was upset before I had said a word.
tc: Although the abandoned village was perfectly peaceful in daylight, at night its empty streets felt so ______ that visitors hurried back to their cars.
'Although ... peaceful in daylight' sets up a contrast, and visitors hurrying away shows the streets felt strangely frightening.
se: The flickering lights and distant footsteps in the deserted hospital were truly ______.
creepy
Both 'eerie' and 'creepy' describe something mysteriously frightening, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: lively, bubbly and enthusiastic in personality or manner
x: Her effervescent personality made her the obvious choice to welcome guests at the wedding reception.
Our new receptionist is so effervescent that even grumpy clients leave the front desk smiling.
Students loved Professor Rahman's effervescent lectures, which turned dry economic theory into lively storytelling.
Critics praised the young actress for an effervescent performance that lifted an otherwise forgettable comedy.
Even after a long shift, he stayed effervescent, cracking jokes and teasing his younger brother at dinner.
tc: Unlike her quiet, reserved brother, Maya was ______, filling every room with laughter and chatter.
'Unlike her quiet, reserved brother' signals a contrast, and 'laughter and chatter' restates the idea of liveliness.
se: The host's ______ manner kept the conversation flowing all evening.
vivacious
Both 'effervescent' and 'vivacious' mean lively and full of energy, so the meaning stays the same.

m: difficult to find, catch, define or achieve
x: A good night's sleep has become elusive since the construction work started next door.
After three years of trying, a promotion still seemed elusive, so she began applying elsewhere.
Scientists have spent decades on the disease, but a definitive explanation of its cause remains elusive.
Police finally caught the elusive suspect after he had slipped past them in three different cities.
For many young couples in Dhaka, an affordable flat close to work remains frustratingly elusive.
tc: Though the team came close several times, victory proved ______, and they finished the season without a single trophy.
'Came close' but finished 'without a single trophy' shows victory was hard to achieve.
se: For philosophers, fairness has always been ______: everyone values it, yet no two people define it in quite the same way.
slippery
Both 'elusive' and 'slippery' describe an idea that is hard to pin down, which the colon clause explains.

m: in a very early stage of development; not yet fully formed
x: My plans for a home vegetable garden are still embryonic; so far I have only bought the seeds.
The merger talks are at an embryonic stage, so please keep the details confidential for now.
Her thesis began as an embryonic idea scribbled in the margin of a lecture handout.
The country's embryonic electric-vehicle market will need heavy investment in charging infrastructure to grow.
Their friendship was still embryonic when he moved abroad, so they slowly lost touch.
tc: The software is far from finished; in fact, it exists only in ______ form, with most of its features yet to be built.
'Far from finished' and 'most of its features yet to be built' show it is at a very early stage.
se: The startup's business model was still ______, and investors wanted to see more detail before committing money.
nascent
Both 'embryonic' and 'nascent' mean just beginning to develop, so the sentence means the same thing.

m: to fill someone with intense delight; to captivate completely
x: The street magician enraptured the children, who forgot all about their ice creams melting in the heat.
Her presentation enraptured the board, and they approved the budget without a single objection.
Students sat enraptured as the visiting astronomer described the birth and death of distant stars.
The orchestra's performance enraptured an audience that had queued for hours in the monsoon rain.
He was enraptured by her laugh the first time they met, and he still is thirty years later.
tc: Far from boring the young audience, the three-hour opera managed to ______ them so completely that hardly anyone checked a phone.
'Far from boring' signals the opposite of boredom, and nobody checking a phone shows complete captivation.
se: A gifted storyteller can ______ listeners of any age with nothing but a voice and a good tale.
captivate
Both 'enrapture' and 'captivate' mean to hold someone's attention with delight, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: the characteristic spirit, values and beliefs of a community, group or era
x: Our family's ethos was simple: work hard, share what you have, and never waste food.
The startup's collaborative ethos disappeared once the new managers introduced strict hierarchies and rigid rules.
This school's ethos encourages students to ask difficult questions rather than simply memorize answers.
Critics argue that the party has abandoned its founding ethos of public service in pursuit of power.
She felt that the volunteer group's ethos of kindness matched her own values perfectly.
tc: Founded by Quaker merchants, the firm still reflects their ______ of honesty and thrift, values that guide every hiring decision.
The phrase 'values that guide every hiring decision' restates the blank as a set of guiding beliefs.
se: Many longtime employees felt the takeover had destroyed the company's ______ of loyalty and mutual respect.
culture
Both 'ethos' and 'culture' refer to a group's shared values, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a pleasing, harmonious combination of sounds, especially in words
x: Some parents choose a baby's name purely for its euphony, without much thought about its meaning.
The copywriter rewrote the slogan three times, trying to balance clarity with euphony.
Poets often bend strict grammar for the sake of euphony, choosing words for how they sound together.
Linguists studying euphony have found that people across cultures prefer certain combinations of vowels and consonants.
Lying in bed, she listened to the euphony of rain on the tin roof and her mother's humming.
tc: The poet avoided harsh consonant clusters and chose soft, flowing words, so the poem is admired chiefly for its ______.
Avoiding 'harsh' sounds and choosing 'soft, flowing words' points to pleasing sound.
se: Readers praised the ______ of her prose, in which every sentence seemed to flow like music.
musicality
Both 'euphony' and 'musicality' mean a pleasing, musical quality of sound, so the meaning is the same.

m: deliberately avoiding giving a direct answer or commitment
x: When I asked my brother who had eaten the last mango, he became suspiciously evasive.
The manager gave an evasive reply when we asked whether there would be layoffs this year.
The student's evasive answers during the viva convinced the examiners he had not written the code himself.
Journalists criticized the spokesperson for being evasive about how many civilians had been affected.
Whenever I mention marriage, he gets evasive and changes the subject to cricket.
tc: Instead of answering the reporter's question directly, the senator was ______, skirting every mention of the scandal.
'Instead of answering ... directly' and 'skirting every mention' show he was deliberately avoiding the question.
se: When asked about the missing funds, the treasurer was ______, offering vague answers and changing the subject.
cagey
Both 'evasive' and 'cagey' describe someone unwilling to give straight answers, so the sentence means the same.

m: a comprehensive, clear explanation or description of a theory, idea or argument
x: Before we started the board game, my uncle gave a lengthy exposition of the rules.
Her exposition of the new budget was so clear that even the interns understood it.
The textbook's opening chapter offers a careful exposition of Newton's laws with everyday examples.
The judge's written ruling included a detailed exposition of the constitutional principles at stake.
In a long letter to his parents, he wrote an honest exposition of why he wanted to study abroad.
tc: Students found the lecturer's ______ of quantum theory remarkably lucid, since he explained each concept step by step.
'Explained each concept step by step' restates the blank as a clear, detailed explanation.
se: The book begins with a thorough ______ of the author's central argument.
explanation
Both 'exposition' and 'explanation' mean a clear setting-out of ideas, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: the belief that events are predetermined, so people are powerless to change them
x: His fatalism about traffic is almost admirable: he simply shrugs and says we'll arrive when we arrive.
A mood of fatalism spread through the office after the third round of budget cuts.
The seminar examined how fatalism in Greek tragedy shapes the choices characters believe they can make.
Public-health officials worry that fatalism about the pandemic will discourage people from getting vaccinated.
She tried to shake off her fatalism and believe that the relationship could still be saved.
tc: Rather than fighting the diagnosis, the patient accepted it with quiet ______, convinced that nothing he did could alter his fate.
'Convinced that nothing he did could alter his fate' defines the belief the blank names.
se: A creeping ______ had settled over the voters, who believed the result was already decided no matter what they did.
resignation
Both 'fatalism' and 'resignation' describe accepting that one cannot change the outcome, so the meaning stays the same.

m: enormous; extremely large in size, amount or scale
x: My cousin served us a gargantuan plate of biryani that could easily have fed four people.
Migrating the company's records to the new system turned out to be a gargantuan task.
Sequencing the human genome required a gargantuan effort from laboratories around the world.
The government now faces gargantuan debts that will take decades to repay.
Her gargantuan appetite for romance novels has kept the local bookshop in business for years.
tc: Far from being modest, the new stadium is ______, with seating for well over a hundred thousand fans.
'Far from being modest' signals the opposite of small, and the huge seating figure confirms enormous size.
se: Rebuilding the city after the earthquake required ______ resources and more than a decade of work.
immense
Both 'gargantuan' and 'immense' mean extremely large, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: splendor and impressiveness, especially of appearance, scale or style
x: We stood in silence, overwhelmed by the grandeur of the mountains at sunrise.
The new headquarters, with its marble lobby and glass atrium, was designed to project corporate grandeur.
Historians debate whether the empire's architectural grandeur concealed serious economic weaknesses.
Despite its faded grandeur, the old colonial hotel still attracts tourists who love history.
He had delusions of grandeur, convinced that he was destined to become a famous filmmaker.
tc: Unlike the plain wooden chapel in her village, the cathedral overwhelmed her with its ______, from the soaring arches to the gilded altar.
The contrast with a 'plain wooden chapel' and the details of soaring arches and gilding point to splendor.
se: Visitors are often struck by the ______ of the palace's main hall.
magnificence
Both 'grandeur' and 'magnificence' mean impressive splendor, so the sentence means the same.

m: to please or satisfy someone; to indulge a desire
x: It gratified my mother enormously when the neighbors praised her rooftop garden.
Positive feedback from clients gratifies the team far more than any bonus could.
She was gratified to learn that her paper had been accepted by a leading journal.
Critics say the policy was designed to gratify wealthy donors rather than help ordinary voters.
He never learned to delay pleasure and expected every whim to be gratified immediately.
tc: Rather than disappoint her loyal fans, the author chose to ______ their wish for a sequel.
'Rather than disappoint' signals the opposite, so the blank must mean to please or satisfy.
se: The chef went to great lengths to ______ every guest's request, however unusual.
satisfy
Both 'gratify' and 'satisfy' mean to fulfil a wish, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: looking exhausted and unwell, especially from fatigue, worry or suffering
x: After a week of nursing the baby through a fever, my sister looked pale and haggard.
By the end of the audit, the accountants were haggard, unshaven and running on coffee.
Students emerged haggard from the exam hall after three hours of advanced calculus.
Rescue workers looked haggard after spending two days searching the flooded villages for survivors.
He was shocked by his father's haggard face when he returned home after five years abroad.
tc: After weeks without proper sleep, the once-vigorous captain looked ______, his eyes sunken and his face lined with worry.
'Weeks without proper sleep', 'sunken' eyes and a face 'lined with worry' describe an exhausted appearance.
se: Years of caring for her sick husband had left her face ______ and lined.
drawn
Both 'haggard' and 'drawn' describe a face that looks tired and strained, so the meaning stays the same.

m: having a strong, exhilarating effect; intoxicating or excitingly powerful
x: The kitchen filled with the heady scent of cardamom, cloves and frying onions.
For a young analyst, the heady experience of presenting to the board was hard to forget.
Those first heady weeks at university, full of new friends and freedom, passed far too quickly.
In the heady days after independence, many citizens believed that anything was possible.
Falling in love at nineteen was a heady mix of excitement, fear and constant daydreaming.
tc: The ______ excitement of opening night soon gave way to the sober reality of poor ticket sales.
'Gave way to the sober reality' contrasts with the blank, which must describe intoxicating excitement.
se: For the whole town, winning the championship after twenty years of defeat felt truly ______.
exhilarating
Both 'heady' and 'exhilarating' describe a thrilling, excited feeling, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: information heard from others that cannot be adequately verified; rumor
x: Don't believe everything your aunts say about the new neighbors; most of it is hearsay.
Promotions should be based on performance, not on office hearsay about who is friendly with whom.
Historians must separate eyewitness accounts from hearsay recorded decades after the events.
The judge ruled that the testimony was hearsay and therefore inadmissible as evidence.
She refused to end the friendship over mere hearsay without first hearing his side of the story.
tc: Because the witness had not seen the crime herself and was only repeating what a neighbor told her, the court dismissed her statement as ______.
'Only repeating what a neighbor told her' defines secondhand, unverified information.
se: The newspaper was criticized for printing a story based on little more than ______.
rumor
Both 'hearsay' and 'rumor' mean unverified talk passed from person to person, so the meaning is the same.

m: requiring enormous strength or effort; extremely difficult
x: Getting three teenagers out of bed before seven on a school day is a herculean task.
Clearing the backlog of customer complaints required a herculean effort from the support team.
Writing a dissertation while working full-time is herculean, but she somehow managed both.
Rescuers made herculean efforts to reach villagers stranded by floodwater after the cyclone.
It took herculean patience to stay calm while my father tried to learn video calling.
tc: Restoring the flooded archive was hardly a simple job; it was ______, requiring months of painstaking work by dozens of conservators.
'Hardly a simple job' and 'months of painstaking work' show the task demanded enormous effort.
se: Feeding an entire refugee camp with so few supplies proved ______ for the small charity.
arduous
Both 'herculean' and 'arduous' mean extremely hard and demanding, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: well known, respected and admired for past achievements
x: Our small town is proud of its one illustrious son, who became a renowned surgeon in London.
She joined the law firm hoping to learn from its illustrious senior partners.
The university boasts an illustrious list of alumni, including three Nobel laureates.
The veteran cricketer ended his illustrious career with a century in his final match.
Despite her illustrious family name, she insisted on being judged by her own work.
tc: Far from being an obscure figure, the composer was ______ across Europe during his lifetime, praised by kings and critics alike.
'Far from being an obscure figure' signals the opposite, and praise from kings and critics confirms fame and respect.
se: The prize has been awarded to many ______ scientists, including several future Nobel laureates.
eminent
Both 'illustrious' and 'eminent' mean famous and highly respected, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: about to happen; approaching, often in a threatening way
x: Dark clouds over the river warned us of an impending storm, so we headed home early.
Rumors of an impending merger made everyone in the office nervous about their jobs.
With final exams impending, the library stayed packed with students until midnight.
Scientists warn of impending water shortages as mountain glaciers continue to shrink.
She sensed impending heartbreak when he started cancelling their weekend plans without explanation.
tc: Sensing ______ disaster as the river kept rising, villagers began moving their livestock to higher ground.
The river 'kept rising' and villagers moving to higher ground show a disaster about to happen.
se: Farmers rushed to harvest their crops before the ______ cyclone reached the coast.
approaching
Both 'impending' and 'approaching' describe something about to arrive, so the sentence means the same.

m: to have an effect, especially a negative one, on something; to encroach
x: Late-night work calls began to impinge on the little time I had with my children.
Employees worry that the new monitoring software impinges on their privacy.
Lab duties should not impinge on the time students need for their own research.
Critics say the law impinges on freedom of the press and must be revised.
She refused to let her parents' expectations impinge on her choice of a partner.
tc: The judge ruled that the new curfew went too far, since it would ______ on citizens' basic freedom of movement.
'Went too far' shows the curfew would intrude on and limit a basic freedom.
se: Residents fear that the new highway will ______ on the protected wetlands.
encroach
Both 'impinge' and 'encroach' mean to intrude harmfully on something, so the meaning stays the same.

m: difficult or impossible to reach, enter, obtain or understand
x: During the monsoon, our ancestral village becomes almost inaccessible because the roads flood.
The files became inaccessible after the server crashed, and IT took two days to recover them.
Many students find his writing inaccessible because it is packed with unexplained jargon.
Quality healthcare remains inaccessible to millions of rural families who cannot afford to travel.
After the divorce, my father seemed emotionally inaccessible, retreating into silence whenever we visited.
tc: Unlike his lively and approachable lectures, the professor's published papers are dense and largely ______ to non-specialists.
'Unlike his ... approachable lectures' and 'dense' signal that the papers are hard for outsiders to understand.
se: Without a four-wheel-drive vehicle, the mountain monastery is practically ______.
unreachable
Both 'inaccessible' and 'unreachable' mean impossible to get to, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: silly and lacking sense or meaning
x: My little brother kept asking inane questions throughout the whole film.
The meeting was full of inane chatter, and nothing useful was decided.
The examiner was irritated by inane answers that showed students had not read the text.
Commentators mocked the advertisement's inane slogan, which seemed to mean nothing at all.
She grew tired of his inane jokes and longed for a serious conversation.
tc: Rather than offering a thoughtful response, the candidate made ______ remarks that revealed he had not understood the question at all.
'Rather than ... thoughtful' signals a contrast, so the remarks must be silly and empty.
se: Instead of discussing the budget, the committee wasted an hour on ______ arguments about the color of the logo.
silly
Both 'inane' and 'silly' mean foolish and pointless, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to deprive of strength or ability; to disable
x: A bad bout of dengue incapacitated my father for nearly two weeks.
A cyberattack incapacitated the company's payment system for an entire afternoon.
Severe exam stress can incapacitate even well-prepared students if they do not learn to manage it.
The strike was designed to incapacitate the country's ports and force the government to negotiate.
Grief over her mother's death incapacitated her for months, and she could barely leave the house.
tc: The new tranquilizer dart is designed to ______ an animal briefly without causing any lasting harm.
A tranquilizer that works 'briefly without ... lasting harm' must temporarily disable the animal.
se: A single well-placed virus could ______ the city's entire power grid.
disable
Both 'incapacitate' and 'disable' mean to make unable to function, so the sentence means the same.

m: in human form; being the perfect embodiment of a quality (placed after the noun)
x: To my nephews, their grandmother is kindness incarnate, always ready with sweets and stories.
The new CEO was efficiency incarnate, replying to every email within minutes.
In the novel, the villain is evil incarnate, a man without a single redeeming quality.
Many voters saw the young reformer as hope incarnate after years of corruption.
When he arrived with flowers after the fight, he looked like apology incarnate.
tc: She seemed to embody generosity in every gesture; to her friends, she was generosity ______.
'Embody generosity in every gesture' restates the idea of a quality taking human form.
se: To the frightened villagers, the warlord was terror ______.
personified
Both 'incarnate' and 'personified' mean a quality given human form, so the meaning stays the same.

m: tending to stir up conflict or strong anger; (literally) designed to start fires
x: My uncle's incendiary comments about politics turned the family dinner into a shouting match.
HR warned employees not to post incendiary messages in the company chat group.
The professor's incendiary article on colonial history provoked furious letters from other scholars.
Authorities blamed incendiary speeches for the riots that broke out after the election.
She regretted sending such an incendiary text to her best friend in a moment of anger.
tc: Rather than calming the angry crowd, the speaker delivered ______ remarks that sent protesters smashing shop windows.
'Rather than calming' signals the opposite, and the smashed windows show the remarks stirred up anger.
se: The editor refused to publish the letter, calling its language needlessly ______.
provocative
Both 'incendiary' and 'provocative' describe language meant to inflame anger, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a natural tendency or preference to act or think in a particular way
x: My first inclination was to stay in bed, but the smell of fresh parathas finally got me up.
He has a strong inclination to agree with whatever the boss says in meetings.
Choose a subject that matches your own inclinations rather than one your parents think is respectable.
Surveys show a growing inclination among young voters to support independent candidates.
She had neither the time nor the inclination to argue with her mother-in-law.
c: neither the time nor the inclination
tc: Although his parents pushed him toward medicine, his natural ______ was always toward painting and music.
'Although his parents pushed him' contrasts their wishes with his own natural preference.
se: Despite her ______ to trust everyone, she was suspicious of the stranger's offer.
tendency
Both 'inclination' and 'tendency' mean a natural leaning toward behaving a certain way, so the sentence means the same.

m: so excellent that nothing else can be compared with it; matchless
x: Nothing beats my mother's fish curry; its flavor is simply incomparable.
The firm's incomparable reputation for reliability has kept clients loyal for decades.
Students flock to her seminars for the incomparable clarity with which she explains statistics.
Reviewers praised the incomparable beauty of the documentary's underwater footage.
The joy of holding his newborn daughter for the first time was incomparable.
tc: Many singers have recorded the song, but none comes close to the original; her performance remains ______.
'None comes close to the original' means nothing can match her performance.
se: The view from the summit is ______, unlike anything else in the region.
unparalleled
Both 'incomparable' and 'unparalleled' mean better than anything else, so the meaning stays the same.

m: not attracting attention; not easily noticed
x: I tried to look inconspicuous as I slipped into the back of the class twenty minutes late.
She chose an inconspicuous seat at the back of the meeting room so she could leave early.
The researcher placed small, inconspicuous cameras around the forest to film shy animals.
Security officers in plain clothes remained inconspicuous among the crowd at the stadium.
He made himself inconspicuous at family weddings, avoiding aunts who asked when he would marry.
tc: Hoping not to draw attention to himself, the spy wore plain gray clothes and stayed as ______ as possible.
'Hoping not to draw attention' defines the quality of being unnoticed.
se: The new security cameras are small and ______, so most shoppers never notice them.
unobtrusive
Both 'inconspicuous' and 'unobtrusive' mean not easily noticed, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: not clearly defined or limited in time, extent or meaning; vague
x: The bridge near our house is closed for an indefinite period while engineers inspect it.
The project has been put on indefinite hold until the new budget is approved.
The professor criticized my essay for its indefinite thesis, which never took a clear position.
Workers at the garment factory began an indefinite strike after talks with management collapsed.
He gave an indefinite answer about the wedding date, which only worried her parents more.
tc: Because no end date was ever set, the factory's closure was described as ______ rather than temporary.
'No end date was ever set' means the closure has no fixed limit in time.
se: The airline has suspended flights to the region until some ______ date in the future.
unspecified
Both 'indefinite' and 'unspecified' mean not fixed or stated, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: careless about what one says or does, especially by revealing private matters
x: My aunt is so indiscreet that the whole family knew about my exam results within an hour.
An indiscreet email to the wrong mailing list revealed the planned layoffs before management was ready.
A lab assistant's indiscreet remarks leaked details of the unpublished research to a rival group.
The minister resigned after indiscreet comments were picked up by a microphone he thought was off.
She regretted being so indiscreet about her friend's divorce at the dinner party.
tc: Although she had promised to keep the secret, she was so ______ that her colleagues heard the whole story by lunchtime.
'Although she had promised to keep the secret' contrasts with her revealing it, so she was careless with private information.
se: Diplomats are trained never to make ______ remarks that could embarrass their government.
unguarded
Both 'indiscreet' and 'unguarded' describe careless remarks that reveal too much, so the sentence means the same.

m: reasoning from specific observations to general conclusions
x: After three rainy Fridays, my inductive conclusion that it always rains on Fridays turned out to be wrong.
Our analytics team uses inductive methods, spotting patterns in customer data before forming any theory.
In the philosophy seminar, we discussed why inductive arguments can never guarantee certain conclusions.
Early naturalists relied on inductive reasoning, collecting thousands of specimens before proposing general laws.
Her inductive guess, based on months of his long silences, was that he was losing interest in the relationship.
tc: Unlike deductive logic, which moves from general rules to particular cases, ______ reasoning builds general principles from particular observations.
The contrast with 'deductive logic' and the phrase 'from particular observations' define reasoning from specifics to generalities.
se: Darwin's theory grew out of ______ research: years of observing finches and fossils before drawing any conclusions.
empirical
Both 'inductive' and 'empirical' describe research built on observation before theory, so the meaning stays the same.

m: a tendency to do nothing or to resist change; lack of movement or energy
x: Sheer inertia kept me on the sofa all Sunday, though I had planned to clean the flat.
Bureaucratic inertia meant the new software sat unused for months after it was purchased.
Many students stay in courses they dislike out of inertia rather than genuine interest.
Reformers struggled to overcome the political inertia that had blocked land reform for decades.
Their marriage continued more through inertia than love, as neither had the energy to leave.
tc: The committee did not reject the proposal outright; through sheer ______, it simply never got around to discussing it.
'Did not reject ... outright' but 'never got around to discussing it' points to a failure to act, not opposition.
se: Many people stay with the same bank for decades out of ______ rather than satisfaction.
apathy
Both 'inertia' and 'apathy' explain staying put through lack of effort or interest, so the sentence means the same.

m: intended or likely to arouse anger, hostility or violence
x: Please avoid inflammatory topics like politics at Grandfather's eightieth birthday lunch.
The manager was disciplined for sending an inflammatory email that insulted the entire sales team.
The debate moderator stopped one student for making inflammatory claims without evidence.
The television channel was fined for broadcasting inflammatory content during the communal unrest.
In the heat of the argument, she said something inflammatory that she still regrets.
tc: Instead of easing tensions, the governor's ______ speech provoked violent protests across the region.
'Instead of easing tensions' and 'provoked violent protests' show the speech stirred up anger.
se: The website removed several posts because of their ______ language about minorities.
incendiary
Both 'inflammatory' and 'incendiary' describe language meant to stir hostility, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: cleverness, originality and inventiveness in solving problems
x: With a little ingenuity, my grandmother turned leftover rice into a delicious breakfast.
The team's ingenuity saved the launch when the main server failed an hour before the demo.
Engineering students showed real ingenuity in designing a low-cost water filter from local materials.
Scientists praised the ingenuity of a rescue plan that used drones to deliver medicine during floods.
His ingenuity in planning surprise dates kept their relationship exciting after many years together.
tc: Lacking proper tools, the stranded sailors relied on sheer ______ to build a working radio from spare parts.
Building a radio from spare parts without proper tools requires inventive cleverness.
se: The puzzle can be solved only with considerable ______ and patience.
cleverness
Both 'ingenuity' and 'cleverness' mean skill at solving problems, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: unaware of or indifferent to something; (also) unconscious
x: He seemed insensible to the cold, wearing only a T-shirt in the January fog.
The manager appeared insensible of the resentment building among his overworked staff.
Absorbed in her experiment, she was insensible to the noise of the construction outside the lab.
Too many policymakers remain insensible to the hardships faced by families in rural areas.
He was completely insensible to her hints that she wanted more than friendship.
tc: So absorbed was the scholar in his reading that he remained ______ to the storm raging outside his window.
'So absorbed ... in his reading' explains why he did not notice the storm.
se: The CEO seemed curiously ______ of the anger his remarks had provoked.
unaware
Both 'insensible' and 'unaware' mean not noticing something, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to say something abruptly, interrupting a conversation or speaker
x: Just as Dad began his favorite story, my sister interjected that we had all heard it before.
May I interject a quick point before we move on to the next item on the agenda?
During the lecture, a student interjected with a question that the professor gladly answered.
The opposition leader repeatedly interjected during the debate, earning a formal warning from the chair.
Whenever her husband exaggerated, she would gently interject a correction.
tc: The chairman asked everyone to let the speaker finish and not ______ until the question period began.
'Let the speaker finish' shows the blank means to break in with a comment.
se: Before the lawyer could finish her argument, the judge tried to ______ a question.
interpose
Both 'interject' and 'interpose' mean to insert a remark into someone else's speech, so the sentence means the same.

m: a person who intrudes into a place or situation where they are not wanted or do not belong
x: At my cousin's wedding, a stranger at the buffet turned out to be an interloper nobody had invited.
Long-serving staff treated the new manager as an interloper and ignored his suggestions.
Biologists see the invasive fish as an interloper that threatens native species in the lake.
Established airlines regard low-cost carriers as interlopers in a market they once controlled.
At family gatherings, her new stepfather still felt like an interloper among old memories.
tc: In the tight-knit village, every newcomer was eyed with suspicion, and the ______ who had bought the old mill was no exception.
'Tight-knit' and 'every newcomer was eyed with suspicion' show the buyer was seen as an unwelcome outsider.
se: The longtime members resented the ______ who had joined the club and immediately tried to change its rules.
intruder
Both 'interloper' and 'intruder' mean an unwelcome person who pushes in, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: unwilling to accept views, beliefs or behavior different from one's own
x: My grandfather can be intolerant of loud music, so we keep the volume low when he visits.
A workplace that is intolerant of mistakes discourages employees from trying new ideas.
The scholar was criticized for being intolerant of any theory that contradicted her own.
Human-rights groups warn that society is becoming more intolerant of religious minorities.
He realized he had been intolerant of his partner's habits and decided to be more patient.
tc: Far from welcoming debate, the regime was deeply ______ of dissent and jailed anyone who criticized it.
'Far from welcoming debate' and jailing critics show an unwillingness to accept opposing views.
se: The editor was so ______ that he refused to publish any opinion different from his own.
narrow-minded
Both 'intolerant' and 'narrow-minded' describe someone who rejects other views, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to make something legally void, or to show that an argument or result is wrong
x: Opening the back of the phone yourself will invalidate the warranty, so take it to the shop.
A single missing signature can invalidate the entire contract, so check every page carefully.
One flawed control group was enough to invalidate the study's main findings.
The high court invalidated the election results after finding widespread ballot fraud.
Telling someone to 'just cheer up' can invalidate their feelings instead of helping them.
tc: The researchers had hoped the new data would support their theory, but it seemed instead to ______ it entirely.
'Hoped ... would support' contrasts with 'instead', so the data must disprove the theory.
se: Any alteration to the will after the owner's death would ______ the entire document.
nullify
Both 'invalidate' and 'nullify' mean to make legally void, so the meaning stays the same.

m: always; on every occasion, without exception
x: Whenever I visit my grandmother, she invariably tells me that I look too thin.
Our Monday meetings invariably run over time because someone raises a new issue at the end.
Students who skip the weekly problem sets invariably struggle on the final exam.
Heavy monsoon rain invariably brings waterlogging to the city's low-lying streets.
He invariably apologizes first after an argument, even when he was not at fault.
tc: Although professional forecasters are sometimes wrong, the old fisherman's predictions were ______ accurate; in forty years he never misjudged a storm.
'Never misjudged a storm' in forty years shows his predictions were right every time.
se: Her lectures ______ began with a joke, a habit her students soon came to expect.
always
Both 'invariably' and 'always' mean on every occasion, so the sentence means the same.

m: done without conscious control or will; not chosen
x: I let out an involuntary yelp when a cockroach ran across my foot.
The factory announced involuntary redundancies after its attempt to find volunteers failed.
In biology class we learned that breathing and heartbeat are largely involuntary processes.
Human-rights groups condemned the involuntary detention of protesters without trial.
She gave an involuntary shiver when she saw her ex-husband walk into the room.
tc: Blinking when dust hits your eye is ______; you cannot stop it even if you try.
'You cannot stop it even if you try' defines an action outside conscious control.
se: The patient's ______ movements were caused by a nerve disorder rather than by any conscious intention.
unconscious
Both 'involuntary' and 'unconscious' describe movements made without deliberate control, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to irritate or annoy
x: It really irks me when people talk loudly on their phones on a quiet bus.
What irked the staff most was not the pay cut but the lack of any explanation.
Students were irked by the last-minute change to the exam timetable.
The ruling irked environmental groups, who had campaigned for stricter limits on pollution.
His habit of checking his phone during dinner irks his wife more than she admits.
tc: Although she tried to appear calm, the constant interruptions began to ______ her, and she finally snapped at her colleague.
'Tried to appear calm' and 'finally snapped' show the interruptions annoyed her.
se: Small things like a dripping tap can ______ even the most patient person.
irritate
Both 'irk' and 'irritate' mean to annoy, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: so opposed or incompatible that agreement or harmony is impossible
x: My brother and I have irreconcilable views on whether pineapple belongs on pizza.
The two founders split up after irreconcilable disagreements over the company's direction.
The two theories rest on irreconcilable assumptions, so at least one of them must be wrong.
Negotiations collapsed because the two governments' demands over the border were irreconcilable.
The couple filed for divorce, citing irreconcilable differences after ten years of marriage.
tc: Despite years of mediation, the two factions' goals remained ______, and the alliance finally fell apart.
'Despite years of mediation' and the alliance falling apart show the goals could never be brought into agreement.
se: Her religious beliefs seemed ______ with the scientific theories she studied at university.
incompatible
Both 'irreconcilable' and 'incompatible' mean unable to exist together in agreement, so the meaning stays the same.

m: impossible to repair, put right or undo
x: Dropping the old laptop in the bathtub caused irreparable damage to its hard drive.
One careless post on social media did irreparable harm to the brand's reputation.
Plagiarism can do irreparable damage to a young researcher's career.
Scientists warn that draining these wetlands would cause irreparable harm to migratory birds.
Their friendship suffered an irreparable rift after he revealed her secret to everyone.
tc: Although the broken vase could be glued, the damage to her trust was ______; she never confided in him again.
'Although the vase could be glued' contrasts with trust that could never be restored.
se: The fire caused ______ damage to the ancient manuscripts.
irreversible
Both 'irreparable' and 'irreversible' mean damage that cannot be undone, so the sentence means the same.

m: impossible to control or hold back, especially of high spirits or enthusiasm
x: My irrepressible niece kept singing all the way home despite her mother's pleas for quiet.
His irrepressible optimism kept the team going through months of failed experiments.
The class was full of irrepressible students who asked questions faster than the teacher could answer.
Even under strict censorship, the people's irrepressible desire for freedom found ways to express itself.
She broke into an irrepressible grin when he finally got down on one knee.
tc: Even after losing her job and her home, she kept laughing and making plans; her spirit was simply ______.
'Even after losing her job and her home' she stayed cheerful, so her spirit could not be held down.
se: The children's ______ enthusiasm could not be dampened even by the rain.
uncontrollable
Both 'irrepressible' and 'uncontrollable' mean impossible to hold back, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: cheerful, merry and lighthearted
x: The jocund old shopkeeper always greeted us with a joke and a free sweet.
Despite the deadline, the office was in a jocund mood after the team won the award.
The poem's jocund opening contrasts sharply with the grim war scenes that follow.
A jocund crowd filled the streets to celebrate the national cricket team's victory.
Her jocund laughter could lift his spirits even on his worst days.
tc: Unlike his gloomy and silent brother, Uncle Karim was ______, always joking and singing at family gatherings.
'Unlike his gloomy and silent brother' signals the opposite, and 'joking and singing' confirms cheerfulness.
se: The festival atmosphere was ______, with music and laughter everywhere.
merry
Both 'jocund' and 'merry' mean cheerful and lighthearted, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: expressing praise and admiration
x: My aunt sent a laudatory message to the family group after my cousin passed the bar exam.
The CEO's laudatory email singled out the warehouse staff for their extra effort.
The reviewer's laudatory comments on her first paper gave her the confidence to keep publishing.
The newspaper ran a laudatory profile of the young engineer who designed affordable solar lamps.
At the farewell party, colleagues gave laudatory speeches that left her in tears.
tc: Far from criticizing the novel, the reviewers were overwhelmingly ______, calling it the finest book of the decade.
'Far from criticizing' signals the opposite, and 'the finest book of the decade' is high praise.
se: The award ceremony featured several ______ speeches about the retiring headmistress.
complimentary
Both 'laudatory' and 'complimentary' mean expressing praise, so the meaning stays the same.

m: expressing strong emotion in an imaginative, beautiful, song-like way
x: My father waxes lyrical whenever he talks about the river near his childhood home.
The brochure's lyrical description of the resort made the office retreat sound like a holiday.
Students admired the lyrical prose of the novel, especially its descriptions of the monsoon.
Critics praised the documentary's lyrical photography of Arctic ice and endless winter light.
In his lyrical letters, he described how much he missed her during the long winter.
tc: Unlike the dry, technical manuals he wrote for work, his travel essays are ______, full of vivid imagery and emotion.
'Unlike the dry, technical manuals' signals a contrast, and 'vivid imagery and emotion' restates the meaning.
se: The poet's ______ descriptions of the countryside made readers long to visit.
poetic
Both 'lyrical' and 'poetic' describe beautiful, emotionally expressive language, so the sentence means the same.

m: relating to trade, merchants or commerce
x: My grandfather came from a mercantile family that had sold spices in Old Dhaka for generations.
The firm's mercantile instincts helped it spot profitable new markets before its rivals did.
The course examines how mercantile networks connected Indian Ocean ports in the sixteenth century.
Venice grew rich as a mercantile power, controlling trade routes across the Mediterranean.
She disliked his mercantile attitude toward friendship, as if every favor had to be repaid.
tc: Unlike the inland farming towns, the port city was thoroughly ______, its wealth built entirely on buying and selling goods.
'Unlike the inland farming towns' and 'buying and selling goods' point to a city devoted to trade.
se: The city's ______ interests pushed the government to lower tariffs on imported goods.
commercial
Both 'mercantile' and 'commercial' mean related to trade, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: so captivating that it holds your attention completely, as if casting a spell
x: We sat on the balcony for an hour, watching the mesmerizing rhythm of the rain on the tin roofs.
Her presentation was so mesmerizing that nobody in the boardroom checked their phones.
Students found the professor's lecture on black holes strangely mesmerizing, despite the dense mathematics.
Scientists filmed the mesmerizing movements of a million starlings swirling over the marshes at dusk.
He still remembers the mesmerizing sound of her laugh from the night they first met.
tc: The dancer's movements were so ______ that the audience forgot to applaud until the music had stopped for several seconds.
The audience forgetting to applaud shows they were completely spellbound, so the blank must mean captivating.
se: The view of the city lights from the hilltop was ______, and we stayed watching it long after dark.
captivating
Both 'mesmerizing' and 'captivating' describe something so beautiful it holds your attention, giving the same meaning.

m: a mistaken belief or wrong understanding of something
x: I bought the larger phone under the misapprehension that it came with a charger.
Many new employees are under the misapprehension that staying late is what impresses their manager.
The tutor corrected a common misapprehension about how compound interest is calculated.
Public fear of the vaccine was fuelled by a widespread misapprehension about its side effects.
She ended the friendship under the misapprehension that he had betrayed her secret.
tc: He accepted the job under the ______ that it was permanent, only to learn later that the contract ended after six months.
'Only to learn later' reveals that his belief was wrong, so the blank means a mistaken belief.
se: The report aims to clear up the public ______ that recycling plastic is always good for the environment.
misconception
Both 'misapprehension' and 'misconception' mean a mistaken belief, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: dark and hard to see through; figuratively, unclear or suspiciously dishonest
x: After the monsoon floods, the pond behind our house turned brown and murky.
The company's accounts are so murky that even the auditors could not trace where the money went.
Historians admit that the origins of the ancient text remain murky.
Investigators are still probing the murky world of offshore shell companies.
Their relationship had a murky past that neither of them liked to talk about.
tc: Unlike the transparent funding of the previous campaign, the financing behind this one was ______, with donations routed through anonymous intermediaries.
'Unlike the transparent' and 'anonymous intermediaries' signal the opposite of clear, so the blank means unclear or shady.
se: The details of how the contract was awarded are still ______, and reporters are demanding answers.
unclear
Both 'murky' and 'unclear' mean not yet understood or explained, giving the same meaning.

m: to think about something deeply and at length, often in a dreamy way
x: Sitting by the window with her tea, she mused about what life would be like in another city.
During the meeting, the director mused aloud on whether the project was worth continuing.
In his essay, the philosopher muses on the nature of memory and identity.
Commentators have long mused over why some nations prosper while others stagnate.
Stuck in Dhaka traffic, he mused on the choices that had brought him to this point in his life.
tc: Rather than reacting at once, she liked to ______ on a problem for days, turning it over quietly in her mind.
'Turning it over quietly in her mind' restates the blank, so it must mean to think deeply.
se: On long train journeys, he would often ______ on how different his life might have been.
reflect
Both 'muse on' and 'reflect on' mean to think quietly and deeply about something.

m: so small or unimportant that it is not worth considering
x: The difference in price between the two brands is negligible, so just buy the one you like.
The new software update had a negligible effect on the team's productivity.
In this experiment, air resistance is negligible and can safely be ignored.
Economists say the tax cut will have a negligible impact on ordinary families.
To her, the risk of rejection seemed negligible compared with the regret of never asking.
tc: Although critics predicted the new law would transform the industry, its actual effect proved ______, with sales barely changing.
'Although' sets up a contrast with 'transform', and 'barely changing' shows the effect was tiny.
se: The extra cost of shipping is ______, so we decided to order everything online.
insignificant
Both 'negligible' and 'insignificant' mean too small to matter, giving the same meaning.

m: quick and light in movement, or quick and clever in thinking
x: The nimble cyclist wove through the traffic jam while cars sat motionless.
Small start-ups are often more nimble than large firms in responding to customer demands.
With a nimble mind, she solved the professor's riddle before anyone else had finished reading it.
The robot's nimble fingers can assemble a smartphone in under a minute, engineers reported.
My grandmother's fingers were still nimble enough to thread a needle at ninety.
tc: Despite his age and bulky frame, the old dancer remained surprisingly ______, gliding across the stage with ease.
'Despite his age and bulky frame' and 'gliding with ease' point to light, quick movement.
se: The ______ squirrel leapt from branch to branch without missing a step.
agile
Both 'nimble' and 'agile' mean quick and light in movement, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a remedy or solution, often useless, promoted with exaggerated claims of success
x: The street vendor sold a nostrum that he claimed would cure everything from headaches to baldness.
Management keeps offering the same tired nostrums, like team-building retreats, for problems that run much deeper.
The historian traces how patent nostrums flooded American markets in the nineteenth century.
Voters are weary of politicians who promise easy nostrums for complex economic problems.
Her aunt swore by a homemade nostrum, but it did nothing for her chronic back pain.
tc: The doctor warned her patients against the ______ advertised online, explaining that no single pill could cure arthritis, diabetes and insomnia at once.
'No single pill could cure' everything shows the product is a dubious cure-all.
se: Economists dismissed the candidate's tax plan as yet another ______ that promised to fix everything overnight.
panacea
Both 'nostrum' and 'panacea' mean a supposed cure for all problems, giving the same meaning.

m: to block or close off an opening, passage, or view
x: Tall new buildings now occlude the view of the river from our old flat.
Engineers found that a buildup of dust had occluded the air vents in the server room.
In the lab, the students learned how a clot can occlude a coronary artery.
Astronomers watched as the moon occluded a distant star for several seconds.
Grief seemed to occlude every happy memory she had of their years together.
tc: If the plaque continues to build up, it may eventually ______ the artery completely, cutting off blood flow to the heart.
'Cutting off blood flow' shows the blank means to block the artery.
se: Doctors feared that the swelling would ______ the patient's airway.
obstruct
Both 'occlude' and 'obstruct' mean to block a passage, giving the same meaning.

m: a very difficult, painful, or unpleasant experience that lasts for some time
x: Getting a visa appointment turned into a three-month ordeal of forms and phone calls.
After the ordeal of the audit, the whole finance team took a long weekend.
For many students, university admission tests are an exhausting ordeal that consumes an entire year.
The freed hostages spoke to reporters about their ordeal on Tuesday evening.
She never fully recovered from the emotional ordeal of her parents' bitter divorce.
tc: The climbers' ______ lasted three days, during which they endured freezing winds without food or shelter.
'Endured freezing winds without food or shelter' describes a long, painful experience.
se: After the ______ of the long flight and the lost luggage, she was happy just to reach her hotel.
nightmare
Both 'ordeal' and 'nightmare' mean a very unpleasant experience, so the meaning stays the same.

m: serving as decoration rather than having a practical use
x: We planted ornamental grasses along the driveway to soften the concrete.
In that company, the deputy chair's role is largely ornamental; real decisions are made elsewhere.
The architecture course examines how ornamental details on Mughal buildings reflect Persian influence.
Critics argue that the new advisory council is merely ornamental and has no real power.
She refused to be an ornamental presence in his life, admired but never truly listened to.
tc: The fireplace in the hotel lobby is purely ______; it has never been lit, since there is no chimney behind it.
A fireplace that is never lit and has no chimney exists only for decoration.
se: The brass handles on the cabinet are ______ and do not actually open anything.
decorative
Both 'ornamental' and 'decorative' mean for show rather than use, giving the same meaning.

m: strikingly strange or unusual, often to the point of seeming ridiculous
x: My cousin turned up to the wedding in an outlandish purple suit with gold buttons.
The consultant's outlandish proposal to move the head office to an island was quickly rejected.
Some of the theories in the paper were so outlandish that reviewers questioned the author's methods.
Conspiracy theories about the moon landing grow more outlandish with each passing year.
He made outlandish promises to win her back, but she had heard them all before.
tc: At first his claims seemed ______, but as more evidence emerged, even his harshest critics admitted he might be right.
'At first ... but' sets up a contrast with being proved right, so the claims first seemed absurdly strange.
se: The film's plot is so ______ that it strains belief even for a comedy.
preposterous
Both 'outlandish' and 'preposterous' mean absurdly strange, giving the same meaning.

m: the many items of equipment or personal belongings needed for a particular activity
x: Our hallway is cluttered with my son's cricket paraphernalia: bats, pads, helmets and gloves.
She moved into the new office with all her paraphernalia of laptops, chargers and sticky notes.
The chemistry lab was full of glass flasks, burners and other scientific paraphernalia.
Police found drug paraphernalia, including scales and syringes, in the abandoned car.
He packed away the paraphernalia of their old relationship: the photos, letters and concert tickets.
tc: The photographer arrived with so much ______ (tripods, lenses, lights and reflectors) that it took three trips to unload the van.
The list of tripods, lenses and lights defines the blank as a collection of equipment.
se: The garage was full of camping ______: tents, stoves, sleeping bags and lanterns.
gear
Both 'paraphernalia' and 'gear' mean the equipment for an activity, so the meaning is the same.

m: a large belly that sticks out
x: After a year of desk work and late-night biryani, he had developed a noticeable paunch.
My boss jokes that his paunch is the result of too many business lunches.
The study links a paunch in middle age to a higher risk of heart disease.
In the cartoon, the corrupt mayor is drawn with a huge paunch and a fat cigar.
She teased her husband gently about his paunch, but secretly she found it endearing.
tc: Years of rich food and no exercise had given the once-slim athlete a soft ______ that strained against his shirt buttons.
'Rich food and no exercise' and 'strained against his shirt buttons' point to a protruding belly.
se: He started jogging every morning to lose the ______ he had gained during the holidays.
potbelly
Both 'paunch' and 'potbelly' mean a large, protruding stomach, giving the same meaning.

m: easily irritated, especially over small things; bad-tempered
x: Without his morning tea, my father is peevish until at least ten o'clock.
The manager grew peevish whenever anyone questioned his scheduling decisions.
Exhausted by the all-night study session, the students were peevish and short with each other.
The senator gave a peevish reply when reporters asked about the missing funds.
She found his peevish complaints about the restaurant embarrassing on their anniversary.
tc: Usually cheerful, the toddler became ______ and whiny whenever he missed his afternoon nap.
'Usually cheerful' contrasts with the blank, and 'whiny' confirms it means irritable.
se: After hours stuck in traffic, the passengers grew ______ and began snapping at the driver.
irritable
Both 'peevish' and 'irritable' mean easily annoyed, so the sentence means the same.

m: to deliberately lie after swearing an oath, usually used as 'perjure oneself'
x: He refused to perjure himself, even though telling the truth meant losing his job.
The company's lawyer assured the clerk that she could not be forced to perjure herself.
In our law seminar, we debated whether a witness who perjures himself to protect a child deserves punishment.
The former official was charged after prosecutors proved he had perjured himself before the committee.
She knew her brother had perjured himself to protect her, and the guilt stayed with her for years.
tc: Asked to give false evidence in court to save his friend, the witness declined, saying he would never ______ himself under oath.
'False evidence in court' and 'under oath' show the blank means to lie while sworn to tell the truth.
se: No honest witness would ______ himself simply to protect his employer.
forswear
'Forswear oneself' and 'perjure oneself' both mean to lie under oath, giving the same meaning.

m: to relate to, concern, or be relevant to something
x: Please keep all receipts that pertain to your travel expenses.
The manager said the new rules pertain only to staff hired after January.
Your essay should discuss only the evidence that pertains to your research question.
The court released documents pertaining to the disputed land deal.
She refused to answer any questions that pertained to her private life.
tc: The judge ruled the letters inadmissible because they did not ______ to the charges being heard, only to an unrelated dispute.
'Only to an unrelated dispute' shows the letters were not relevant, so the blank means to relate.
se: The new safety regulations ______ only to factories with more than fifty workers.
apply
Both 'pertain to' and 'apply to' mean are relevant to, giving the same meaning.

m: to spread through and be present in every part of something
x: The smell of frying onions pervaded the whole house by lunchtime.
A sense of anxiety pervaded the office as rumours of layoffs spread.
Themes of loss and exile pervade the poet's later work.
Corruption pervades every level of the city's administration, according to the report.
Even years later, a quiet sadness pervaded their conversations about their late son.
tc: Fear did not stay confined to one district; it began to ______ the entire city, until no neighbourhood felt safe.
'Did not stay confined' and 'the entire city' show the blank means to spread throughout.
se: A feeling of optimism seemed to ______ the campus in the weeks before graduation.
permeate
Both 'pervade' and 'permeate' mean to spread through every part, giving the same meaning.

m: of crucial importance because other things depend on it
x: Choosing the right flatmate turned out to be a pivotal decision in my first year abroad.
Her pivotal role in landing the contract earned her a promotion.
The discovery of DNA's structure was a pivotal moment in modern biology.
Swing voters will play a pivotal part in deciding the election.
Meeting his mentor at nineteen was pivotal in shaping the man he became.
tc: Far from being a minor episode, the battle was ______, determining the outcome of the entire war.
'Far from being a minor episode' and 'determining the outcome' show the blank means crucially important.
se: The coach believes the final over will be ______ in deciding the match.
crucial
Both 'pivotal' and 'crucial' mean decisively important, so the meaning stays the same.

m: grand and showy ceremony or display, especially on official occasions
x: Their wedding was held with great pomp, with a horse-drawn carriage and three hundred guests.
The company launched its new product with all the pomp of a royal coronation.
Our history lecturer described the pomp of the Mughal court in vivid detail.
The new president was sworn in amid much pomp and ceremony.
She preferred quiet dinners at home to the pomp of formal family gatherings.
tc: Unlike his predecessor's lavish inauguration, the new mayor took office without any ______, signing the oath in a small room with only two witnesses.
'Unlike his predecessor's lavish inauguration' signals the blank means grand ceremony.
se: The royal visit was marked by great ______, with parades, banners and a military band.
pageantry
Both 'pomp' and 'pageantry' mean showy ceremonial display, giving the same meaning.

m: power or strength, especially of a drug, argument, or influence
x: Cheap painkillers often lose their potency if you store them in a hot, humid room.
The marketing team badly underestimated the potency of word-of-mouth recommendations from loyal customers.
Researchers tested the potency of the new antibiotic against resistant bacteria.
The potency of social media as a political tool became clear during the protests.
She was surprised by the potency of her own anger when she finally confronted him.
tc: Because the vaccine must be kept cold, storing it at room temperature can sharply reduce its ______ and leave patients unprotected.
'Leave patients unprotected' shows the vaccine loses its strength, so the blank means power.
se: Scientists are studying why the drug's ______ declines after only a few months on the shelf.
efficacy
Both 'potency' and 'efficacy' refer to how strongly the drug works, giving the same meaning.

m: preying on or exploiting others, especially the weak, for one's own gain
x: Be careful with those cheap online loans; many come with predatory interest rates.
Several employees accused the supervisor of predatory behaviour toward young interns.
Biology students observed the predatory habits of spiders in the campus garden.
Regulators have promised to crack down on predatory lenders who target the elderly.
She sensed something predatory in his charm and kept her distance.
tc: Far from helping struggling families, the lender was ______, deliberately trapping borrowers in debts they could never repay.
'Far from helping' and 'deliberately trapping borrowers' show the blank means exploitative.
se: Consumer groups condemned the bank's ______ practices, which targeted borrowers with poor credit.
exploitative
Both 'predatory' and 'exploitative' mean taking unfair advantage of the vulnerable, giving the same meaning.

m: to be an early sign or indication of something that will happen later
x: The dark clouds over the field seemed to prefigure the rain that ruined the match.
The small losses in the first quarter prefigured the company's eventual collapse.
Critics argue that the novelist's early short stories prefigure the themes of her later masterpieces.
Some economists believe the housing bubble prefigured the wider financial crisis.
Their first argument, about something trivial, prefigured the deeper conflicts in their marriage.
tc: The minor tremors that shook the village that morning seemed to ______ the devastating earthquake that struck at nightfall.
The morning tremors came before the later earthquake, so the blank means to be an early sign of it.
se: In the novel, the hero's childhood fear of water seems to ______ his drowning in the final chapter.
foreshadow
Both 'prefigure' and 'foreshadow' mean to hint at a later event, giving the same meaning.

m: belonging to the earliest ages of the world; ancient and primitive
x: We hiked through a primeval forest where some of the trees were over a thousand years old.
Our team retreat was held in a lodge on the edge of a primeval rainforest.
Geology students studied rocks that formed in the primeval oceans of the early Earth.
Conservationists are fighting to protect the Sundarbans, one of the last primeval mangrove forests in the region.
A primeval fear of the dark took hold of her as the lights went out.
tc: Untouched by logging for thousands of years, the ______ woodland looks much as it did before humans ever arrived.
'Untouched for thousands of years' and 'before humans ever arrived' show the blank means extremely ancient.
se: Scientists believe life first emerged in the ______ oceans billions of years ago.
primordial
Both 'primeval' and 'primordial' mean existing at the very beginning of time, giving the same meaning.

m: easily shocked by matters of sex or nudity; excessively proper or modest
x: My aunt is so prudish that she changes the channel whenever a couple kisses on screen.
Some staff found the new dress code prudish, especially its ban on sleeveless shirts.
The literature professor mocked the prudish censors who once banned the novel.
Victorian society is often described as prudish, though historians say the reality was more complicated.
He worried she would think him prudish for blushing at the joke.
tc: Far from being ______, the novelist wrote frankly about desire and was unembarrassed by the scandal her books caused.
'Far from' signals the opposite of writing frankly and being unembarrassed, so the blank means easily shocked.
se: Critics called the film's censorship ______, arguing that adults could easily handle a brief love scene.

m: to resist or endure something without being damaged or giving way

weather

m: a person who is fanatical and uncompromising in pursuing their beliefs or ideals

fanatic
Both 'zealot' and 'fanatic' describe an uncompromising extremist, so the meaning is unchanged.

scrape
Both 'abrade' and 'scrape' mean to damage a surface by rubbing against it.

m: a general idea or concept not tied to any particular real example

concept
Both 'abstraction' and 'concept' describe something general and theoretical rather than concrete.

implore
Both 'adjure' and 'implore' mean to urge earnestly, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: praising someone excessively or in a fawning way

flattering
Both 'adulatory' and 'flattering' describe excessive praise, matching praise for even weak work.

m: happening by chance; not inherent, essential or planned

se: Scientists stressed that the link between the two events was ______ and not evidence of any real cause.
accidental
Both 'adventitious' and 'accidental' mean happening by chance rather than through a real cause.

m: to refer to or call attention to something in speech or writing (usually 'advert to')

Both 'advert to' and 'refer to' mean to mention or direct attention to something.

m: the scope, extent or range of something's authority or influence

purview
Both 'ambit' and 'purview' mean the range of authority, so the sentence means the same.

m: the quality of being friendly, pleasant and good-natured
x: The shopkeeper's amiability made us return to his small store again and again.

geniality
Both 'amiability' and 'geniality' mean friendly warmth that makes people comfortable.

m: harsh criticism or a critical, disapproving remark

criticism
Both 'animadversion' and 'criticism' mean harsh disapproval, matching 'called it dishonest'.

m: the act of taking control of a territory and adding it to one's own

m: a short, witty saying that expresses a general truth

maxim

x: His braggadocio about his fishing skills ended abruptly when he came home with nothing but a sunburn.
Behind the sales manager's braggadocio was a team that had missed its targets three quarters in a row.
At the seminar, a young scholar's braggadocio irritated professors who had spent decades on the same question.
Political rallies often reward braggadocio more than careful policy, and candidates know it.
I fell for his braggadocio on our first date, but by the third I found it exhausting.
tc: For all his ______ about being the best player in the club, he lost every match of the tournament without winning a single set.
'For all his... about being the best' set against his total failure shows the blank means empty boasting.
se: The boxer's pre-fight ______ fooled no one, since everyone knew he had barely trained.
bluster
Both 'braggadocio' and 'bluster' mean loud, empty boasting, which 'fooled no one' because he was unprepared.

m: great technical skill and brilliance, especially in an artistic performance
x: The young violinist played the final movement with such bravura that the audience leapt to its feet.
Her presentation to the board was a bravura performance, handling every hostile question with ease.
This novel opens with a bravura passage describing an entire city waking up in a single sentence.
Even critics who disliked the film admitted that its opening chase sequence was a piece of real bravura.
Watching my grandfather tell stories at weddings, all timing and bravura, made me want to become an actor.
tc: Rather than playing the difficult concerto cautiously, the pianist attacked it with dazzling ______, racing through the hardest passages flawlessly.
'Rather than... cautiously' and 'racing through... flawlessly' signal bold, brilliant technical skill.
se: The dancer's ______ in the final solo left even the hardened critics speechless.
virtuosity
Both 'bravura' and 'virtuosity' mean dazzling technical skill, the kind that would leave critics speechless.

m: a member of a gang of robbers who attack travelers, especially in mountains or forests
x: In the eighteenth century, travelers crossing the mountain pass hired armed guards to protect them from brigands.
An old ballad tells of a brigand who robbed rich merchants and shared the loot with poor villagers.
Our history professor described how brigands controlled the trade routes after the empire collapsed.
Reports of brigands attacking trucks on the remote highway have alarmed transport companies.
My little brother loved playing the brigand in our games, ambushing anyone who walked past the garden.
tc: Before setting out, the merchant was warned that a notorious ______ and his gang had been ambushing travelers on the forest road.
'His gang had been ambushing travelers' identifies the blank as a robber who preys on people on the road.
se: Legend has it that the cave was once the hideout of a fearsome ______ who terrorized the region.
bandit
Both 'brigand' and 'bandit' mean a violent robber, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: abundantly full of or thickly covered with something; usually followed by 'with'
x: The kitchen drawer was bristling with old receipts, rubber bands and keys nobody could identify.
My manager's reply was bristling with questions, which meant my proposal was far from approved.
Last week my thesis came back from my supervisor bristling with red ink and margin notes.
The border region, bristling with troops and checkpoints, felt more like a war zone than a holiday destination.
She walked into the meeting bristling with confidence after a long talk with her father the night before.
tc: Far from being sparsely defended, the fortress was ______ with cannons along every wall.
'Far from being sparsely defended' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean densely full.
se: The streets near the stadium were ______ with fans hours before the final began.
teeming
Both 'bristling with' and 'teeming with' mean crowded or full of, giving the same picture of packed streets.

m: a strongly worded, critical attack in speech or writing
x: After another monsoon flood, local columnists fired a broadside at the city council over its broken drainage system.
The CEO's email was a broadside against middle managers who had ignored the new safety rules.
In a famous broadside, a young economist accused the whole field of ignoring real-world data.
Opposition parties launched a fresh broadside against the government's handling of fuel prices.
After my sister's broadside about my messy room, I spent the whole weekend cleaning.
tc: Instead of the polite disagreement everyone expected, the senator delivered a blistering ______ against her own party's leadership.
'Instead of the polite disagreement' and 'blistering' show the blank means a fierce verbal attack.
se: The editorial was a scathing ______ against the new tax, calling it reckless and unfair.
diatribe
Both 'broadside' and 'diatribe' mean a bitter written attack, matching 'scathing' and 'reckless and unfair'.

m: a trite, unoriginal remark, often meant to soothe or placate
x: When I failed my driving test, my uncle offered the usual bromide that everything happens for a reason.
The manager's speech was full of bromides about teamwork, but nobody heard a word about pay rises.
Graduation speakers often fall back on bromides like 'follow your passion' instead of giving real advice.
Voters are tired of politicians who answer hard questions about inflation with comforting bromides.
I didn't need bromides from my friend after the breakup; I just needed her to listen.
tc: Hoping for practical advice, the grieving widow was instead offered the stale ______ that time heals all wounds.
'Stale' and the overused saying 'time heals all wounds' show the blank means a trite, soothing remark.
se: The coach's halftime talk was nothing but one tired ______ after another.
platitude
Both 'bromide' and 'platitude' mean an overused, empty remark, which fits 'tired'.

m: a comic imitation that mocks a serious subject by exaggerating it or treating it absurdly
x: Our school play turned into a burlesque of the principal's morning speeches, and even he laughed.
His imitation of the board meeting was a perfect burlesque of corporate jargon.
The professor argued that the poem is not a tribute to heroic epics but a burlesque of them.
A satirical show's burlesque of the election debates attracted millions of viewers online.
My brother's burlesque of my singing was so accurate that I felt hurt for a moment before laughing.
tc: Far from being a respectful adaptation, the production turned the original tragedy into broad ______, exaggerating every solemn moment until it became ridiculous.
'Far from being a respectful adaptation' and 'exaggerating... until it became ridiculous' define the blank as mocking imitation.
se: The comedy troupe's sketch was pure ______, mocking the pomposity of the royal court.
parody
Both 'burlesque' and 'parody' mean a mocking comic imitation, so the sentence means the same.

m: to stop someone and keep them in conversation, often when they would rather leave
x: Every time I go to the shop, the owner buttonholes me to complain about his neighbors.
At the conference, a nervous startup founder buttonholed investors in the corridor between sessions.
Students buttonholed the professor after class to ask whether the exam would include last week's material.
Lobbyists buttonholed lawmakers outside the chamber, hoping to change their votes at the last minute.
At my cousin's wedding, an aunt buttonholed me for twenty minutes about when I would finally get married.
tc: Hoping to slip out unnoticed, the minister was dismayed when a persistent journalist managed to ______ him at the door and refused to let him go.
'Refused to let him go' when he hoped to slip out shows the blank means to detain someone in conversation.
se: Whenever my neighbor sees me in the lift, he tries to ______ me about the building's parking problems.
corner
Both 'buttonhole' and 'corner' mean to trap someone into an unwanted conversation.

m: a hidden store of things, such as weapons, money or supplies
x: While renovating the old house, we found a cache of letters hidden under the floorboards.
Police discovered a cache of weapons in a warehouse on the edge of the city.
Our university archive contains a cache of unpublished manuscripts that scholars have only begun to study.
Squirrels bury caches of nuts in autumn and rely on memory to find them in winter.
My grandmother kept a secret cache of sweets in her cupboard, which she shared only with me.
tc: Hikers stumbled upon the smugglers' ______, a hollow tree stuffed with stolen jewelry and cash hidden from view.
The restatement 'a hollow tree stuffed with... hidden from view' defines the blank as a hidden store.
se: During the raid, soldiers uncovered a large ______ of ammunition buried beneath the farmhouse.
stockpile
Both 'cache' and 'stockpile' mean a stored supply, and 'buried' makes clear it was hidden.
