m: a generally accepted rule or standard, or the body of works regarded as authoritative
x: In my mother's kitchen, the first canon was simple: nobody eats until everyone is seated.
Our firm's canons of professional conduct forbid accepting gifts from clients.
This course introduces students to the Western literary canon as well as Bengali writers often left out of it.
Critics argued that the museum's collection reflected a narrow canon dominated by European painters.
He judged every relationship by his own canons of loyalty, which few friends could ever satisfy.
tc: The architect ignored every established ______ of classical design, yet her unconventional building won the top prize.
'Ignored every established' and 'unconventional' show she broke accepted rules, so the blank means a rule or standard.
se: Plagiarism violates the most basic ______ of academic honesty.
principle
Both 'canon' and 'principle' mean a fundamental rule, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: the killing of a large number of people, especially in battle or a disaster
x: Witnesses described scenes of carnage after the bus plunged off the bridge.
Our emergency team had trained for months, but nothing prepared them for the carnage at the factory collapse.
Historians still debate whether the generals could have avoided the carnage of the trench battles.
Aid agencies called for a ceasefire to stop the carnage in the besieged city.
Even years later, he could not talk to his children about the carnage he had witnessed in the war.
tc: The battlefield, once a quiet meadow, was strewn with bodies after a day of relentless ______.
'Strewn with bodies' tells us the blank means mass killing.
se: Reporters were barred from the town, but satellite images later revealed the full extent of the ______.
slaughter
Both 'carnage' and 'slaughter' mean large-scale killing, so the sentence means the same.

m: to complain or find fault continually, especially about trivial matters
x: My father carps about the electricity bill every month, even when it is lower than last time.
Instead of carping about the new software, why not ask the IT team for proper training?
Some reviewers carped about minor typos while ignoring the book's original argument.
Opposition politicians carped at the budget but offered no alternative plan of their own.
She grew tired of a partner who carped at everything from her cooking to her choice of friends.
tc: Although the hotel was spotless and the staff attentive, one guest continued to ______ about the color of the towels.
'Although... spotless and attentive' signals contrast, so the blank means to complain about something trivial.
se: Critics will always find something to ______ about, no matter how good the film is.
quibble
Both 'carp' and 'quibble' mean to raise petty objections, so the sentence means the same.

m: clever but misleading reasoning, especially used to justify questionable moral behavior
x: Only through elaborate casuistry could he convince himself that borrowing from the office cash box wasn't stealing.
The company's lawyers used legal casuistry to argue that the pollution was technically not their responsibility.
Our ethics professor warned us that casuistry can make almost any action seem acceptable.
Commentators dismissed the minister's defense of the contract as pure casuistry.
I recognized my own casuistry when I told myself that skipping my sister's birthday was for her own good.
tc: His argument seemed logical at first, but closer inspection revealed it to be mere ______, designed to excuse conduct that was plainly dishonest.
'Seemed logical at first' but was 'designed to excuse' dishonesty defines the blank as deceptive moral reasoning.
se: The defense rested on ______ so slippery that even the judge struggled to follow it.
sophistry
Both 'casuistry' and 'sophistry' mean clever but misleading argument, which fits 'slippery'.

m: the release of strong or pent-up emotions, bringing a sense of relief
x: After a stressful week, a long cry during a sad film can provide unexpected catharsis.
For many employees, the farewell party for the unpopular boss was a kind of catharsis.
Aristotle believed that tragedy offers the audience catharsis through pity and fear.
Winning the final brought a moment of collective catharsis to a country exhausted by crisis.
Writing a long letter to her late father gave her the catharsis she had needed for years.
tc: Having kept his grief hidden for months, he finally experienced a powerful ______ when he broke down and wept at the memorial.
Grief 'kept hidden for months' that finally pours out in weeping points to an emotional release.
se: For the survivors, testifying in court provided a long-awaited emotional ______.
release
Both 'catharsis' and 'emotional release' mean letting out pent-up feelings, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: very formal and polite; marked by elaborate ritual or etiquette
x: Our landlord greets us with a ceremonious bow every time he comes to collect the rent.
A ceremonious handover of the project files felt absurd for a team of only four people.
Visiting scholars were surprised by how ceremonious the university's graduation dinner turned out to be.
The two leaders exchanged ceremonious greetings before the tense talks began.
After the fight, my brother and I were ceremonious with each other for days, saying please and thank you like strangers.
tc: Unlike his casual younger colleagues, the old ambassador remained ______ in all things, rising and bowing whenever a guest entered the room.
'Unlike his casual younger colleagues' and 'rising and bowing' show the blank means very formal.
se: The butler's ______ manner made the young visitors feel slightly awkward.
formal
Both 'ceremonious' and 'formal' describe stiff, correct behavior that could make casual guests uneasy.

m: a person who changes their opinions or behavior to suit the situation
x: At family gatherings he is a chameleon, agreeing with whoever happens to be speaking.
A good salesperson is something of a chameleon, adjusting her style to every customer.
Our professor called the poet a literary chameleon who reinvented his voice in every collection.
Voters see the party's leader as a political chameleon, shifting positions whenever the polls move.
I realized my friend was a chameleon when I saw her mock the same people she had flattered the day before.
tc: Consistent in nothing, the senator was the consummate ______, adopting the views of whichever group he happened to be addressing.
'Consistent in nothing' and 'adopting the views of whichever group' define the blank as someone who changes to suit his audience.
se: Voters soon learned that the mayor was a shameless ______ who would switch sides whenever it suited his career.
opportunist
Both 'chameleon' and 'opportunist' describe someone who changes positions for personal advantage.

m: marked by alternating success and failure, often including some discreditable episodes
x: Our old car has a checkered history, breaking down on every family trip but somehow always getting us home.
Despite his checkered career, the new manager won the team's trust within weeks.
This university has a checkered record on free speech, defending some students while silencing others.
The bank's checkered past, including two fraud scandals, made regulators wary of its latest merger.
Her checkered relationship with her stepfather improved once she moved out and they began writing to each other.
tc: The candidate's ______ past, which included two bankruptcies and a brief stint in jail, worried the investors.
'Two bankruptcies and a brief stint in jail' show the blank means marked by failures and discredit.
se: The hospital has a somewhat ______ record on patient safety, with excellent years followed by serious lapses.
uneven
Both 'checkered' and 'uneven' describe a record that mixes good periods with bad ones.

m: a rude, ill-mannered, or mean-spirited person
x: Only a churl would refuse to say thank you when someone holds the door open.
Our new supervisor turned out to be a churl who never greeted anyone in the morning.
At the seminar, one churl kept interrupting the speaker to point out irrelevant mistakes.
It would take a churl to criticize volunteers who spent the night pumping water out of flooded homes.
I felt like a churl for refusing my grandmother's third helping of rice.
tc: Everyone else thanked the hosts warmly, but one ______ complained loudly about the food and left without saying goodbye.
The contrast with guests who 'thanked the hosts warmly' and the rude behavior that follows show the blank means an ill-mannered person.
se: It would take a real ______ to mock a child's first attempt at singing in public.
boor
Both 'churl' and 'boor' mean a rude, insensitive person, so the sentence means the same.

m: using more words than necessary; expressing ideas in a roundabout, indirect way
x: His circumlocutory explanation of why he was late only made his mother more suspicious.
That memo was so circumlocutory that nobody could tell whether the meeting had been cancelled.
Reviewers criticized the thesis for its circumlocutory style and asked for a shorter, clearer version.
Official statements are often deliberately circumlocutory, avoiding any clear admission of blame.
Rather than giving a circumlocutory answer, she simply told him she was not ready to get married.
tc: Instead of answering the simple question directly, the spokesperson gave a reply so ______ that it wandered for ten minutes without reaching a point.
'Instead of answering... directly' and 'wandered... without reaching a point' define the blank as roundabout and wordy.
se: The lawyer's ______ phrasing made a simple contract almost impossible to understand.
roundabout
Both 'circumlocutory' and 'roundabout' describe indirect, wordy expression that obscures meaning.

m: to climb or move awkwardly using both hands and feet
x: During rush hour in Dhaka, commuters clamber onto the roofs of overcrowded buses and trains.
The technician clambered into the cramped ceiling space to fix the office Wi-Fi router.
Our geology team had to clamber down a steep ravine to collect samples from the stream.
Rescue workers clambered through the rubble of the collapsed building, searching for survivors.
My daughter clambered into my lap and fell asleep halfway through the story.
tc: Lacking ropes or proper boots, the hikers had to ______ up the steep, crumbling slope on their hands and knees.
'On their hands and knees' up a 'crumbling slope' shows the blank means to climb awkwardly.
se: The toddler tried to ______ over the arm of the sofa to reach the biscuits.
scramble
Both 'clamber' and 'scramble' mean to climb clumsily using hands and feet.

m: sheltered or secluded from the outside world and its realities
x: After a cloistered childhood in a small village, she found the noise of the city overwhelming.
Executives in their cloistered offices often have little idea what customers actually want.
Critics argue that some economists live cloistered academic lives far removed from real markets.
A new report criticized the cloistered world of the judiciary, where few judges come from poorer backgrounds.
He felt safe in their cloistered little marriage, but she longed to travel and meet new people.
tc: Having spent decades in ______ research labs, the scientist was startled by the rough-and-tumble of public debate.
Being 'startled by the rough-and-tumble of public debate' implies she had been shut away from the outside world.
se: Raised in a ______ household with no television, the boy knew little about popular culture.
sheltered
Both 'cloistered' and 'sheltered' mean protected from the wider world, explaining his ignorance of popular culture.

m: of the same age, date or period; existing at the same time
x: My grandmother's sewing machine is coeval with the house itself; both arrived in 1962.
The two companies are roughly coeval, but one has grown far faster than the other.
Archaeologists believe the pottery fragments are coeval with the temple's foundations.
Researchers found that the rise of literacy was coeval with the spread of cheap printed newspapers.
Being almost exactly coeval, the two cousins shared every childhood milestone, from first teeth to first exams.
tc: Radiocarbon dating showed that the wooden boat was ______ with the nearby settlement, both dating to around 800 BC.
'Both dating to around 800 BC' restates the blank as being of the same age.
se: The poet was ______ with several famous painters of the period, though they never met.
contemporary
Both 'coeval with' and 'contemporary with' mean living at the same time, so the sentence means the same.

m: a strongbox for valuables; in the plural, the funds or treasury of an organization
x: The museum displays a carved wooden coffer that once held a merchant's gold coins.
This new contract will bring millions of dollars into the company's coffers.
Rising tuition fees have filled the university's coffers while students sink deeper into debt.
Every year, tax revenues from the garment industry swell the national coffers.
My grandmother kept her wedding jewelry in a small brass coffer beside her bed.
tc: Thieves forced open the merchant's ______ and made off with every gold coin it held.
Something 'forced open' that held 'every gold coin' must be a box for valuables.
se: The family's deeds and jewels were locked in an iron ______ under the stairs.
strongbox
Both 'coffer' and 'strongbox' mean a secure box for valuables, so the sentence means the same.

m: related by origin, especially of words or languages descended from the same ancestor
x: English 'mother' and Bengali 'mata' are cognate words, both descended from an ancient Indo-European root.
Spanish and Italian are cognate languages, so learning one makes the other much easier.
Our firm hires engineers as well as graduates from cognate disciplines such as physics and mathematics.
Scientists found that the two viruses are cognate, sharing a common ancestor from decades ago.
Learning German was easier for me than I expected, because so many of its words are cognate with English ones.
tc: Although they look very different today, the two words are ______, both deriving from the same Latin root.
'Both deriving from the same Latin root' restates the blank as related by origin.
se: Economics and political science are ______ disciplines, and many students take courses in both.
related
Both 'cognate' and 'related' mean connected by shared origins or subject matter.

m: the gathering together and comparison of information, texts or data in order to organize them
x: The collation of everyone's holiday photos into a single album took my mother an entire weekend.
My first job involved the collation of sales figures from twelve regional offices.
That scholar spent years on the collation of the surviving manuscripts to produce a reliable edition.
Careful collation of data from hundreds of weather stations allowed scientists to map the cyclone's path.
Writing my grandfather's biography began with the collation of letters he had sent from abroad.
tc: Before the report could be written, someone had to undertake the tedious ______ of hundreds of survey responses, sorting and comparing them line by line.
'Sorting and comparing them line by line' defines the blank as gathering and comparing information.
se: The ______ of evidence from different witnesses revealed several contradictions.
comparison
Both 'collation' and 'comparison' mean examining sources side by side, which is how contradictions are revealed.

m: courtesy and considerate behavior toward others, especially mutual respect between groups or nations
x: In our apartment building, a spirit of comity means neighbors share umbrellas and parking spaces without complaint.
The merger succeeded partly because of the comity between the two firms' senior partners.
Academic comity requires scholars to acknowledge rivals' work even when they disagree with it.
This treaty was meant to restore comity between the two nations after years of border disputes.
Their old friendship had cooled, but a certain comity survived, and they still exchanged greetings at Eid.
tc: After decades of bitter rivalry, the two parties finally entered a new era of ______, cooperating politely on issues they once fought over.
'After decades of bitter rivalry' and 'cooperating politely' signal a change to mutual courtesy.
se: Diplomats worked hard to preserve the ______ between the two countries during the trade dispute.
goodwill
Both 'comity' and 'goodwill' mean friendly, respectful relations, which diplomats try to protect.

m: to mix or blend together
x: In the old market, the smells of fried fish and ripe mangoes commingle in the humid air.
Accountants warn small business owners never to commingle personal and company funds.
A new exhibition at the museum commingles ancient artifacts with contemporary art.
Along the coast, rising seas let salt water commingle with fresh water, threatening rice farms.
At the farewell party, joy and sadness commingled as we said goodbye to our oldest friend.
tc: Rather than keeping the two collections separate, the curator chose to ______ them, placing old and new works side by side.
'Rather than keeping... separate' signals the opposite, so the blank means to mix together.
se: In her novel, history and fantasy ______ so smoothly that readers cannot tell where one ends and the other begins.
blend
Both 'commingle' and 'blend' mean to mix seamlessly, so the sentence means the same.

m: the reduction of a legal penalty or sentence to a less severe one
x: After years of appeals, the prisoner's family celebrated the commutation of his death sentence to life imprisonment.
Our law firm's pro bono team spent months preparing a petition for commutation.
Students in the criminal law class debated whether commutation undermines the authority of the courts.
Yesterday the governor announced the commutation of sentences for dozens of elderly inmates.
When my father heard about the commutation, he wept with relief for his old friend.
tc: The president's ______ of the sentence meant that, instead of being executed, the prisoner would serve thirty years in jail.
'Instead of being executed... would serve thirty years' shows the penalty was reduced.
se: The ______ of her prison term allowed her to return home three years early.
reduction
Both 'commutation' and 'reduction' mean shortening the sentence, which is why she came home early.

m: a series of interconnected things or events linked together like a chain
x: A concatenation of small disasters, from a missed alarm to a flat tire, made me miss my cousin's wedding.
Our project failed through a concatenation of delays, each one triggering the next.
In programming, string concatenation simply means joining pieces of text end to end.
Investigators said the bridge collapse resulted from a concatenation of failures by regulators, engineers and builders.
Our friendship began through an unlikely concatenation of events: a lost umbrella, a shared rickshaw and a wrong turn.
tc: The accident was not caused by any single error but by a whole ______ of linked failures, each making the next one more likely.
'Not... any single error' and 'linked failures, each making the next one more likely' define the blank as a chain of events.
se: The detective pieced together the ______ of events that led to the robbery.
chain
Both 'concatenation' and 'chain' mean a linked series of events, so the sentence means the same.

m: strong sexual desire; lust
x: Medieval preachers warned their congregations against gluttony, greed and concupiscence.
In the novel, the villain hides his concupiscence behind a respectable career as a bank manager.
Augustine wrote at length about concupiscence as a source of humanity's moral struggle.
Critics complained that the advertising campaign appealed more to concupiscence than to common sense.
In the poem, the young lover's concupiscence slowly gives way to genuine tenderness.
tc: The monks took vows of chastity, struggling daily to suppress any trace of ______.
'Vows of chastity' and 'suppress' indicate the blank means sexual desire.
se: The preacher thundered against the ______ he saw in the town's dance halls.
lust
Both 'concupiscence' and 'lust' mean strong sexual desire, the target of the preacher's anger.

m: to talk together informally; to chat
x: My aunts confabulate in the kitchen for hours after every family dinner.
During coffee breaks, the engineers confabulate about football rather than the project deadline.
Graduate students gathered in the corridor to confabulate about the new department head.
Delegates confabulated in small groups in the hotel lobby before the final vote.
On summer evenings, my grandparents would sit on the veranda and confabulate about old times.
tc: The meeting was supposed to be formal, but the old friends could not resist the urge to ______ casually about their families before getting down to business.
'Supposed to be formal, but' and 'casually' signal the blank means to chat informally.
se: The neighbors liked to ______ over the fence every evening.
chat
Both 'confabulate' and 'chat' mean to talk informally, so the sentence means the same.

m: the act of formally granting a title, degree, honor or right
x: Heavy rain forced the school to postpone the conferral of medals at sports day.
The board approved the conferral of partner status on three senior associates.
Degree conferral will take place at the university's convocation ceremony in December.
Parliament fiercely debated the conferral of citizenship on long-term refugees.
My mother cried during the conferral of my brother's doctorate, which she had dreamed of for years.
tc: The university postponed the ______ of the honorary degree after protesters revealed the recipient's links to corruption.
An honorary degree is formally granted by a university, so the blank means the act of granting it.
se: The ______ of knighthood was the proudest moment of the old actor's life.
bestowal
Both 'conferral' and 'bestowal' mean the formal granting of an honor.

m: trusting; willing to share private thoughts and secrets with others
x: In a confiding tone, the shopkeeper told me he was planning to close the business.
My colleague is so confiding that I now know more about her marriage than I want to.
Our professor's confiding manner encouraged even shy students to speak about their struggles.
In a rare confiding interview, the retired general admitted serious doubts about the war.
Children are naturally confiding, so they need to learn which adults deserve their trust.
tc: Unlike her guarded and secretive brother, she was so ______ that she told strangers her life story within minutes.
'Unlike her guarded and secretive brother' signals the opposite, so the blank means trusting and open.
se: The old man's ______ nature made him an easy target for swindlers.
trusting
Both 'confiding' and 'trusting' describe someone who readily trusts others, which makes him easy to cheat.

m: in agreement or harmony; consistent with something
x: His actions are rarely congruent with his promises, so I've stopped trusting his plans for the weekend.
Make sure your CV is congruent with what you say in the interview.
Results from the second experiment were congruent with the original hypothesis.
Critics said the new policy was not congruent with the government's stated commitment to the environment.
We broke up because our goals were simply not congruent: she wanted to travel, and I wanted to settle down.
tc: The witness's story was entirely ______ with the physical evidence, so detectives saw no reason to doubt it.
'Saw no reason to doubt it' shows the story matched the evidence, so the blank means consistent.
se: The company's marketing message is not ______ with its actual treatment of workers.
consistent
Both 'congruent with' and 'consistent with' mean in agreement with, so the sentence means the same.

m: to join or combine two or more things
x: The two villages slowly conjoined as new houses filled the fields between them.
Our team tried to conjoin the marketing and sales databases into one system.
This course conjoins history and economics to explain why empires rise and fall.
Under the new constitution, the two provinces were conjoined under a single administration.
Their lives were conjoined by marriage, but their temperaments remained completely different.
tc: Rather than keeping the two departments apart, the new director decided to ______ them under one manager.
'Rather than keeping... apart' signals the opposite, so the blank means to join together.
se: The architect planned to ______ the old library and the new science building with a glass walkway.
join
Both 'conjoin' and 'join' mean to connect, so the sentence means the same.

m: relating to marriage or the relationship between husband and wife
x: After forty years of conjugal life, my grandparents still argue about how to cook rice.
Under the company's new policy, conjugal partners are covered by the staff health insurance plan.
Anthropologists study how conjugal customs differ across cultures and generations.
Last year the court ruled that prisoners have a limited right to conjugal visits.
Their conjugal happiness was tested when he lost his job and they moved in with his parents.
tc: Unlike the single men in the barracks, the soldier enjoyed ______ life with his wife in a small house near the base.
'Unlike the single men' and 'with his wife' show the blank means relating to marriage.
se: The novel explores the strains of ______ life in a crowded joint family.
marital
Both 'conjugal' and 'marital' mean relating to marriage, so the sentence means the same.

m: in agreement or harmony; consistent, usually followed by 'with'
x: Buying an expensive car would not be consonant with my plan to save for a flat.
The new hiring policy is consonant with the firm's commitment to diversity.
Her findings are consonant with earlier studies on sleep and memory.
Journalists asked whether the minister's lavish lifestyle was consonant with his speeches about austerity.
He chose a career consonant with his values, even though it paid far less than banking.
tc: The CEO claimed to value transparency, yet her secretive decisions were hardly ______ with that ideal.
'Claimed to value transparency, yet... secretive' shows a mismatch, so the blank means in agreement.
se: Her decision to quit was ______ with everything she had said about wanting more freedom.
consistent
Both 'consonant with' and 'consistent with' mean in agreement with, so the sentence means the same.

m: self-restraint, especially in controlling one's desires or appetites
x: With remarkable continence, he ate only one sweet from the box his aunt had sent.
Her continence at the office party, where she drank only water, impressed her new boss.
Ancient philosophers praised continence as the virtue that keeps passion under the control of reason.
This religious order demands strict continence from all its members.
His continence in the face of her insults surprised everyone who knew his temper.
tc: Far from indulging his appetites, the monk was known for his strict ______, eating little and refusing all luxuries.
'Far from indulging his appetites' signals the opposite, so the blank means self-restraint.
se: The athlete's ______ during months of training, avoiding sweets and late nights, paid off in the final.
temperance
Both 'continence' and 'temperance' mean disciplined restraint of one's appetites.

m: insolent, scornful language or treatment; humiliating insult
x: The waiter endured the drunken customer's contumely with remarkable patience.
No employee should have to put up with the contumely of a manager who shouts insults at meetings.
Her theory was met with contumely by senior professors, who later had to admit she was right.
Refugees often face the contumely of officials who treat them as criminals.
After years of her mother-in-law's contumely, she finally moved her family into a separate flat.
tc: Instead of the respect he had earned, the veteran received only ______ from the young officers, who mocked his age and old-fashioned methods.
'Instead of the respect' and 'mocked' show the blank means scornful, insulting treatment.
se: She bore the critics' ______ with quiet dignity and kept writing.
scorn
Both 'contumely' and 'scorn' mean contemptuous treatment, which she endured with dignity.

m: a natural consequence or result that follows directly from something else
x: One corollary of moving to a bigger flat is a much higher electricity bill.
A corollary of the new remote-work policy was that the office cafeteria lost most of its customers.
In geometry class we learned the theorem first and then worked through its corollaries.
Rising sea levels bring an inevitable corollary: more frequent flooding in low-lying coastal cities.
For him, the natural corollary of falling in love was asking her parents for permission to marry.
tc: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive, and a predictable ______ is that fewer families buy new homes.
Fewer home purchases follow directly from costlier borrowing, so the blank means a resulting consequence.
se: Unemployment is often the unhappy ______ of rapid automation in factories.
consequence
Both 'corollary' and 'consequence' mean a result that follows from something, so the sentence means the same.

m: to cancel or reverse an order, especially by issuing a contrary one
x: My mother told us we could stay up late, but my father quickly countermanded her decision.
The regional manager countermanded the store's discount offer only hours after it was announced.
Our dean countermanded the professor's decision to cancel the final exam.
The general countermanded the order to advance after receiving news of enemy reinforcements.
It hurt my pride when my older sister countermanded my instructions to the children in front of everyone.
tc: The captain had ordered the crew to abandon ship, but the admiral arrived just in time to ______ that command and keep them at their posts.
The admiral keeps the crew at their posts, reversing the captain's order, so the blank means to cancel an order.
se: The head office can ______ any order issued by a branch manager.
rescind
Both 'countermand' and 'rescind' mean to cancel an order, so the sentence means the same.

m: having an excessive desire to possess something, especially something belonging to someone else
x: Every morning he cast a covetous eye at his neighbor's new motorbike.
Some colleagues were covetous of her corner office and its view of the river.
Our professor warned that covetous rival labs might try to steal the team's unpublished data.
Covetous developers have long had their eyes on the city's last remaining wetlands.
Her sister's covetous glances at her wedding jewelry made the whole family uncomfortable.
tc: Content with his modest belongings, the old man never felt ______ of the luxuries his wealthy neighbors enjoyed.
'Content with his modest belongings' explains why he 'never felt' the blank, which must mean eager to possess others' things.
se: The children cast ______ looks at the cake long before it was time to cut it.
greedy
Both 'covetous' and 'greedy' describe eager desire for something, so the sentence means the same.

m: (of handwriting or writing) cramped and difficult to read or understand
x: I could barely read the crabbed note my landlord had pushed under the door.
Our accountant's crabbed handwriting on the invoices caused endless errors.
Historians spent months deciphering the crabbed manuscripts of a medieval monk.
The treaty's crabbed legal language left both governments arguing over what it actually meant.
My father's crabbed letters from abroad, full of tiny cramped lines, are among my most precious possessions.
tc: Unlike his secretary's neat, legible notes, the doctor's prescriptions were so ______ that no pharmacist could read them.
'Unlike... neat, legible notes' and 'no pharmacist could read them' show the blank means hard to read.
se: The old diary, written in faded and ______ script, took the historian weeks to transcribe.
illegible
Both 'crabbed' and 'illegible' describe writing that is hard to read, explaining the weeks of work.

m: a gradual, steady increase in loudness or intensity, or the peak of such an increase
x: The rain on the tin roof rose to a crescendo, and we could barely hear each other.
Complaints about the new parking rules reached a crescendo at Friday's staff meeting.
Our orchestra practiced building a long crescendo before the final crash of cymbals.
Calls for the minister's resignation grew to a crescendo after the leaked emails were published.
Her anxiety rose to a crescendo as she waited for the university admission results.
tc: The protest began with a few quiet voices but grew steadily louder until it reached a deafening ______ outside parliament.
'Began with a few quiet voices' and 'grew steadily louder' describe a gradual rise to a peak.
se: Applause built to a ______ as the champion lifted the trophy.
climax
Both 'crescendo' and 'climax' mean the peak of rising intensity, so the sentence means the same.

m: the unfair practice of giving jobs or favors to friends and associates
x: Residents accused the building committee of cronyism after it hired the chairman's cousin as caretaker.
Staff morale collapsed when promotions seemed to depend on cronyism rather than performance.
A recent study found that cronyism in university hiring discouraged talented young researchers from applying.
Anti-corruption activists say cronyism has turned public contracts into rewards for political loyalty.
I refused to recommend my best friend for the job because I didn't want anyone to suspect cronyism.
tc: Instead of hiring the most qualified candidates, the mayor filled every post with old golfing partners, a blatant act of ______.
Filling posts with friends 'instead of the most qualified candidates' defines the blank as favoritism toward friends.
se: The scandal exposed widespread ______ in the awarding of government contracts.
favoritism
Both 'cronyism' and 'favoritism' mean unfairly favoring friends, so the sentence means the same.

m: wicked and cruel, typically in a cowardly or underhanded way
x: Some dastardly prankster let the air out of every tire on our street last night.
Leaking a colleague's private messages to get her fired was a dastardly thing to do.
In the old adventure novels we read at school, the villain always has a dastardly plan.
Police condemned the dastardly attack on unarmed villagers as they slept.
I never forgave him for his dastardly betrayal of my sister's trust.
tc: Rather than facing his rival openly, the villain hatched the most ______ scheme imaginable: poisoning him in secret.
'Rather than facing his rival openly' and 'poisoning him in secret' show the blank means cowardly and wicked.
se: Setting fire to the school while the children slept was a truly ______ act.
despicable
Both 'dastardly' and 'despicable' mean shockingly wicked, so the sentence means the same.

m: a person who wastes time or moves slowly and idly
x: My younger son is a hopeless dawdler, so we leave for school ten minutes early.
The manager warned that dawdlers on the new project would be moved to other teams.
Teachers had to round up the dawdlers who were still chatting in the corridor after the bell.
City officials plan new signs asking dawdlers on busy metro escalators to stand to one side.
I'm a confessed dawdler on Sunday mornings, and my wife has learned not to plan anything before noon.
tc: While her brisk classmates finished the test in an hour, Ayesha, a habitual ______, was still on the second question when time ran out.
The contrast with 'brisk classmates' and being 'still on the second question' show the blank means a slow, time-wasting person.
se: The tour guide had no patience for any ______ who lingered in the gift shop after the bus was ready to leave.
straggler
Both 'dawdler' and 'straggler' mean someone who lags behind the group, so the sentence means the same.

m: to set or mark the boundaries or limits of something
x: We used flowerpots to demarcate our small balcony garden from the neighbor's side.
The contract clearly demarcates the responsibilities of the client and the contractor.
In her thesis, she carefully demarcates the scope of her study before presenting her data.
A joint commission was set up to demarcate the disputed river border between the two countries.
Early in our marriage, we demarcated our work time and family time to avoid arguments.
tc: To prevent further disputes between the farmers, surveyors were brought in to ______ exactly where one field ended and the next began.
'Exactly where one field ended and the next began' defines the blank as marking boundaries.
se: Before the match, groundstaff painted white lines to ______ the playing area.
delimit
Both 'demarcate' and 'delimit' mean to mark out the limits of an area, so the sentence means the same.

m: relating to ordinary people or their everyday, informal language
x: Rickshaw art in Dhaka is a vivid demotic tradition, painted for ordinary people rather than for galleries.
The ad agency wanted a demotic slogan that would sound natural in everyday conversation.
This poet deliberately wrote in a demotic style, using the speech of farmers and factory workers.
Populist leaders often adopt demotic language to present themselves as ordinary people.
My grandfather's letters were formal, but his conversation was warm, funny and wonderfully demotic.
tc: Rejecting the elevated diction of earlier poets, she wrote in the ______ idiom of street conversations.
'Rejecting the elevated diction' and 'street conversations' show the blank means the language of ordinary people.
se: The novel's dialogue is refreshingly ______, capturing how teenagers really talk.
colloquial
Both 'demotic' and 'colloquial' mean informal, everyday speech, matching 'how teenagers really talk'.

m: a formal statement given under oath outside court, later used as evidence
x: My neighbour had to take a day off work to give a deposition about the car accident she witnessed.
Lawyers for both sides spent three hours taking the accountant's deposition before the trial began.
In her law school seminar, students practised drafting questions for a mock deposition.
According to court documents, the former manager stated in a sworn deposition that he had warned the company about the defect.
Reading his brother's deposition, which contradicted everything he had said at home, left Karim feeling betrayed.
tc: Because the witness was too ill to attend the trial, her ______, recorded under oath a month earlier, was read aloud to the jury.
'Recorded under oath' and being read in place of live evidence point to a sworn out-of-court statement.
se: The judge allowed the jury to hear the doctor's ______, which had been given under oath before the trial.
testimony
Both 'deposition' and 'testimony' refer to sworn evidence given by a witness, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: an act of attacking, plundering or destroying, often repeated over time
x: Farmers near the forest put up electric fences to protect their crops from the depredations of wild elephants.
No biscuit tin in our office survives the depredations of the sales team for more than a day.
The historian's lecture described the depredations of Viking raiders along the coasts of England and Ireland.
Environmental groups warn that illegal logging and mining are causing serious depredation in the country's last rainforests.
After years of watching her brother's depredations on the family business, she finally refused to lend him another taka.
tc: Centuries of ______ by raiders who looted temples and burned crops had left the region impoverished.
'Raiders who looted temples and burned crops' defines the blank as plundering and destruction.
se: Years of ______ by invading armies had stripped the province of its wealth.
pillage
Both 'depredation' and 'pillage' mean violent plundering, and both explain how the province lost its wealth.

m: to uproot, especially to remove people from their native land or culture
x: The war deracinated thousands of families, scattering them across refugee camps in three countries.
Moving to a new city for work every two years left him feeling deracinated and lonely.
Her dissertation examines how colonial schooling deracinated young people from their own languages and traditions.
Critics argue that the dam project will deracinate entire villages that have farmed the riverbanks for centuries.
Leaving Sylhet for a cold flat in London, my grandfather felt deracinated, cut off from everything familiar.
tc: Officials feared the new highway would ______ communities that had lived in the valley for centuries, scattering them far from their ancestral land.
'Scattering them far from their ancestral land' restates the idea of uprooting people.
se: The policy aimed to ______ nomadic tribes from their traditional lands and settle them in towns.
uproot
Both 'deracinate' and 'uproot' mean to tear people away from their home ground, giving the same meaning.

m: a state of disuse; no longer being used or practised
x: After the microwave arrived, my grandmother's old clay oven fell into desuetude in the corner of the kitchen.
Our company's suggestion box has fallen into such desuetude that nobody remembers who holds the key.
Legal scholars still debate whether laws that have lapsed into desuetude can be enforced.
Many minority languages are slipping into desuetude as younger speakers switch to more widely used tongues.
Their friendship, once so close, had drifted into desuetude after she moved abroad.
tc: Once a lively hub, the old railway station has sat in ______ for decades, its platforms cracked and its ticket windows boarded up.
'Cracked' platforms and 'boarded up' windows show the station is no longer used.
se: Having been replaced by email, the office fax machine slowly fell into ______.
disuse
Both 'desuetude' and 'disuse' describe the state of no longer being used.

m: to transfer power, duties or responsibility to a lower level or another person
x: When my father fell ill, the job of running the household devolved on my elder sister.
Our new manager plans to devolve more decision-making to individual team leaders.
The university decided to devolve control of the research budget to each faculty.
A new law will devolve powers over health and education from the central government to local councils.
After their mother's death, the care of their younger brother devolved upon the two of them, and it brought them closer.
tc: Rather than keeping every decision in the head office, the company chose to ______ authority to its regional branches.
'Rather than keeping every decision in the head office' signals the opposite: handing authority down.
se: The president promised to ______ power to the provinces so that they could manage their own schools.
transfer
Both 'devolve' and 'transfer' mean passing power from the centre to the provinces.

m: demanding total obedience; domineering and unwilling to consider others' views
x: My uncle's dictatorial way of choosing restaurants means we always end up eating at the same place.
Staff complained that the new director's dictatorial style left no room for discussion in meetings.
Our thesis supervisor was helpful but rather dictatorial about formatting, rejecting any chapter with a single misplaced comma.
Opposition parties accused the government of seizing dictatorial powers under the emergency law.
She ended the relationship because his dictatorial attitude made her feel like an employee rather than a partner.
tc: Far from inviting input, the coach was so ______ that players were punished merely for questioning his tactics.
'Far from inviting input' and punishing questions show a leader who demands total obedience.
se: Employees resented the manager's ______ approach, in which every decision came from him alone.
autocratic
Both 'dictatorial' and 'autocratic' describe someone who rules alone without consulting others.

m: strong disapproval, especially on moral grounds
x: My aunt's raised eyebrow showed her disapprobation when I arrived at the wedding in jeans.
The proposal to shorten lunch breaks met with loud disapprobation from the entire staff.
Despite the committee's disapprobation, the young researcher published her controversial findings.
Plans to build a casino next to the old mosque drew widespread public disapprobation.
He could bear any criticism except the silent disapprobation of his own father.
tc: Expecting applause, the comedian was startled by the ______ of an audience that booed and walked out.
'Expecting applause' contrasts with booing and walking out, so the blank means strong disapproval.
se: The senator's remarks drew sharp ______ from members of his own party.
disapproval
Both 'disapprobation' and 'disapproval' mean the party members strongly objected to his remarks.

m: to cause someone trouble or inconvenience
x: I hope it won't discommode you if I leave my bicycle in your hallway overnight.
The fire drill was scheduled for early morning so as not to discommode customers.
Students were badly discommoded when the library closed for renovations during exam week.
Residents complained that the roadworks had discommoded thousands of commuters for months.
She never wanted to discommode her friends, so she rarely asked anyone for help.
tc: The hotel staff went out of their way not to ______ the guests, carrying out repairs only while the rooms were empty.
Doing repairs only in empty rooms shows the staff were trying not to inconvenience guests.
se: We are sorry to ______ you, but the lift will be out of service until Friday.
inconvenience
Both 'discommode' and 'inconvenience' mean to cause someone trouble, so the apology means the same.

m: deeply unhappy and impossible to comfort
x: After losing his favourite toy on the bus, my little nephew sat disconsolate by the window all evening.
Tom was disconsolate after missing the promotion and barely spoke to anyone at the office for a week.
A few disconsolate students lingered outside the exam hall, convinced they had failed.
Disconsolate fans filed out of the stadium after Bangladesh lost the final by just two runs.
She was disconsolate for months after the breakup, refusing every invitation from her friends.
tc: Although his friends tried every joke they knew, the grieving man remained ______, staring silently at the floor.
'Although' his friends tried to cheer him, he 'remained' sad, so the blank means unable to be comforted.
se: The ______ child sat on the steps, weeping because her kitten had run away.
dejected
Both 'disconsolate' and 'dejected' describe a deeply unhappy child, giving the same meaning.

m: to deprive someone of a right, especially the right to vote
x: Moving house just before the election nearly disenfranchised me, because my name was still registered at the old address.
Workers on short-term contracts feel disenfranchised, since they have no say in company decisions.
Her political science thesis studies how literacy tests were once used to disenfranchise poor voters.
Critics warn that strict new ID requirements could disenfranchise millions of elderly and low-income citizens.
Growing up as the youngest of six, he often felt disenfranchised at family meetings where his opinion was ignored.
tc: The new rule would ______ citizens living abroad by removing their names from the voting rolls.
'Removing their names from the voting rolls' explains that citizens would lose the right to vote.
se: Activists argued that closing rural polling stations would ______ thousands of farmers who could not travel to town.
disfranchise
Both 'disenfranchise' and 'disfranchise' mean to take away people's ability to vote.

m: to pour out or release contents; to give up something, especially unwillingly
x: Every morning, crowded buses disgorge thousands of commuters at the busy Farmgate junction in Dhaka.
The office printer jammed and then suddenly disgorged forty copies of the same report.
Our geology class watched footage of a volcano disgorging rivers of molten lava.
A court ordered the bank to disgorge the profits it had made by misleading its customers.
Once she began to talk, she disgorged years of pent-up anger at her parents.
tc: When the doors finally opened, the packed train began to ______ its passengers onto the platform in a great rush.
A 'packed' train releasing people 'in a great rush' shows the blank means to pour out.
se: The judge ordered the fraudster to ______ every dollar he had taken from his victims.
surrender
Both 'disgorge' and 'surrender' mean to hand over ill-gotten money unwillingly.

m: official permission to be excused from a rule or usual requirement
x: Because of her broken leg, my sister was given special dispensation to skip the school sports day.
The manager granted him a dispensation from the dress code during the hot summer months.
International students may apply for dispensation from the language requirement if they studied in English.
The church granted the couple a dispensation allowing them to marry during Lent.
He felt hurt that his brother always seemed to receive dispensations their parents never gave him.
tc: Normally every student must attend the field trip, but Hasan received ______ because of a family emergency.
'Normally every student must... but' signals an excuse from the usual rule.
se: The council granted the festival a special ______ to play music after midnight.
exemption
Both 'dispensation' and 'exemption' mean official release from a rule, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a long, detailed and formal discussion or essay on a subject
x: I only asked my uncle about his car, but he launched into a twenty-minute disquisition on engine oil.
Her email to the team turned into a disquisition on punctuality that nobody read to the end.
The professor's disquisition on medieval trade routes filled nearly three hundred pages.
In a lengthy disquisition published in the weekend paper, an economist examined the causes of inflation.
On their first date, he delivered a disquisition on his favourite films while she quietly checked her watch.
tc: What the students expected to be a brief reply turned into an hour-long ______ on the history of the semicolon.
'Hour-long' contrasted with 'brief reply' points to a long, formal discussion.
se: The philosopher's ______ on free will was so thorough that it took readers weeks to finish.
treatise
Both 'disquisition' and 'treatise' mean a long, systematic written discussion of a subject.

m: to hide one's true feelings or intentions by pretending
x: Children are rarely good at dissimulating, so their faces usually show exactly how they feel.
During the negotiation, she dissimulated her eagerness to sign and asked for more time.
The novel's narrator constantly dissimulates, and readers discover his true motives only in the final chapter.
Investigators concluded that company officials had dissimulated about the safety risks for years.
He loved her deeply but dissimulated his feelings, afraid that she would not feel the same.
tc: Though she was furious about the decision, she managed to ______ so well that her colleagues believed she was perfectly content.
'Though she was furious' contrasts with colleagues thinking she was content, so she must have hidden her feelings.
se: Skilled poker players learn to ______, hiding their excitement when they are dealt a strong hand.
dissemble
Both 'dissimulate' and 'dissemble' mean to conceal one's true feelings behind a false front.

m: swelling or stretching of something, especially a body part, caused by pressure from inside
x: Eating a huge plate of biryani too quickly left him with painful distension of the stomach.
The nurse noted mild abdominal distension and asked the patient when he had last eaten.
Students in the physiology lab measured the distension of a balloon as the air pressure increased.
Doctors say that severe abdominal distension in malnourished children is a sign of serious protein deficiency.
She grew anxious about the distension in her ankles after the long flight and called her doctor.
tc: The X-ray showed that gas trapped in the intestine had caused visible ______, making the patient's belly swell like a drum.
'Making the patient's belly swell like a drum' restates the meaning of swelling from inside pressure.
se: Overeating can lead to uncomfortable ______ of the abdomen.
bloating
Both 'distension' and 'bloating' describe the stomach swelling after too much food.

m: distracted and inattentive, usually because of worry
x: She seemed distrait at dinner, pushing her food around and missing half of what we said.
Worried about his sick mother, the usually sharp accountant was distrait throughout the meeting.
Still thinking about his visa interview, the distrait student stared blankly at the exam paper.
Witnesses described the pilot as distrait and anxious in the hours before the flight.
When I asked what was wrong, he gave me a distrait smile and changed the subject.
tc: Normally attentive in class, Maya was so ______ after hearing about her father's accident that she didn't notice when the teacher called her name.
'Normally attentive' contrasts with not noticing her name, so the blank means distracted by worry.
se: Worried about the results, he was ______ all evening and barely followed the conversation.
preoccupied
Both 'distrait' and 'preoccupied' mean too absorbed in worry to pay attention.

m: the practice of trying to foretell the future or discover hidden knowledge by supernatural means
x: At the village fair, an old man offered divination by reading the lines on people's palms.
Setting next quarter's sales target felt less like planning and more like divination.
The anthropology course included a unit on divination practices in ancient China and West Africa.
Economists sometimes joke that forecasting interest rates is closer to divination than to science.
She refused to rely on divination of any kind, insisting that her future was hers to shape.
tc: Ancient priests practised ______, studying the flight of birds to foretell whether a battle would be won.
'Studying the flight of birds to foretell' the outcome defines supernatural prediction.
se: In the ancient world, kings rarely went to war without consulting experts in ______.
soothsaying
Both 'divination' and 'soothsaying' mean predicting the future by supernatural means.

m: feeling or expressing great sorrow or grief
x: Our dog gives a dolorous whine every time we leave the house without him.
His dolorous email announcing the budget cuts made the whole team expect the worst.
The poem's dolorous final stanza mourns the death of the poet's young son.
Reporters heard dolorous accounts from families who had lost everything in the monsoon floods.
She sang a dolorous folk song that reminded her of her late grandmother.
tc: Unlike the cheerful melodies of his early albums, the singer's new record is slow and ______, full of songs about loss and grief.
'Unlike the cheerful melodies' and 'songs about loss and grief' point to a sorrowful quality.
se: The ______ tolling of the church bells announced the death of the old king.
mournful
Both 'dolorous' and 'mournful' describe a sound full of grief, fitting a royal death.

m: the period of old age, especially when the mind becomes weak
x: My grandfather, now in his dotage, tells the same story about the 1971 war every evening.
Even in her dotage, the company's founder still came to the office every Monday to check on her old employees.
Some historians argue that the emperor's poor decisions in his dotage hastened the empire's decline.
A recent study suggests that regular reading may delay the memory loss many people fear in their dotage.
He joked that he would need someone patient to look after him in his dotage, and she promised to be that person.
tc: Once a brilliant scientist, he was now in his ______, forgetting names and repeating questions he had asked minutes earlier.
'Once a brilliant scientist' contrasted with forgetfulness points to the mental decline of old age.
se: In her ______, the old novelist often confused her grandchildren's names.
senility
Both 'dotage' and 'senility' refer to old age marked by mental decline, so the sentence means the same.

m: brave, determined and persistent, especially in difficult situations
x: Our doughty neighbour, at seventy-five, still shovels the snow from her own driveway every winter.
The union's doughty negotiator refused to leave the table until the workers' pay rise was agreed.
She was a doughty champion of open-access research long before it became fashionable.
Doughty rescue workers waded through chest-deep floodwater to reach stranded families.
Through every setback in his illness, he remained a doughty companion who never let her lose hope.
tc: Though outnumbered and exhausted, the ______ defenders held the bridge for three days without retreating.
Holding the bridge 'though outnumbered and exhausted' shows courage and persistence.
se: The ______ old campaigner spent forty years fighting for clean drinking water in rural areas.
stalwart
Both 'doughty' and 'stalwart' describe someone brave and unwavering over a long struggle.

m: to force or pressure someone into doing something
x: My mother dragooned all of us into cleaning the house before the guests arrived.
New employees were dragooned into organizing the office party, whether they liked it or not.
Several graduate students were dragooned into marking exams over the holiday.
Historians record that villagers were dragooned into building roads for the colonial administration.
He resented being dragooned into a marriage his parents had arranged without asking him.
tc: Rather than persuading volunteers, the officer chose to ______ the reluctant villagers into carrying supplies.
'Rather than persuading' and 'reluctant' show the villagers were forced.
se: The coach tried to ______ his exhausted players into an extra hour of practice.
coerce
Both 'dragoon' and 'coerce' mean to force someone to do something against their will.

m: bad-tempered and irritable, as if suffering from indigestion
x: The dyspeptic old man next door shouts at any child whose ball lands in his garden.
Our dyspeptic editor rarely praises anything, so a single 'good' from him feels like a medal.
In a dyspeptic review, the critic dismissed the professor's new book as tedious and pointless.
Voters, increasingly dyspeptic about rising prices, punished the ruling party at the polls.
Lack of sleep had made her dyspeptic, and she snapped at her husband over nothing.
tc: Known for his ______ temper, the columnist found fault with every new restaurant and seemed to enjoy nothing.
Finding fault with everything and enjoying nothing points to an irritable, sour temper.
se: After a long flight and a lost suitcase, Daniel was feeling ______ and snapped at the hotel clerk.
irritable
Both 'dyspeptic' and 'irritable' describe a bad-tempered mood that makes someone snap at others.

m: a sudden outburst of emotion or activity; also, the act of boiling
x: Her sudden ebullition of laughter at the dinner table startled the quiet guests.
The meeting ended in an ebullition of anger when the manager announced unpaid overtime.
In the chemistry lab, students recorded the temperature at which ebullition began in each liquid.
Historians describe the decade as an ebullition of artistic creativity after years of censorship.
News of the cricket victory set off an ebullition of joy across the streets of Dhaka.
tc: The usually reserved professor surprised everyone with his sudden ______ of rage when a student's phone rang during the lecture.
'Usually reserved' contrasts with a 'sudden... of rage', so the blank means an outburst.
se: News of the ceasefire produced a sudden ______ of joy in the capital.
outburst
Both 'ebullition' and 'outburst' mean a sudden burst of strong emotion.

m: weak and ineffectual, often from being overrefined or pampered
x: My grandfather calls city boys effete because they have never done a day's work in the fields.
The board dismissed the old management as effete, unable to make a hard decision when one was needed.
In the essay, the author argues that the empire's effete ruling class had grown too comfortable to defend its borders.
The populist candidate railed against what he called an effete elite out of touch with ordinary workers.
She found his effete manners charming at first, but soon longed for someone with more spirit.
tc: Once a vigorous and daring dynasty, the royal family had grown ______ after generations of luxury, unable either to govern or to fight.
'Once a vigorous and daring dynasty' contrasted with 'generations of luxury' points to weakness from pampering.
se: Critics dismissed the club's members as ______ aristocrats who had never done anything useful.
decadent
Both 'effete' and 'decadent' describe pampered, self-indulgent people who have lost vigour.

m: shining brightly; radiant
x: An effulgent full moon rose over the river, lighting up the fishing boats.
Her effulgent smile at the job interview made an immediate impression on the panel.
Our astronomy textbook includes striking photographs of effulgent nebulae taken by space telescopes.
Thousands crowded the square to see the effulgent lights of the New Year festival.
Holding her newborn daughter, she looked more effulgent than he had ever seen her.
tc: Unlike the dim, flickering lamps of the old hall, the new chandelier was ______, flooding the room with brilliant light.
'Unlike the dim, flickering lamps' and 'flooding the room with brilliant light' point to shining brightly.
se: The ______ sunset turned the whole sky gold and pink.
radiant
Both 'effulgent' and 'radiant' describe something shining brightly.

m: excessive concern with one's own interests; selfishness
x: It was pure egoism that made him take the biggest piece of cake without asking anyone else.
Her colleagues grew tired of the egoism that led her to claim credit for every team success.
Our philosophy seminar debated whether ethical egoism can ever justify helping others.
Some economists argue that markets work because they harness individual egoism for the common good.
Their marriage struggled because his egoism left little room for her needs and dreams.
tc: Far from being motivated by ______, the volunteer gave away most of her savings to help strangers.
'Far from' signals the opposite of her generous behaviour, so the blank means selfishness.
se: His decision to skip his sister's wedding for a business trip was seen as an act of pure ______.
selfishness
Both 'egoism' and 'selfishness' mean putting one's own interests first, giving the same judgment.

m: energy, style and enthusiasm in the way something is done
x: My aunt hosts dinner parties with such elan that guests always ask when the next one will be.
She presented the quarterly report with elan, turning dry figures into a lively story.
The young pianist played the difficult sonata with remarkable elan at her graduation recital.
Commentators praised the Bangladesh openers for batting with elan against a fierce bowling attack.
He loved her for the elan with which she faced every challenge, even the hardest ones.
tc: Although the actor was nearly eighty, he performed the dance number with such ______ that the audience leapt to its feet.
'Although... nearly eighty' and the standing ovation show he performed with energy and style.
se: The chef served each dish with ______, adding a dramatic flourish to every plate.
flair
Both 'elan' and 'flair' mean stylish energy, matching the 'dramatic flourish'.

m: the skill of speaking clearly and expressively, especially in public
x: My parents sent me to elocution lessons because they said I mumbled at the dinner table.
Her clear elocution made her the obvious choice to present the company's plans to investors.
Many schools in Dhaka hold annual elocution contests where students recite poems by Tagore and Nazrul.
Radio announcers in the 1950s were trained in elocution to sound formal and precise.
He admired the actor's elocution so much that he practised speaking in front of the mirror every night.
tc: Although the speaker's ideas were excellent, his poor ______ meant that half the audience could not understand his mumbled words.
'Mumbled words' that the audience could not understand point to poor speaking skill.
se: Actors at the drama school spend hours on ______, learning to pronounce every syllable clearly.
diction
Both 'elocution' and 'diction' refer to the clarity of one's speech, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to entangle or trap someone or something in a difficult situation
x: A small bird had become enmeshed in the netting over our vegetable garden.
Without meaning to, the new intern got enmeshed in an office feud between two senior managers.
Her research shows how quickly teenagers can become enmeshed in online misinformation.
The minister's family business became enmeshed in a corruption scandal just weeks before the election.
Family therapists warn that parents and children can become so enmeshed that neither has a separate identity.
tc: Hoping to stay neutral, the diplomat was careful not to ______ himself in the bitter quarrel between the two neighbouring states.
'Hoping to stay neutral' shows he wanted to avoid getting entangled in the quarrel.
se: Lawyers warned the company that the dispute could ______ it in years of costly litigation.
embroil
Both 'enmesh' and 'embroil' mean to entangle someone in a difficult conflict.

m: devoted to pleasure, especially the enjoyment of fine food and drink
x: My uncle's epicurean tastes mean he will drive across the city for the perfect plate of kacchi biryani.
The company's annual dinner was an epicurean feast of seven courses and fine wines.
Her book traces how epicurean attitudes toward food spread through eighteenth-century Paris.
This year's food festival offers epicurean delights from more than forty countries.
A shared epicurean love of long dinners and good coffee was what first brought them together.
tc: Unlike his ______ brother, who spent fortunes on fine wines and rare cheeses, Tom ate simple meals of rice and lentils.
The brother's spending on 'fine wines and rare cheeses' contrasts with Tom's simple meals, showing devotion to fine food.
se: The resort is famous for its ______ dinners, where guests enjoy rare wines and exquisite dishes.
gourmet
Both 'epicurean' and 'gourmet' describe refined food and drink enjoyed for pleasure.

m: an inferior follower or imitator of a great artist or thinker
x: My cousin's band is just an epigone of a famous rock group, copying both their haircuts and their songs.
The start-up's founders insisted they were innovators, not epigones of the big tech companies.
Critics dismissed the young painter as a mere epigone of Picasso who added nothing new.
After the great architect's death, his epigones filled the city with poor imitations of his buildings.
She feared she would always be seen as her famous mother's epigone rather than as a writer in her own right.
tc: The critic argued that the novelist was no innovator but the ______ of a greater master, copying his style without his genius.
'No innovator' and 'copying his style without his genius' define an inferior imitator.
se: Scholars regard the composer as the ______ of Beethoven, imitating his style without matching his brilliance.
imitator
Both 'epigone' and 'imitator' describe a lesser follower who copies a master.

m: a state of balance or equilibrium between forces or interests
x: After a stressful week, a quiet afternoon of gardening restores my equipoise.
A good manager keeps the team in equipoise between ambition and realistic deadlines.
Medical ethicists say a clinical trial is justified only when there is genuine equipoise about which treatment works better.
The treaty aimed to create an equipoise of power between the two rival nations.
Meditation helped her find some emotional equipoise after the difficult divorce.
tc: The architect placed the heavy stone tower opposite the glass wing so that the two halves of the building stood in perfect ______.
Placing a heavy part 'opposite' another so the halves match points to balance.
se: Through daily yoga she learned to keep her mind in ______, even during stressful exams.
balance
Both 'equipoise' and 'balance' mean a calm, stable state of mind.

m: the quality of being fair and impartial
x: My mother divided the jewellery among us with scrupulous equity, down to the last bangle.
The new pay policy is meant to ensure equity between staff in different departments.
Researchers studied equity in university admissions, asking whether rural students had the same chances as urban ones.
Campaigners argue that the tax reform does little to improve social equity.
In a good friendship, there is a natural equity of give and take.
tc: To ensure ______, the judge ordered both parties to share the legal costs equally rather than placing the burden on one side.
Sharing costs 'equally rather than placing the burden on one side' shows the goal is fairness.
se: The committee reviewed salaries to promote ______ between male and female employees.
fairness
Both 'equity' and 'fairness' mean just and equal treatment, so the sentence means the same.

m: deserving respect and admiration
x: Our estimable neighbour has quietly tutored the street's children for free for over twenty years.
She was an estimable colleague, always honest and generous with her time.
The prize recognizes the professor's estimable contributions to the study of tropical diseases.
Thanks to the estimable work of local volunteers, every flood victim received food within two days.
He hoped that one day his children would think of him as an estimable man.
tc: Although critics often attacked her politics, even they admitted that her honesty and devotion to the poor were truly ______.
'Although critics attacked her... even they admitted' signals praise, so the blank means worthy of respect.
se: Everyone at the ceremony praised the retiring judge for his ______ career of honest public service.
admirable
Both 'estimable' and 'admirable' mean deserving respect, giving the same praise.

m: full of high praise
x: My aunt's eulogistic description of the new restaurant made us all eager to try it.
The farewell email to the retiring manager was so eulogistic that she joked it sounded like an obituary.
Reviewers found the biography too eulogistic, since it ignored the scientist's well-known mistakes.
State media published eulogistic articles celebrating the government's tenth year in power.
Reading his friends' eulogistic birthday messages, he felt deeply appreciated.
tc: Expecting harsh criticism, the young author was astonished by the ______ review, which called her novel a masterpiece.
'Expecting harsh criticism' contrasts with calling the novel 'a masterpiece', so the review was full of praise.
se: The speaker's ______ remarks about the retiring teacher brought tears to the audience's eyes.
laudatory
Both 'eulogistic' and 'laudatory' mean full of praise, so the remarks mean the same.

m: extremely bad or unpleasant
x: The hotel's coffee was so execrable that we walked to a café across town every morning.
His execrable handwriting meant his secretary had to retype every note he gave her.
The examiner described the essay's grammar as execrable and returned it for revision.
Human rights groups condemned the prison's execrable conditions, including overcrowding and a lack of clean water.
She apologized for her execrable behaviour at the party and promised it would never happen again.
tc: Far from being the masterpiece the studio promised, the film was ______, with wooden acting and a plot that made no sense.
'Far from being the masterpiece' plus 'wooden acting' shows the film was extremely bad.
se: The critics agreed that the play's acting was ______ and urged audiences to stay at home.
atrocious
Both 'execrable' and 'atrocious' mean extremely bad, so the critics' verdict is unchanged.

m: a detailed critical explanation or interpretation of a text, especially scripture
x: My father's dinner-table exegesis of a single newspaper cartoon lasted longer than the meal itself.
The lawyer offered a careful exegesis of the contract, explaining what each clause really meant.
Her doctoral thesis is an exegesis of three early Persian poems.
Scholars of religion have produced centuries of exegesis on just a few verses of scripture.
He was touched when his daughter wrote a thoughtful exegesis of his favourite song for a school project.
tc: Readers found the poem baffling until the scholar's line-by-line ______ explained the meaning of each obscure image.
A 'line-by-line' account that 'explained the meaning' defines a critical interpretation of a text.
se: The seminar was devoted to close ______ of the founding documents, examining the meaning of every phrase.
interpretation
Both 'exegesis' and 'interpretation' mean explaining the meaning of a text.

m: a person or thing serving as a typical or excellent model
x: My grandmother was an exemplar of patience, never raising her voice even with the noisiest grandchildren.
The manager held up Sara's report as an exemplar of clear, concise writing.
Teachers gave students several exemplars of high-scoring essays to study before the exam.
Scientists regard the national park as an exemplar of successful wildlife conservation.
To him, his older brother was an exemplar of everything he hoped to become.
tc: Praised for its clarity and elegance, the bridge is considered the ______ of modern engineering design and is copied by architects around the world.
Being 'copied by architects around the world' shows the bridge serves as a model.
se: Her selfless work in the clinic made her the ______ of compassion in the community.
epitome
Both 'exemplar' and 'epitome' mean a perfect example of a quality.

m: the state of being very small in amount; scantiness
x: Opening the fridge, we laughed at the exiguity of its contents: some bread, two eggs and one tomato.
Given the exiguity of the budget, the team had to cancel its overseas training trip.
The historian apologized for the exiguity of surviving records from the twelfth century.
Aid agencies warned that the exiguity of clean water in the camps could lead to disease.
Despite the exiguity of his salary, he sent money home to his parents in Rajshahi every month.
tc: The researchers could draw no firm conclusions because of the ______ of their data, which came from only four patients.
'Only four patients' explains that the data were extremely scanty.
se: Because of the ______ of the harvest, many families had barely enough rice to last the winter.
scantiness
Both 'exiguity' and 'scantiness' mean a very small amount, explaining the shortage of rice.

m: to take property from its owner, especially by government action for public use
x: My grandfather never forgot how officials expropriated his family's orchard to build a highway.
Without asking anyone, the new director expropriated the staff room and turned it into his private office.
Her economics thesis compares countries that expropriated foreign oil companies in the twentieth century.
The government plans to expropriate farmland along the river to build a new port.
He felt that his older sister had expropriated their mother's affection, leaving none for him.
tc: Instead of buying the land at a fair price, the regime chose to ______ it, seizing the estates of anyone who opposed it.
'Instead of buying' and 'seizing the estates' show the land was taken by force.
se: The revolutionary government moved quickly to ______ the factories owned by foreign investors.
confiscate
Both 'expropriate' and 'confiscate' mean to take property away from its owners by authority.

m: to speak or perform without preparation; to improvise
x: When the power went out, we had to extemporize a dinner of cold sandwiches by candlelight.
My slides failed to load, so I extemporized for twenty minutes and hoped nobody noticed.
Good jazz students learn to extemporize freely over a simple chord progression.
The prime minister abandoned his prepared text and extemporized for nearly an hour.
Nervous at his sister's wedding, he forgot his toast and had to extemporize, which made everyone laugh warmly.
tc: Having lost his notes moments before the lecture, the professor had no choice but to ______, speaking without any preparation.
'Speaking without any preparation' directly defines the blank.
se: When the lead actor forgot his lines, the rest of the cast had to ______ until he remembered them.
improvise
Both 'extemporize' and 'improvise' mean to perform without a script.

m: coming from outside; not part of the essential nature of something
x: A child who reads only to earn stickers is driven by extrinsic rewards rather than a love of books.
Bonuses and promotions are extrinsic motivators, but many employees value meaningful work far more.
The study controlled for extrinsic factors, such as weather and diet, that might affect the results.
Economists argue that the slowdown was caused by extrinsic shocks, such as falling global demand, rather than domestic policy.
She realized that her happiness had depended too much on extrinsic things like praise and money.
tc: The painting's value is not ______ but inherent: it lies in the brilliance of the brushwork, not in the fame of its previous owners.
'Not ... but inherent' signals that the blank is the opposite of inherent, meaning coming from outside.
se: The judge ruled that the documents were ______ to the case and would not be considered.
extraneous
Both 'extrinsic' and 'extraneous' mean coming from outside and not essential to the matter.

m: so absurd or disorganized that it is ridiculous
x: Our attempt to assemble the flat-pack wardrobe became farcical when we realized we had built it upside down.
The meeting turned farcical as three managers argued over who had booked the room.
Students called the exam farcical, since half the questions covered topics that had never been taught.
International observers described the election as farcical after ballot boxes were found already full.
Looking back, she found their constant breakups and reunions almost farcical.
tc: The trial was so ______ that the judge fell asleep, the key witness forgot his own name, and the verdict was announced before closing arguments.
The list of absurd events shows the trial was ridiculous.
se: Critics called the government's plan to ease traffic by banning bicycles ______.
ludicrous
Both 'farcical' and 'ludicrous' mean absurd to the point of being laughable.

m: smug or complacent foolishness
x: I only saw the fatuity of buying a year's supply of bread when half of it went mouldy.
Everyone in the office rolled their eyes at the fatuity of the new rule banning coffee at desks.
The professor exposed the fatuity of the argument with a single simple counterexample.
Commentators mocked the fatuity of a campaign slogan that promised more of everything for everyone.
She was embarrassed by the fatuity of the love letters she had written as a teenager.
tc: Instead of wisdom, the speech offered only ______, a string of empty clichés delivered with complete self-satisfaction.
'Instead of wisdom' and 'empty clichés delivered with complete self-satisfaction' define smug foolishness.
se: The committee was astonished by the ______ of a proposal to cut costs by switching off the hospital's air conditioning in summer.
foolishness
Both 'fatuity' and 'foolishness' mean a lack of good sense, so the committee's reaction is the same.

m: loyalty, especially sworn loyalty to a lord or leader
x: Our old dog showed absolute fealty to my grandmother, following her from room to room.
