The new chief executive expected fealty from senior staff and quickly replaced anyone who questioned him.
In medieval Europe, knights swore fealty to their lords in return for land and protection.
Party members were expected to show complete fealty to the leadership, whatever their private doubts.
She valued his fealty more than any gift, knowing he would stand by her through anything.
tc: Though he disagreed with the king, the old knight never wavered in his ______, refusing every bribe offered by the rebels.
'Never wavered' and 'refusing every bribe' show steadfast loyalty.
se: The new governors were required to swear ______ to the emperor before taking office.
allegiance
Both 'fealty' and 'allegiance' mean sworn loyalty to a ruler.

m: lively, determined and ready to fight or argue
x: Our feisty little terrier barks at dogs three times his size.
The feisty new recruit challenged the manager's figures in her very first meeting.
A feisty graduate student, she refused to let her supervisor dismiss her findings without evidence.
In a feisty televised debate, the two candidates traded sharp attacks on the economy.
He fell for her feisty spirit the moment she told him his argument was nonsense.
tc: Unlike her shy, quiet sister, Nadia was ______ and never backed down from an argument, even with her teachers.
'Unlike her shy, quiet sister' and 'never backed down' point to a spirited, combative nature.
se: The ______ underdogs fought hard for every point and nearly beat the champions.
plucky
Both 'feisty' and 'plucky' describe small but determined fighters.

m: to search persistently, especially to discover something hidden (often 'ferret out')
x: My mother can ferret out a hidden chocolate bar anywhere in the house within minutes.
The auditors spent weeks ferreting out errors buried in the company's accounts.
She ferreted around in the university archives until she found the original letters.
Investigative journalists ferreted out evidence that officials had accepted bribes.
He tried to keep the surprise party a secret, but his wife ferreted it out in a day.
tc: The detective was determined to ______ out the truth, however carefully the suspects tried to hide it.
'However carefully the suspects tried to hide it' shows the detective must search persistently to uncover it.
se: She began to ______ around in her bag for the train ticket she was sure she had packed.
rummage
Both 'ferret around' and 'rummage around' mean to search busily through something.

m: an authoritative order or decree, usually issued without consultation
x: In our house, bedtime was set by parental fiat, and no amount of arguing could change it.
The new office hours were imposed by fiat, without consulting a single employee.
Universities cannot simply raise academic standards by fiat; they must also invest in teaching.
A presidential fiat dissolved parliament overnight, leaving the country without a legislature.
She resented the way he made decisions about their finances by fiat, as though her opinion didn't matter.
tc: Rather than allowing the members to vote, the chairman settled the matter by ______, simply announcing the decision himself.
'Rather than allowing the members to vote' and 'announcing the decision himself' point to an authoritative order.
se: The new holiday was created by royal ______, without any debate in parliament.
decree
Both 'fiat' and 'decree' mean an official order issued by authority.

m: to obtain something by clever, persuasive or slightly dishonest means
x: Somehow my brother finagled two free tickets to the sold-out concert.
Our sales manager finagled a bigger budget by convincing the director that a rival was about to launch.
He finagled his way onto the research team even though he had missed the application deadline.
The report accused the developer of finagling planning permission through personal connections with officials.
Every Eid, my little cousin finagles extra money from all the aunts with his sweetest smile.
tc: Unable to get tickets honestly, the clever student managed to ______ his way into the concert by pretending to be a stagehand.
'Unable to get tickets honestly' and the pretence show he got in by trickery.
se: He somehow managed to ______ an invitation to the exclusive party through a friend of a friend.
wangle
Both 'finagle' and 'wangle' mean to obtain something through cunning or persuasion.

m: a person who passionately stirs up trouble or supports a radical cause
x: My aunt was the family firebrand, always the first to start an argument about politics at dinner.
The union's young firebrand urged workers to walk out if management refused their demands.
As a student firebrand at Dhaka University, he led protests demanding greater press freedom.
The firebrand preacher's speeches drew huge crowds and alarmed the authorities.
She loved his passion but worried that the firebrand she had married would never settle down.
tc: Unlike her cautious, moderate colleagues, the senator was the party's ______, known for fiery speeches that stirred crowds to protest.
'Unlike her cautious, moderate colleagues' and 'fiery speeches that stirred crowds' define a passionate agitator.
se: Authorities arrested the young ______ after he urged crowds to storm the government offices.
agitator
Both 'firebrand' and 'agitator' mean someone who stirs people up to protest or revolt.

m: to become tired, weak, or less enthusiastic; to lose energy or interest
x: By late afternoon my energy began to flag, so I made myself another cup of strong tea.
Attendance at the weekly team meetings started to flag once people realized the real decisions were made elsewhere.
Her concentration flagged during the third hour of the exam, and she made several careless mistakes.
Public interest in the inquiry flagged after months of delays and inconclusive hearings.
Whenever my spirits flag, a phone call from my mother in Chittagong always cheers me up.
tc: The marathon runner started strongly, but her pace began to ______ in the final miles as exhaustion set in.
'Started strongly, but' and 'as exhaustion set in' show the blank must mean to weaken or tire.
se: As the debate dragged on past midnight, the audience's attention began to ______.
wane
Both 'flag' and 'wane' mean to grow weaker, describing attention fading during a long debate.

m: becoming weaker, more tired, or less vigorous; declining
x: A short walk in the fresh air did wonders for my flagging energy after lunch.
The company launched an aggressive advertising campaign to revive its flagging sales.
Our professor told a few jokes to rouse the flagging attention of the students in the back rows.
Economists warned that the stimulus package might not be enough to lift a flagging economy.
His kind words lifted her flagging spirits after a long week of job rejections.
tc: The coach's rousing halftime speech restored the team's ______ morale, and they played the second half with renewed energy.
'Restored' and 'renewed energy' show the morale had been weakening before the speech.
se: The new menu was meant to revive the restaurant's ______ business.
declining
'Revive' implies the business was weakening, and both 'flagging' and 'declining' express that.

m: fully developed or qualified; of a young bird, having feathers and able to fly
x: After three years of training, she is finally a fully fledged member of the nursing staff.
What began as a weekend hobby has grown into a fully fledged business with twelve employees.
The newly fledged sparrows spent the morning hopping clumsily between the branches of our mango tree.
Diplomats worry that the minor border dispute could escalate into a fully fledged war.
Leaving home for university made him feel, for the first time, like a fully fledged adult.
tc: Only after the chicks were ______ and able to fly did the mother bird stop bringing food to the nest.
'Able to fly' defines the blank: the young birds had grown their feathers and matured.
se: Within a decade, the small reading group had become a fully ______ literary society with its own journal.
developed
Both 'fully fledged' and 'fully developed' describe the group growing into a complete, mature society.

m: floating wreckage or debris; also, useless odds and ends that have been discarded
x: After the storm, the beach was littered with flotsam: broken planks, plastic bottles and tangled fishing nets.
Rescuers searched the flotsam for any sign of the fishermen from the capsized trawler.
My desk drawer is full of the flotsam of a busy year: dead pens, old receipts and loose screws.
Marine biologists study how flotsam can carry invasive species thousands of kilometres across the ocean.
Sorting through my late grandfather's papers, I found precious letters among the flotsam of a long life.
tc: After the ship sank, ______ from the wreck, including splintered timber, crates and life jackets, drifted ashore for weeks.
The list of floating pieces from a wreck defines the blank as floating wreckage.
se: The river was choked with ______ after the flood: branches, plastic sheets and broken furniture.
debris
Both 'flotsam' and 'debris' name the floating rubbish listed after the colon.

m: to confuse or bewilder someone completely
x: The new ticket machines at the station flummoxed even the most experienced commuters.
My manager was flummoxed when the client suddenly cancelled a contract they had praised just a week earlier.
The final question on the physics paper flummoxed nearly everyone in the class.
The rare symptoms flummoxed doctors at three hospitals before a specialist finally made the diagnosis.
His sudden silence flummoxed her; she could not tell whether he was angry or simply tired.
tc: The puzzle was designed to ______ even expert solvers, and indeed no one in the competition managed to finish it.
'No one managed to finish it' shows the puzzle was meant to confuse completely.
se: The magician's final trick was clever enough to ______ even the skeptics in the front row.
baffle
Both 'flummox' and 'baffle' mean to leave someone completely puzzled.

m: to trick someone into accepting something inferior, or to put someone off with excuses (usually 'fob off')
x: The shopkeeper tried to fob off a cracked phone screen on me, claiming it was brand new.
Whenever I ask for a raise, my boss fobs me off with vague promises about next year.
The students refused to be fobbed off with a photocopied handout instead of the textbook they had paid for.
Residents complained that the council had fobbed them off for months instead of fixing the broken drains.
Don't fob me off with excuses; just tell me honestly why you missed my birthday dinner.
tc: Instead of dealing with the customer's complaint, the agent tried to ______ her off with a meaningless discount voucher.
'Instead of dealing with the complaint' and 'meaningless voucher' show the agent was putting her off with something worthless.
se: The trader tried to ______ cheap copies on unsuspecting tourists, passing them off as genuine antiques.
foist
Both 'fob' and 'foist' mean to trick someone into accepting something inferior as genuine.

m: to search widely for food or supplies; to rummage around looking for something
x: I foraged in the fridge for something to eat but found only half a lemon and some yogurt.
Before the deadline, the team foraged through old files for any data that could support the proposal.
Monkeys from the nearby forest often forage in the campus bins, much to the students' amusement.
Researchers tracked how bees forage for nectar across fields treated with different pesticides.
Lonely in a new city, she foraged through her phone contacts for anyone she might call for a chat.
tc: During the harsh winter, deer must ______ widely, often travelling miles each day to find enough food.
'Travelling miles each day to find enough food' defines the blank as searching widely for food.
se: Hungry after the late shift, he went to ______ in the kitchen for leftovers.
rummage
Both 'forage' and 'rummage' mean to search around for something, here leftover food.

m: to determine or decide an outcome in advance, as if by fate
x: My grandmother believed that whom you marry is foreordained long before you are born.
Nothing about the merger was foreordained; it succeeded only because both teams worked tirelessly.
Some historians argue that the empire's collapse was foreordained by its crushing debts.
The novel's characters seem foreordained to repeat their parents' mistakes, no matter how hard they try.
Students from poor villages should not feel that failure in the university admission tests is foreordained.
tc: The ancient Greeks believed that the gods could ______ a person's fate at birth, leaving no room for free will.
'At birth' and 'no room for free will' show the blank means to decide in advance.
se: Fatalists believe that some cosmic force must ______ every event in our lives.
predetermine
Both 'foreordain' and 'predetermine' mean to settle events beforehand.

m: to give up or renounce something solemnly, often under oath
x: After a terrible hangover on his birthday, he forswore alcohol for the rest of the year.
To win the contract, the firm had to forswear any business dealings with its client's competitors.
She forswore social media for the month before her GRE so that she could study without distractions.
The rebel group formally forswore violence as part of the peace agreement.
He had forsworn love after his engagement collapsed, yet he found himself smiling at her messages.
tc: Determined to get healthy, he decided to ______ sugar entirely, giving away every chocolate bar in the house.
'Entirely' and 'giving away every chocolate bar' show he was firmly giving sugar up.
se: The new leader promised to ______ the use of force against peaceful protesters.
renounce
Both 'forswear' and 'renounce' mean to formally give up a practice.

m: to associate in a friendly way, especially with people one is expected to keep apart from
x: Auditors are warned not to fraternize too closely with the clients whose accounts they check.
Managers at the firm are discouraged from fraternizing with junior staff outside the office.
During the conference, graduate students fraternized happily with professors over tea and samosas.
Soldiers on both sides famously fraternized during the Christmas truce of 1914, exchanging gifts and songs.
Her parents did not approve of her fraternizing with the boys from the rival school.
tc: Prison guards were strictly forbidden to ______ with inmates, so even a casual friendly chat could lead to dismissal.
'Even a casual friendly chat' was forbidden, so the blank means to associate in a friendly way.
se: At the party, the new interns were eager to ______ with the senior partners.
mingle
Both 'fraternize' and 'mingle' mean to socialize in a friendly way with others.

m: to wear thin or unravel at the edges; of nerves or relationships, to become strained
x: The collar of my favourite shirt has started to fray after years of washing.
Tempers frayed in the office as the deadline approached and the server crashed yet again.
Stuck for three hours in Dhaka traffic, even the calmest passengers had begun to fray at the edges.
Relations between the two countries have frayed since the trade talks collapsed last spring.
Years of small resentments had slowly frayed their friendship until they barely spoke.
tc: The rope had been rubbing against the sharp rock for hours, and the climbers watched anxiously as it began to ______.
Hours of 'rubbing against the sharp rock' would cause the rope to wear thin and unravel.
se: Months of constant pressure had begun to ______ the bond between the two business partners.
strain
Both 'fray' and 'strain' describe pressure weakening a relationship.

m: gloomy and solemn, as if suited to a funeral
x: The waiting room was painted a funereal grey that made everyone feel slightly worse.
After the quarterly losses were announced, the mood in the boardroom was positively funereal.
The lecturer spoke in such a funereal tone that even his jokes sounded like condolences.
A funereal silence fell over the stadium after the home team collapsed in the final overs.
She dressed in funereal black for weeks after the breakup, which her friends found rather dramatic.
tc: Far from the festive celebration the organizers had promised, the reception's atmosphere was ______, with guests speaking in hushed voices.
'Far from the festive celebration' and 'hushed voices' signal a gloomy, solemn mood.
se: The usually lively café felt ______ after news of the owner's death spread.
somber
Both 'funereal' and 'somber' describe a gloomy, mournful mood after a death.

m: pompous, inflated speech or writing that sounds grand but says little
x: The restaurant menu's fustian about 'artisanal journeys of flavour' made us laugh before we had even ordered.
The report was full of corporate fustian about synergy and paradigm shifts but contained no real numbers.
Our writing tutor circled every bit of fustian in my essay and wrote 'Say it simply!' in the margin.
Strip away the fustian from the candidate's speech and you are left with very little actual policy.
His love letters were embarrassing fustian, full of grand phrases but empty of genuine feeling.
tc: Voters expected plain, direct language from the new mayor, but his inaugural address was pure ______, crammed with lofty phrases that meant almost nothing.
The contrast with 'plain, direct language' and 'lofty phrases that meant almost nothing' define the blank as pompous talk.
se: Underneath all the ______, the party's manifesto offered no practical solutions.
bombast
Both 'fustian' and 'bombast' mean inflated language that hides a lack of substance.

m: producing income or profit; paid
x: After six months of searching, my cousin finally found gainful employment at a software firm in Dhaka.
The charity offers training to help former prisoners find gainful work after their release.
Many students take part-time jobs, but few find work that is both gainful and related to their studies.
The government's new scheme aims to move thousands of young people into gainful employment.
Her parents were relieved when she finally found something gainful to do after graduating.
tc: Unlike his volunteer work at the shelter, his new position was ______, finally providing a steady income for his family.
The contrast with 'volunteer work' and 'steady income' show the blank means paid.
se: Retired engineers often look for ______ work that lets them use their skills.
paid
Both 'gainful' and 'paid' describe work that earns money.

m: an opening move or remark made to gain an advantage, often involving some risk
x: Asking about her favourite books was my usual conversational gambit at parties.
Offering a deep discount on the first order was a clever gambit to win the client's trust.
In the debate, his opening gambit was to concede a minor point and then attack the main argument.
The prime minister's call for early elections was widely seen as a risky political gambit.
Her gambit of pretending not to care only made him more anxious about the relationship.
tc: Sacrificing a pawn early in the game was a deliberate ______ intended to lure his opponent into a trap.
A deliberate sacrifice 'intended to lure his opponent into a trap' is a calculated opening move.
se: Announcing a fake rival offer was his favourite ______ for pushing buyers to pay more.
ploy
Both 'gambit' and 'ploy' mean a calculated move to gain an advantage.

m: the complete range or scope of something
x: The shop sells the whole gamut of spices, from cheap turmeric to rare saffron.
Our new director has worked across the full gamut of jobs in this company, from intern to manager.
The course covers the entire gamut of modern economic theory in just twelve weeks.
Public reaction to the new law has run the gamut from outrage to quiet approval.
Waiting for my GRE scores, I ran the gamut of emotions from hope to sheer panic.
tc: The actress displayed the entire ______ of emotions in a single scene, moving from joy to grief to rage within minutes.
'Moving from joy to grief to rage' shows she covered the complete range of emotions.
se: The museum's collection covers the whole ______ of Bengali art, from ancient terracotta to contemporary painting.
spectrum
Both 'gamut' and 'spectrum' mean the full range, here from ancient to contemporary.

m: a broad, vague statement or idea that lacks specific detail
x: When I asked about the refund, the customer service agent responded only with polite generalities.
The CEO's speech was full of generalities about innovation but said nothing about the job cuts.
My supervisor told me to replace the generalities in my thesis introduction with concrete evidence.
Voters are tired of politicians who speak in comforting generalities instead of offering real plans.
Her apology was a vague generality that never mentioned what she had actually done wrong.
tc: Rather than giving specific examples, the candidate answered every question with some vague ______ about hard work and teamwork.
'Rather than giving specific examples' signals the blank means a broad, vague statement.
se: His essay never rises above the level of ______; it does not offer a single concrete example.
generalization
Both 'generality' and 'generalization' mean broad, vague statements lacking concrete detail.

m: unintelligible or meaningless speech or writing; nonsense
x: My baby nephew babbles happy gibberish at the ceiling fan every morning.
The translation software turned our carefully written brochure into complete gibberish.
Written at four in the morning, my lab report read like gibberish when I checked it later that day.
Researchers submitted computer-generated gibberish to the journal to expose its weak peer review.
When I'm nervous on a first date, I tend to talk gibberish and then regret it all night.
tc: The encrypted message looked like pure ______ until the analysts found the key that made it readable.
'Until... made it readable' shows the message had seemed meaningless.
se: After the stroke, his speech was briefly reduced to ______, though he recovered within days.
babble
Both 'gibberish' and 'babble' mean speech that cannot be understood.

m: to coat thinly with gold, or to make something appear more attractive than it really is
x: Craftsmen spent weeks gilding the old temple's carved doors before the festival.
The marketing team gilded the quarterly figures with optimistic language that fooled no one.
Late afternoon sunlight gilded the pages of my textbook as I studied by the window.
Critics accused the ministry of gilding a failed policy with glossy reports and photo opportunities.
Memory tends to gild our first love, erasing the arguments and leaving only the sweetness.
tc: Not content with the statue's plain bronze finish, the wealthy patron paid artisans to ______ it with real gold leaf.
'With real gold leaf' defines the blank as coating something in gold.
se: The press release tried to ______ a disappointing year with talk of exciting opportunities ahead.
sugarcoat
Both 'gild' and 'sugarcoat' mean to make something bad look more attractive than it is.

m: expressed in short, wise-sounding sayings that are often hard to understand
x: My grandfather answered every question with gnomic proverbs that left us more confused than before.
The CEO's gnomic email, which simply said 'Change is coming', sent the whole office into a panic.
Students struggled to interpret the philosopher's gnomic fragments, each only a sentence or two long.
The central bank's gnomic statements are carefully worded to avoid unsettling the markets.
Her gnomic reply, 'Some doors close for a reason', left him unsure whether she was ending things.
tc: The old monk's teachings were ______: brief, riddle-like sayings that his disciples spent years trying to decode.
The phrase after the colon, 'brief, riddle-like sayings', defines the blank.
se: The poet's ______ final line has been debated by critics for decades.
cryptic
Both 'gnomic' and 'cryptic' describe brief wording whose meaning is hard to pin down.

m: very light, thin, and delicate
x: She wore a gossamer scarf that floated behind her in the evening breeze.
The designers chose gossamer curtains for the new office so that natural light could pour in.
Under the microscope, the insect's gossamer wings revealed an intricate network of veins.
Engineers have developed a gossamer fabric that is lighter than paper yet remarkably strong.
After the argument, their friendship felt gossamer-thin, as though one more harsh word might tear it.
tc: Unlike the thick wool curtains in the living room, the bedroom drapes were ______, so thin that sunlight passed straight through them.
The contrast with 'thick wool' and 'so thin that sunlight passed through' define the blank as delicate and light.
se: The bride's ______ veil fluttered in the gentle evening breeze.
gauzy
Both 'gossamer' and 'gauzy' describe fabric that is thin, light and delicate.

m: to behave showily in order to impress onlookers or win approval
x: Instead of helping fix the leak, my neighbour grandstanded about it at every residents' meeting.
He tends to grandstand in meetings, repeating other people's ideas loudly as if they were his own.
Our professor warned that students who grandstand in seminars rarely impress the examiners.
Several senators used the hearing to grandstand for the cameras rather than question the witnesses.
She was tired of her boyfriend grandstanding in front of her friends instead of just being himself.
tc: Rather than quietly negotiating a solution, the councillor chose to ______ before the television crews, making dramatic promises he could not keep.
The contrast with 'quietly negotiating' and the 'dramatic promises' for cameras show showy behaviour.
se: Some lawyers like to ______ in front of the jury, waving documents and raising their voices.
showboat
Both 'grandstand' and 'showboat' mean to show off to impress an audience.

m: to complain or grumble, especially about something minor
x: My father grouses about the electricity bill every month but never switches off the fans.
Employees groused that the new open-plan office made it impossible to concentrate.
Students always grouse about the cafeteria food, yet its queue is the longest on campus.
Farmers have groused for years about the low prices paid by middlemen in the city markets.
Instead of grousing about your roommate, why not just talk to him honestly?
tc: Though he loved his job, he couldn't help but ______ about the endless paperwork that kept him from teaching.
'Though he loved his job' signals a contrast, so the blank means to complain.
se: Passengers continued to ______ about the delay long after the train had finally departed.
grumble
Both 'grouse' and 'grumble' mean to complain in a discontented way.

m: strong and healthy, especially of an older person
x: At eighty-five, my grandfather is still hale enough to walk to the mosque five times a day.
Our hale old caretaker still climbs the office stairs faster than most of the young staff.
The study found that hale older adults who exercised regularly performed better in memory tests.
Photographs of the hale former governor at the rally helped quiet rumours about his health.
She came back from the holiday looking hale and hearty, and her friends were relieved to see her smile.
tc: Despite his advanced age, the retired general remained ______, hiking in the mountains every summer.
'Despite his advanced age' and 'hiking in the mountains' show he stayed strong and healthy.
se: Though nearly ninety, the old fisherman was still ______ and hauled in his nets every morning.
vigorous
Both 'hale' and 'vigorous' describe an old person who is still strong and active.

m: regarded as holy or greatly respected; sacred
x: For cricket fans, Lord's is hallowed ground, and visiting it was a dream come true for me.
Our office treats the founder's original desk as a hallowed relic that no one may touch.
She walked through the hallowed halls of the old university library, awed by its silence.
The ceremony was held at a hallowed memorial where thousands of soldiers are buried.
Sunday lunch with the whole family was a hallowed tradition in our house.
tc: To the villagers the ancient banyan tree was ______, and anyone who harmed it was accused of sacrilege.
Harming it counts as 'sacrilege', so the tree must be regarded as holy.
se: The old stadium is ______ ground for the club's supporters.
sacred
Both 'hallowed' and 'sacred' describe a place treated with deep reverence.

m: a bossy, bad-tempered old woman who constantly scolds
x: In the play, the landlady is a shrieking harridan who yells at her tenants from the stairs.
Unfairly, the strict office manager was dismissed as a harridan by junior staff behind her back.
The novel's heroine escapes from her aunt, a cruel harridan who keeps her locked indoors.
Critics note that older women in films are too often portrayed as either saints or harridans.
He feared his mother-in-law would be a harridan, but she turned out to be warm and funny.
tc: The children were terrified of their neighbour, an elderly ______ who scolded anyone who stepped near her garden.
'Elderly' and 'scolded anyone' define the blank as a bad-tempered, scolding old woman.
se: In the old comedy, the hero's wife is portrayed as a nagging ______ who criticizes his every move.
shrew
Both 'harridan' and 'shrew' name a bad-tempered, scolding woman.

m: haughty, proud arrogance of manner
x: The waiter at the expensive restaurant treated our questions about the menu with icy hauteur.
Her hauteur in meetings alienated colleagues who might otherwise have supported her ideas.
The visiting professor's hauteur toward undergraduates made his lectures deeply unpopular.
Voters were put off by the candidate's aristocratic hauteur and his refusal to visit poorer districts.
Behind his hauteur, she sensed a shy man who was terrified of being rejected.
tc: The duchess looked down at the servants with such ______ that they felt utterly beneath her notice.
'Looked down at' and 'beneath her notice' point to proud arrogance.
se: The critic's ______ toward popular novels won him few friends among ordinary readers.
arrogance
Both 'hauteur' and 'arrogance' mean a proud, superior attitude toward others.

m: to bully or intimidate someone with loud, aggressive talk
x: My older brother used to hector me into doing his chores by threatening to reveal my secrets.
The manager hectored his team for an hour about missed targets, which only lowered morale further.
No student learns well when a teacher hectors them in front of the whole class.
The interviewer hectored the minister, interrupting every answer before it was complete.
She refused to be hectored into marrying someone her relatives had chosen for her.
tc: Rather than gently persuading the witness, the lawyer chose to ______ him, shouting questions until he broke down.
The contrast with 'gently persuading' and 'shouting questions' show the blank means to bully aggressively.
se: The coach would ______ his players whenever they lost, screaming insults from the sideline.
bully
Both 'hector' and 'bully' mean to intimidate people with loud, harsh words.

m: the period of greatest success, popularity, or vigour
x: In its heyday, this old cinema hall in Old Dhaka drew huge crowds every night.
The typewriter company employed thousands of workers in its heyday during the 1960s.
During the heyday of the Silk Road, scholars travelled thousands of miles to study in distant cities.
Newspapers in their heyday could shape public opinion in a way social media does today.
My parents love to talk about their heyday, when they danced until dawn at family weddings.
tc: The town, now quiet and half-empty, was once a thriving port; in its ______, ships from across the world crowded its harbour.
The contrast between 'now quiet' and 'once a thriving port' shows the blank means its period of greatest success.
se: In her ______, the singer filled stadiums across the country.
prime
Both 'heyday' and 'prime' mean the period of someone's greatest success.

m: like a sermon; preachy and moralizing in tone
x: My uncle's homiletic speeches at family dinners always end with a lesson about saving money.
The manager's homiletic email on punctuality annoyed staff who had never once been late.
The book's homiletic tone undermines its research, since every chapter ends with a moral lesson.
Critics found the documentary too homiletic, lecturing viewers instead of letting the facts speak.
She wanted sympathy, not his homiletic advice about learning from her mistakes.
tc: The novel was meant to entertain, but readers found it disappointingly ______, as if the author were delivering a sermon on every page.
'As if the author were delivering a sermon' defines the blank as preachy.
se: His ______ graduation speech, full of moral lessons, bored most of the students.
preachy
Both 'homiletic' and 'preachy' describe a speech that lectures listeners on morals.

m: to deceive or trick someone
x: Some rickshaw drivers hoodwink tourists into paying triple the usual fare.
A clerk hoodwinked the accounts department for years with fake invoices.
Students who copy essays from the internet rarely hoodwink experienced examiners.
Thousands of investors were hoodwinked by a scheme that promised impossibly high returns.
She felt hurt and foolish when she discovered he had hoodwinked her about his past.
tc: The con artist managed to ______ dozens of elderly victims, persuading them to hand over their savings for a fake investment.
'Con artist' and 'fake investment' show the blank means to deceive.
se: The forger was skilled enough to ______ even expert art dealers.
dupe
Both 'hoodwink' and 'dupe' mean to trick someone into believing something false.

m: opposed to freedom of thought or behaviour; narrow-minded and intolerant
x: My landlord's illiberal rules forbid any guests after nine, even on weekends.
The company's illiberal dress code even dictates the colour of employees' socks.
Some universities have been accused of illiberal attempts to silence unpopular speakers.
Observers warned that the new media law marked a worrying illiberal turn for the country.
He was hurt by his parents' illiberal views about whom he should be allowed to marry.
tc: Though the government claimed to champion free expression, its ______ policies shut down independent newspapers one after another.
'Though... claimed to champion free expression' signals a contrast, so the policies were intolerant of freedom.
se: Thousands of citizens protested the ______ new laws restricting public assembly.
repressive
Both 'illiberal' and 'repressive' describe laws that restrict people's freedoms.

m: without limits or boundaries; limitless
x: Standing on the beach at Cox's Bazar as a child, I thought the sea was illimitable.
Our new manager seems to have an illimitable appetite for meetings.
Astronomers once believed the universe to be illimitable in both space and time.
Investors' appetite for the new technology seemed illimitable until the market suddenly crashed.
Her patience with her younger brother appeared illimitable, no matter how often he teased her.
tc: Unlike the cramped city streets he had grown up with, the desert seemed ______, stretching endlessly toward the horizon.
The contrast with 'cramped' and 'stretching endlessly' define the blank as limitless.
se: The young inventor's supply of new ideas seemed ______.
boundless
Both 'illimitable' and 'boundless' mean having no limit.

m: filled with or showing intense feeling
x: She made an impassioned plea to her parents to let her study abroad.
After an impassioned debate, the board voted to keep the old factory open.
The student's impassioned defence of her thesis impressed even the most sceptical examiner.
Activists delivered impassioned speeches outside parliament demanding cleaner air for the city.
His impassioned letter, written at two in the morning, finally convinced her to give him another chance.
tc: Unlike his usual dry, monotone lectures, the professor's farewell address was ______, and several students were moved to tears.
The contrast with 'dry, monotone' and 'moved to tears' show the speech was full of emotion.
se: The lawyer's ______ appeal to the jury left several of them in tears.
fervent
Both 'impassioned' and 'fervent' describe an appeal full of intense feeling.

m: persistent in making requests or demands, to the point of being annoying
x: Importunate vendors followed us down the beach, insisting that we buy shell necklaces.
She ignored the importunate emails from a supplier demanding an immediate meeting.
The professor finally granted the importunate student an extension just to stop his daily visits.
Politicians often complain about importunate lobbyists who wait for hours outside their offices.
His importunate phone calls after the breakup made her feel harassed rather than loved.
tc: The ______ salesman refused to leave the doorstep, repeating his offer again and again despite our firm refusals.
'Refused to leave' and 'again and again despite our firm refusals' show annoying persistence.
se: Tired of her ______ requests for money, her brother finally stopped answering her calls.
insistent
Both 'importunate' and 'insistent' describe requests repeated so often they become tiresome.

m: the act of deceiving others by pretending to be someone else
x: The man's imposture as a bank official fooled several elderly customers.
His imposture was exposed when HR discovered that his engineering degree had been forged.
Archived letters reveal the scholar's long imposture as an expert in Sanskrit.
Police uncovered the imposture after the fake doctor prescribed a dangerous dose to a patient.
She felt that her confidence at work was an imposture and feared her colleagues would see through it.
tc: For three years he posed as a licensed surgeon, and his ______ was discovered only when a patient checked the medical register.
'Posed as a licensed surgeon' defines the blank as pretending to be someone else.
se: The spy's ______ as a diplomat lasted for nearly a decade.
impersonation
Both 'imposture' and 'impersonation' mean falsely pretending to be someone.

m: dishonesty; lack of moral integrity
x: The shop's improbity became clear when customers noticed that its scales were rigged.
An internal audit uncovered years of financial improbity in the purchasing department.
The university dismissed the researcher for improbity after he fabricated laboratory results.
Public anger grew as reports of improbity among senior officials filled the newspapers.
Her husband's improbity in money matters slowly destroyed her trust in him.
tc: Once famous for his honesty, the judge was disgraced when evidence of his ______, including bribes accepted over many years, came to light.
The contrast with 'famous for his honesty' and the mention of bribes show the blank means dishonesty.
se: The inquiry found no evidence of ______ on the part of the treasurer.
dishonesty
Both 'improbity' and 'dishonesty' mean a lack of honesty or integrity.

m: not suitable or relevant in the circumstances; out of place
x: His joke about funerals was wildly inapposite at his niece's birthday party.
The lawyer argued that the precedent cited by the other side was inapposite to this case.
My supervisor said the quotation in my introduction was interesting but inapposite to my argument.
Critics called the minister's comparison of the protests to a war both inapposite and inflammatory.
She found his cheerful message inapposite, given that she had just told him about her father's illness.
tc: Although the speaker's statistics were accurate, they were ______, since they concerned a completely different industry from the one under discussion.
'Concerned a completely different industry' shows the figures were not relevant.
se: The judge ruled that the defence's analogy was ______ and could not guide her decision.
irrelevant
Both 'inapposite' and 'irrelevant' mean not applicable to the matter at hand.

m: to accuse someone or show that they are guilty of wrongdoing
x: The fingerprints on the broken window inculpated the neighbour's teenage son.
The leaked emails inculpated two senior managers in the bribery scheme.
The study's data appeared to inculpate a common food additive in the rise of childhood allergies.
Prosecutors hoped the witness's testimony would inculpate the leader of the gang.
Afraid of inculpating her best friend, she refused to say who had broken the vase.
tc: Instead of clearing the suspect as his lawyer had hoped, the new video evidence seemed to ______ him even further.
'Instead of clearing the suspect' signals the opposite, so the blank means to show him guilty.
se: The accountant feared that the missing records would ______ him in the fraud.
implicate
Both 'inculpate' and 'implicate' mean to show someone is involved in wrongdoing.

m: not in keeping with good taste or proper behaviour; improper
x: Shouting into your phone on a crowded bus is rather indecorous.
His indecorous remarks at the office party led to a formal warning from HR.
At many universities it is considered indecorous for students to address professors by their first names.
The senator's indecorous behaviour during the memorial service caused a public outcry.
She thought it indecorous to discuss her salary with friends, so she changed the subject.
tc: In a temple where visitors spoke only in whispers, his loud laughter seemed shockingly ______.
The contrast between whispering visitors and 'loud laughter' shows his behaviour was improper.
se: Many guests thought it ______ for the bride's uncle to dance on the table.
unseemly
Both 'indecorous' and 'unseemly' mean not fitting for the occasion or proper behaviour.

m: impossible to doubt; unquestionable
x: It is an indubitable fact that Dhaka traffic gets even worse during the monsoon.
Her indubitable talent for negotiation earned her a promotion within a year.
The clinical trial provided indubitable proof that the vaccine was effective.
Historians consider the letters indubitable evidence that the treaty was signed under pressure.
His love for her was indubitable, even if he was hopeless at expressing it.
tc: Unlike earlier studies, whose conclusions were hotly disputed, this one offered ______ evidence that no serious scientist could challenge.
The contrast with 'hotly disputed' and 'no serious scientist could challenge' show the evidence was beyond doubt.
se: The DNA results were ______ proof of the suspect's presence at the scene.
undeniable
Both 'indubitable' and 'undeniable' mean impossible to doubt or dispute.

m: failing to produce the intended result; lacking the ability to get things done
x: My attempts to stop the leaking tap with tape proved completely ineffectual.
The team's ineffectual manager let problems pile up until the project collapsed.
Our ineffectual study group spent more time chatting than reviewing for the exam.
Critics called the new traffic rules ineffectual, pointing out that congestion had only got worse.
He felt ineffectual and helpless as he watched his closest friend struggle with depression.
tc: Despite countless meetings and warnings, the committee's response was ______, and the pollution continued unchecked.
'The pollution continued unchecked' shows the response failed to have any effect.
se: The government's ______ efforts to curb inflation frustrated ordinary families.
ineffective
Both 'ineffectual' and 'ineffective' describe efforts that fail to achieve their goal.

m: lack of fairness or justice; an unfair situation
x: My sister complained about the inequity of doing all the housework while our brothers played cricket.
Employees protested the inequity in pay between men and women doing the same job.
Her research examines inequity in access to higher education across rural districts.
The report highlighted growing inequity in healthcare between rich and poor neighbourhoods.
He resented the inequity in their friendship, in which he always gave and she always took.
tc: Workers were outraged by the ______ of a system that gave huge bonuses to executives while cutting their own wages.
Rewarding executives while cutting workers' wages describes an unfair situation.
se: The new policy aims to reduce the ______ in school funding between wealthy and poor areas.
inequality
Both 'inequity' and 'inequality' describe an unfair gap in funding between areas.

m: so wrong that it can never be atoned for or forgiven
x: Forgetting my mother's birthday felt like an inexpiable sin, though she forgave me by dinner.
For the law firm, leaking a client's confidential data was an inexpiable breach of trust.
In our ethics seminar, we debated whether any act is truly inexpiable.
Survivors of the massacre still regard it as an inexpiable crime that no apology can undo.
He carried the inexpiable guilt of the accident with him for the rest of his life.
tc: The betrayal was so grave that the old man considered it ______; no apology or act of penance could ever make amends.
'No apology or act of penance could ever make amends' defines the blank.
se: To the grieving family, the driver's decision to flee the scene seemed ______.
unforgivable
Both 'inexpiable' and 'unforgivable' describe an act that can never be pardoned.

m: unfortunate or inappropriate, especially in wording or timing
x: Wearing a white dress to someone else's wedding was an infelicitous choice.
The CEO's infelicitous remark about 'trimming dead wood' upset the entire workforce.
My editor circled several infelicitous phrases in my thesis that obscured its argument.
The minister apologized for his infelicitous comparison of flood victims to beggars.
She immediately regretted her infelicitous joke about his weight, which clearly hurt him.
tc: The translation was accurate but ______, full of awkward phrases that no native speaker would ever use.
'Accurate but' and 'full of awkward phrases' show the wording was poorly chosen.
se: The spokesperson's ______ choice of words turned a minor issue into a major scandal.
unfortunate
Both 'infelicitous' and 'unfortunate' describe a badly chosen, inappropriate phrase.

m: an ungrateful person
x: We spent a whole weekend helping him move house, and the ingrate didn't even say thank you.
After his mentor got him promoted, he criticized her publicly, and colleagues called him an ingrate.
Not wanting to seem an ingrate, the scholarship student wrote a long thank-you letter to the donors.
The tycoon's memoir portrays his former employees as ingrates who forgot his generosity.
My aunt raised me after my parents died, and I would be an ingrate to forget her sacrifices.
tc: Despite all the sacrifices his parents had made for his education, he never once thanked them, behaving like the worst kind of ______.
'Never once thanked them' despite their sacrifices points to an ungrateful person.
se: Having accepted their hospitality for a month, he left without a word of thanks, like a true ______.
churl
In this context both 'ingrate' and 'churl' describe someone rudely ungrateful for kindness received.

m: lacking physical sensation or feeling; unconscious or unfeeling
x: After the dentist's injection, my jaw was insensate for nearly three hours.
My boss seemed insensate to the stress his constant demands were causing the team.
Medical students practised suturing on insensate rubber models before working with real patients.
Rescuers found the climber lying insensate in the snow and airlifted him to hospital.

debatable

m: a charlatan who tricks people, especially to get their money
x: The man selling miracle hair oil at the bus station was clearly a mountebank.
The so-called consultant turned out to be a mountebank who had invented his entire resume.
The historian described how traveling mountebanks sold fake medicines at medieval fairs.
The financial adviser was exposed as a mountebank after his clients lost their life savings.
She felt foolish for trusting a mountebank who had promised to cure her mother's illness.
tc: Though he claimed to be a qualified doctor, the man selling colored water as a cure was exposed as the worst kind of ______.
'Claimed to be a qualified doctor' while 'selling colored water as a cure' points to a fraud.
se: The villagers eventually exposed the faith healer as the ______ he was, after his cures failed again and again.
charlatan
Both 'mountebank' and 'charlatan' mean a deceitful fraud, so the sentence means the same.

m: stubborn and unreasonable
x: My son turns mulish whenever I suggest he eat his vegetables.
The project stalled because of the director's mulish refusal to consider any other designs.
The student's mulish insistence that his answer was correct annoyed the examiner.
Negotiators complained about the mulish stance of both parties, which made compromise impossible.
Her mulish pride kept her from apologizing, even though she knew she was wrong.
tc: No amount of reasoning could move him; he remained ______ in his refusal to change his plans.
'No amount of reasoning could move him' defines stubbornness.
se: Her ______ refusal to listen to advice cost her the best job offer she had ever received.
stubborn
Both 'mulish' and 'stubborn' mean unreasonably obstinate, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: the quality of being likely to change
x: The mutability of the weather in spring means you should always carry an umbrella.
The mutability of market demand makes long-term planning difficult for small firms.
Her paper explores the mutability of language, showing how word meanings shift over centuries.
Scientists are studying the mutability of the virus to predict which new strains may emerge.
As he grew older, he came to accept the mutability of friendships and stopped mourning lost ones.
tc: Fashion is defined by its ______; what is popular this season will almost certainly be out of style next year.
The clause after the semicolon explains that fashion constantly changes.
se: The poet often reflects on the ______ of human affairs, reminding readers that nothing lasts forever.
changeability
Both 'mutability' and 'changeability' mean the tendency to change, so the sentence means the same.

m: lack of foresight or long-term thinking; shortsightedness
x: Spending my entire bonus in a week was a classic case of financial myopia.
The company's myopia about online sales left it far behind its competitors.
The study blamed policy myopia for the country's failure to invest in early-childhood education.
Environmental groups criticized the government's myopia in approving new coal plants.
His emotional myopia meant he never noticed how unhappy his wife had become.
tc: Focused only on next quarter's profits, the board's ______ left the company unprepared for long-term change.
'Focused only on next quarter's profits' and 'unprepared for long-term change' describe a lack of foresight.
se: Economists blamed the government's ______ for its failure to plan for an aging population.
shortsightedness
Both 'myopia' and 'shortsightedness' mean a failure to think ahead, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a person who claims to communicate with the dead, often to predict the future; a sorcerer
x: My little sister loves fantasy games, and her favorite character is a necromancer who raises skeleton armies.
Joking about the impossible deadline, my boss said we would need a necromancer to revive the dead project.
The lecture explored why people in medieval Europe feared necromancers who claimed to summon spirits.
In some old societies, villagers paid a local necromancer to consult their ancestors about the coming harvest.
In his grief, he even considered visiting a necromancer to speak with his late wife once more.
tc: In the legend, the ______ summoned the spirits of dead kings to reveal where their treasure was buried.
'Summoned the spirits of dead kings' to learn secrets defines a necromancer.
se: The old ______ claimed he could raise the dead with a single spell.
sorcerer
Both 'necromancer' and 'sorcerer' name a practitioner of dark magic, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a newly invented word or expression
x: My niece fills her text messages with neologisms that I have to look up online.
Corporate neologisms like 'upskilling' spread through the office faster than any memo.
Linguists track neologisms to understand how language responds to new technology.
The dictionary added several pandemic-era neologisms this year, including 'doomscrolling'.
He invented a little neologism for their shared habit of eating dessert first, and she loved it.
tc: When no existing word could describe the phenomenon, the scientist invented the ______ that is now found in every textbook.
'No existing word' and 'invented' show the blank is a newly created word.
se: The word 'selfie' started life as an internet ______ but is now ordinary English.
coinage
Both 'neologism' and 'coinage' mean a newly invented word, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: lack of knowledge or awareness; ignorance
x: His nescience about household finances surprised his wife, who had assumed he knew how to pay the bills.
The new manager's nescience of local customs led to several awkward meetings with suppliers.
Socrates argued that recognizing one's own nescience is the beginning of wisdom.
Scientists warn that public nescience about vaccines allows misinformation to spread more easily.
She found his nescience of her feelings hard to forgive after all their years together.
tc: The candidate's ______ of basic economics was exposed when he could not explain what inflation means.
'Could not explain what inflation means' shows a lack of knowledge.
se: The professor was shocked by the students' ______ of even the most famous events in their nation's history.
ignorance
Both 'nescience' and 'ignorance' mean lack of knowledge, so the sentence means the same.

m: a person or thing that has no equal
x: My mother is a nonpareil in the kitchen; nobody makes biryani quite like her.
In the world of contract law, she is regarded as a nonpareil whom every firm tries to hire.
The physicist was a nonpareil among his generation, winning every major prize in the field.
For years the batsman was the nonpareil of Bangladeshi cricket, admired even by his rivals.
To him, she was simply a nonpareil, the most remarkable person he had ever known.
tc: Unrivaled by any other pianist of her era, she was considered the true ______ of the concert stage.
'Unrivaled by any other pianist' defines someone without equal.
se: Many critics regarded the novelist as the ______ of her generation, a writer with no true equal.
paragon
Both 'nonpareil' and 'paragon' mean an unmatched, model example, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: in a way that is widely known, usually for something bad
x: He is notoriously bad at remembering birthdays, so his friends no longer take offense.
Our IT department is notoriously slow to respond to requests for new equipment.
Predicting earthquakes is notoriously difficult, even with the most advanced computer models.
Dhaka's traffic is notoriously bad, especially during the monsoon season.
The bus to her office is notoriously unreliable, so she usually leaves an hour early.
tc: The mountain road is ______ dangerous; every year several vehicles plunge off its sharp bends.
The clause after the semicolon shows the road's danger is well known from repeated accidents.
se: The airline is ______ unreliable, with delays and cancellations that have angered travelers for years.
infamously
Both 'notoriously' and 'infamously' mean widely known for something bad, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: of no value or importance; useless or having no force
x: My efforts to keep the cat off the sofa proved nugatory; she simply waited until I left the room.
The new rule, passed without any warning, rendered our earlier agreement with the landlord completely nugatory.
The reviewer dismissed the study's contribution as nugatory, since it merely repeated earlier findings.
Without proper enforcement, the new environmental law will be nugatory.
His apology felt nugatory to her after so many broken promises.
tc: Because the court later ruled the contract invalid, all the clauses the lawyers had argued over became ______.
'Ruled the contract invalid' means the clauses lost all force and value.
se: Without funding to enforce it, the anti-pollution law is essentially ______.
worthless
Both 'nugatory' and 'worthless' mean having no real value or effect, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to push oneself or one's ideas on others in an unwelcome way
x: I didn't want to obtrude on their family dinner, so I waited outside.
A good manager offers guidance without obtruding her own opinions on every decision.
In a strong thesis, the writer's personal biases should not obtrude on the analysis.
Critics warn that commercial interests increasingly obtrude on scientific research, shaping which questions get studied.
He tried not to let his jealousy obtrude when she talked about her old friends.
tc: A tactful guest would never ______ his political views on the hosts at a family celebration.
'Tactful' and 'never' indicate the blank means forcing one's views on others unwelcomely.
se: The author is careful not to ______ her own opinions on the reader, letting the characters speak for themselves.
impose
Both 'obtrude' and 'impose' mean to force something on others, so the sentence means the same.

m: a blockage or closing of a passage, pipe, or blood vessel
x: The plumber found that the slow drain was caused by an occlusion of hair and soap deep in the pipe.
Engineers at the plant traced the pressure drop to an occlusion in the main cooling pipe.
Medical students learn to recognize the warning signs of an occlusion of the retinal artery.
Doctors confirmed that a blood clot had caused a complete occlusion of the artery, triggering the stroke.
Her grandfather's sudden stroke, caused by an arterial occlusion, brought the scattered family back together.
tc: Blood could no longer reach the lower leg because of the ______ in the main artery, so surgeons had to clear it immediately.
'Blood could no longer reach' and 'had to clear it' point to a blockage.
se: The scan revealed a partial ______ of the artery, which explained the patient's chest pain.
blockage
Both 'occlusion' and 'blockage' mean an obstruction, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: general or widespread hatred and disgust, and the disgrace that comes with it
x: The driver who blocked the narrow lane for an hour earned the odium of the entire neighborhood.
The manager earned the odium of his staff by taking credit for their work.
The study traces how the odium once attached to divorce has faded over two generations.
The government faced public odium after officials were caught stealing flood relief funds.
She could not bear the odium of her relatives after she broke off the engagement.
tc: The banker who profited from the crisis became an object of public ______, despised by the very people he had ruined.
'Despised by the very people he had ruined' restates widespread hatred.
se: The senator's corruption brought him the ______ of voters who had once admired him.
contempt
Both 'odium' and 'contempt' mean strong public disapproval and dislike, so the sentence means the same.

m: excessively flattering in an oily, insincere way
x: The oleaginous salesman complimented my taste so often that I left without buying anything.
Everyone in the office was tired of his oleaginous praise of the boss at every meeting.
The student's oleaginous email begged the professor for a better grade with lavish flattery.
Reporters mocked the minister's oleaginous speech welcoming the foreign investors.
She found her sister's new boyfriend oleaginous, all smiles and compliments that never seemed sincere.
tc: The waiter's ______ manner, full of flattery and fawning bows, made the guests feel more uncomfortable than welcome.
'Full of flattery and fawning bows' defines an oily, ingratiating manner.
se: The ambassador's ______ flattery of the king embarrassed the rest of the delegation.
unctuous
Both 'oleaginous' and 'unctuous' mean oily and insincerely flattering, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to state one's opinion, often freely or without being asked
x: My aunt likes to opine on everyone's marriage prospects at family weddings.
In the meeting, the new intern was asked to opine on the redesigned website.
Students were asked to opine on whether the novel's ending was hopeful or tragic.
Television pundits opine endlessly about elections they know very little about.
Her mother opined that he was not good enough for her, which only made her love him more.
tc: Though he had never visited the country, the commentator was happy to ______ at length on its politics.
The contrast with 'never visited' shows he freely gave opinions he had little basis for.
se: Everyone at the dinner table felt free to ______ on how the young couple should raise their child.
comment
'Opine on' and 'comment on' both mean to give one's views, so the sentence means the same.

m: taking advantage of situations for personal gain without regard for principles
x: My cousin's sudden friendliness when he heard I had bought a car looked like pure opportunism.
Colleagues accused him of opportunism after he switched teams just before the layoffs.
The historian argued that the alliance was driven by opportunism rather than shared ideals.
Voters grew tired of the opportunism of politicians who changed parties before every election.
She realized his affection was mere opportunism when he vanished as soon as her money ran out.
tc: The politician switched parties three times in five years, a record of ______ that left voters doubting he believed in anything.
Switching parties repeatedly and seeming to believe in nothing points to unprincipled self-interest.
se: Critics said the company's sudden interest in environmental causes was pure ______, aimed only at winning new customers.
self-interest
Both 'opportunism' and 'self-interest' describe acting only for one's own gain, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: (of a voice or speech) full, rich, and imposing; sometimes pompous
x: My grandfather recited poems in an orotund voice that filled the whole house.
The chairman's orotund speech at the annual meeting impressed shareholders but said little of substance.
The professor's orotund lectures were famous for their rolling sentences and dramatic pauses.
The newsreader's orotund delivery gave even minor stories an air of great importance.
She teased him gently about the orotund way he read her love letters aloud.

'Deep and rich' and carrying to the back of the theater describe a full, imposing voice.
se: The old preacher's ______ voice filled the vast church from end to end.
sonorous
Both 'orotund' and 'sonorous' describe a full, deep, resonant voice, so the sentence means the same.

m: having become rigid and fixed in attitudes or habits, and unable to change or adapt

Critics argued that the department's curriculum had grown ossified, still teaching methods the field abandoned decades ago.
Reformers warned that an ossified bureaucracy would never respond quickly enough to a public health emergency.
She worried that their marriage had become ossified, a set of polite habits rather than a living partnership.

'Far from being open to new ideas' and the automatic rejection of every proposal point to a word meaning rigid and unchanging.
se: The party's leadership had grown ______, clinging to policies that no longer matched voters' concerns.
rigid
Both 'ossified' and 'rigid' describe leaders stuck in fixed ways and unable to adapt.

m: serving no practical purpose; unnecessary or futile

In her thesis, she argued that the extra variable was otiose because it explained none of the observed variation.
Some lawmakers called the proposed committee otiose, since three existing agencies already did the same work.
After the apology had been made, any further argument between the two friends seemed otiose.

se: With the automated system now handling all bookings, the manual ledger has become ______.
redundant
Both 'otiose' and 'redundant' mean no longer needed, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: to try to do more than one can manage, or to go beyond the limits of one's authority

overstep
Both 'overreach' and 'overstep' mean to go beyond the limits of one's authority.

m: a song, speech, or piece of writing expressing enthusiastic praise

The professor's new book is less a history of the railway than a paean to the engineers who built it.
The documentary has been criticized as a paean to the industry rather than an honest investigation of it.

tribute
Both 'paean' and 'tribute' mean an expression of praise and honour, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

fuss
Both 'palaver' and 'fuss' mean tiresome, drawn-out bother, contrasted with the quick online process.

m: to become less interesting or appealing through familiarity or excess

As the campaign dragged on, the candidate's slogans palled and audiences began to drift away.
Her jokes, so charming on their first date, had palled by the end of their second year together.

se: The excitement of the new job started to ______ once the work became routine.
wane
Both 'pall' and 'wane' mean to weaken or lose appeal, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: stylish, confident flair in the way one does things

The young lecturer explained thermodynamics with a panache that kept even the back rows awake.
The opener batted with panache at Mirpur, hitting three sixes in the first over of the match.
What attracted her to him was not his looks but the panache with which he laughed off his own mistakes.

flair
Both 'panache' and 'flair' mean confident style, so the actor's delivery is described the same way.

m: a particular way of speaking or set of words used by a specific group

The contrast between the medical term and what people ordinarily say shows the blank means a way of speaking.

jargon
Both 'parlance' and 'jargon' refer to the special vocabulary of a group, here the military.

m: unfair bias in favour of one person, group, or side

The referee's obvious partiality toward the home team angered the visiting supporters.
Even as children, the twins resented any sign of partiality from their parents.

favoritism
Both 'partiality' and 'favoritism' mean unfairly preferring certain people, so the criticism is the same.

m: a person who has suddenly gained wealth or status but is seen as lacking refinement

The novel's hero is a parvenu who buys a country estate but cannot master the manners that come with it.

tc: The established families sneered at every ______ who arrived with new money but none of their inherited manners.
'New money' without 'inherited manners' defines someone newly rich but unrefined.
se: The aristocrats snubbed the merchant as the kind of ______ whose wealth was too recent to be respectable.
upstart
Both 'parvenu' and 'upstart' mean someone who has risen suddenly and is looked down on for it.

m: having keen insight or understanding; perceptive
x: A percipient neighbour noticed that the old man's newspapers were piling up and called for help.

The professor praised the essay as the most percipient analysis of the novel she had read in years.
Percipient observers had predicted the housing bubble long before the banks admitted there was a problem.
Children are often more percipient than adults realise, sensing tension at home even when nobody argues openly.

'Unlike his colleagues, who missed the warning signs' contrasts them with someone sharply perceptive.
se: She is a remarkably ______ reader of people, often understanding their motives before they do.
perceptive
Both 'percipient' and 'perceptive' mean quick to notice and understand, so the sentence means the same.

m: the concluding part of a speech, usually meant to inspire or move the audience
x: In his peroration at the wedding, the best man finally stopped joking and spoke sincerely about friendship.
The CEO's peroration urged employees to see the merger as an opportunity rather than a threat.
Students of rhetoric study how a good peroration gathers the speech's arguments into one emotional appeal.
The candidate's stirring peroration brought the convention delegates to their feet.
She rehearsed the peroration of her farewell speech so often that she could say it with her eyes closed.
tc: After an hour of dry statistics, the speaker finally reached the ______, ending with a passionate call to action that moved the crowd.
'Finally reached' and 'ending with' show the blank refers to the closing part of the speech.
se: The lawyer's ______ reminded the jury once more of the victim's family waiting outside.
summation
Both 'peroration' and 'summation' mean the final part of an address, here the lawyer's closing words to the jury.

m: a benefit or privilege that comes with a job or position, in addition to salary

The new law limits the perquisites that government ministers can claim, including official cars and foreign trips.
For her, the greatest perquisite of retirement was finally having time to visit her grandchildren.
tc: Beyond her salary, the most valuable ______ of the post was a rent-free flat in the city centre.
'Beyond her salary' signals an extra benefit that comes with the job.
se: Free tuition for employees' children is one ______ that makes the job especially attractive.
perk
Both 'perquisite' and 'perk' mean an extra benefit of employment, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: light, playful teasing or banter
