The professor's lectures mixed serious analysis with a gentle persiflage that students enjoyed.
Commentators noted that the debate began with friendly persiflage before turning sharply hostile.
Beneath their constant persiflage, the two old friends clearly cared deeply for each other.
tc: The talk show host's light ______ kept the mood relaxed, though he never let his teasing become cruel.
'Light' and the later restatement 'his teasing' show the blank means playful banter.
se: Their friendly ______ about each other's football teams went on for most of the evening.
banter
Both 'persiflage' and 'banter' mean good-humoured teasing, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a person who quibbles over trivial details, especially a lawyer who uses petty or dishonest tactics
x: My landlord is a real pettifogger who once charged me for a scratch you could barely see.
The deal collapsed because a pettifogger in the legal department objected to every comma in the contract.
The reviewer was dismissed as a pettifogger who cared more about footnote formatting than about the argument itself.
In the novel, a small-town pettifogger wins cases by exploiting technicalities rather than proving facts.
She refused to argue with her brother over the bill, saying she would not become a pettifogger over twenty taka.
tc: Instead of addressing the substance of the case, the lawyer acted like the worst kind of ______, objecting to trivial technicalities for hours.
Ignoring the substance while 'objecting to trivial technicalities' defines a petty quibbler.
se: Nobody but the most tiresome ______ would reject an excellent proposal because of a single misplaced comma.
nitpicker
Both 'pettifogger' and 'nitpicker' mean someone who fusses over tiny details, so the sentence means the same.

m: a bitter, forceful speech or piece of writing attacking someone
x: After the neighbour's dog dug up her roses again, she delivered a philippic over the garden fence.
The director's email was a philippic against the sales team, blaming them for the company's losses.
In a philippic published in the journal, the professor attacked his rival's methods as careless and dishonest.
The opposition leader's philippic against corruption dominated the evening news.
When he finally came home at midnight, his wife greeted him with a philippic about broken promises.
tc: Far from offering mild criticism, the editorial was a scathing ______ that accused the minister of betraying the public.
'Far from offering mild criticism' and 'scathing' point to a bitter verbal attack.
se: The coach launched into a furious ______ against the referees after the match.
tirade
Both 'philippic' and 'tirade' mean an angry, sustained verbal attack.

m: petty, trivial, or of little value or importance
x: Let's not argue over something as picayune as who forgot to buy the milk.
The auditor spent days on picayune expense claims while ignoring the millions missing from the main account.
Reviewers called his objections picayune, since none of them affected the paper's central findings.
With the economy in crisis, voters had little patience for parliament's picayune squabbles over procedure.
Their marriage survived serious hardships but nearly ended over picayune quarrels about household chores.
tc: Compared with the serious safety problems at the factory, the inspector's complaint about faded paint seemed ______.
'Compared with the serious safety problems' contrasts real dangers with a trivial complaint.
se: The board wasted the entire meeting on ______ matters such as the colour of the new letterhead.
trivial
Both 'picayune' and 'trivial' mean unimportant, as the letterhead example shows.

m: pleasantly sharp or spicy in taste; also, stimulating and interesting
x: Grandmother's tamarind chutney has a piquant flavour that goes perfectly with fried snacks.
The speaker added a piquant anecdote about her first failed startup, and the audience instantly warmed to her.
The memoir offers piquant details about student life in the 1970s that no textbook would include.
Food scientists study why piquant spices such as chilli trigger a pleasurable burning sensation.
Their conversation had a piquant edge, full of teasing that hinted at something more than friendship.
tc: Unlike the bland soup served earlier, the second course came in a ______ sauce of lime, ginger and green chilli.
'Unlike the bland soup' and the sharp ingredients point to a word meaning pleasantly sharp or spicy.
se: A squeeze of lemon makes the otherwise mild curry pleasantly ______.
tangy
Both 'piquant' and 'tangy' describe a pleasantly sharp taste, contrasted with 'mild'.

m: the quality of expressing something briefly, clearly, and forcefully
x: My father's advice was famous for its pithiness: 'Study hard, sleep early, never lie.'
Her emails are admired across the office for their pithiness; she never uses ten words where three will do.
The examiner praised the essay's pithiness, noting that every sentence advanced the argument.
Political slogans owe much of their power to pithiness rather than to careful reasoning.
He loved her pithiness, since she could end any argument with a single well-chosen remark.
tc: Unlike his rambling predecessor, the new spokesman was known for the ______ of his statements, which rarely ran beyond two sentences.
'Unlike his rambling predecessor' and statements of two sentences point to brevity and force.
se: Readers loved the ______ of her columns, which made complex issues clear in a few hundred words.
conciseness
Both 'pithiness' and 'conciseness' mean saying a lot in few words.

m: complete and unlimited; also, attended by all the members of a group
x: Only a plenary meeting of the whole family, aunts and cousins included, could decide where we would spend Eid.
The board granted the new CEO plenary authority to restructure the company as she saw fit.
The conference opens with a plenary session at which all delegates hear the keynote address.
The constitution gives parliament plenary power over taxation, leaving the courts little room to intervene.
When she went abroad for treatment, she gave her brother plenary power to manage her affairs.
tc: Rather than giving the envoy only limited authority, the president granted him ______ powers to negotiate on the nation's behalf.
'Rather than ... only limited authority' signals the opposite: complete, unrestricted power.
se: The emergency law gives the governor ______ authority to close schools and offices.
full
Both 'plenary' and 'full' mean complete and unrestricted authority.

m: the quality of bending easily; also, readiness to be influenced or controlled by others
x: The bamboo's pliancy lets it bend in monsoon storms without snapping.
Management valued his pliancy, but his colleagues saw it as a lack of backbone.
Researchers tested the pliancy of the new polymer by bending it thousands of times.
Opposition parties criticized the regulator's pliancy in the face of pressure from large banks.
She mistook his pliancy for kindness until she realised he simply agreed with whoever spoke last.
tc: Unlike the brittle plastic that cracked at the first bend, the new material showed remarkable ______ even in freezing temperatures.
'Unlike the brittle plastic that cracked' contrasts it with a material that bends easily.
se: Leather that has been properly oiled regains its ______ and no longer cracks when folded.
suppleness
Both 'pliancy' and 'suppleness' mean the ability to bend without cracking.

m: a writer of inferior or trivial poetry
x: My uncle, a cheerful poetaster, insists on reading his rhymes aloud at every family wedding.
The magazine's editor rejected hundreds of submissions from poetasters hoping to see their names in print.
Literary historians have rescued some writers once dismissed as poetasters and shown their real merit.
The critic's review dismissed the prize-winner as a poetaster whose verses relied on clichés.
In her diary she called herself a mere poetaster, though her letters to him were full of lovely lines.
tc: The anthology was supposed to feature the century's finest poets, yet it included verses by every second-rate ______ with a famous friend.
'Second-rate' and the contrast with 'finest poets' point to an inferior poet.
se: Critics dismissed him as nothing but a third-rate ______ whose rhymes were as predictable as a greeting card.
versifier
Both 'poetaster' and 'versifier' here mean a writer of mediocre verse.

m: an irritatingly self-important, grand, or solemn manner
x: His pomposity at family gatherings, lecturing everyone about investments, makes his cousins roll their eyes.
The new director's pomposity, including his insistence on being called 'Sir', quickly alienated the staff.
The professor's prose suffers from pomposity, with simple ideas buried under grand Latin phrases.
Satirists have always delighted in puncturing the pomposity of politicians.
She fell for him partly because he had none of the pomposity she had found in other successful men.
tc: Despite his high rank, the general spoke with no ______ at all, chatting with junior soldiers as if they were old friends.
'Despite his high rank' and his friendly chatting show he lacked self-important airs.
se: The mayor's ______ made him an easy target for cartoonists.
pretentiousness
Both 'pomposity' and 'pretentiousness' mean a self-important manner that invites mockery.

m: a person who behaves affectedly to impress others, pretending to be something they are not
x: He carries a guitar everywhere, but everyone knows he's a poseur who can barely play three chords.
The office poseur talks constantly about strategy but has never delivered a single project on time.
Among graduate students, he was regarded as a poseur who quoted philosophers he had never actually read.
The art world, some critics argue, is full of poseurs who mistake obscurity for depth.
She realised he was a poseur when his stories about travelling the world kept changing.
tc: He claimed to be a wine expert, but when he could not tell red from white in a blind tasting, everyone saw him as the ______ he really was.
His false claim of expertise, exposed by the tasting, marks him as someone pretending to be what he is not.
se: Real climbers had no patience for the ______ who bought expensive gear but never left the café at the bottom of the mountain.
phony
Both 'poseur' and 'phony' mean someone who only pretends to be the real thing.

m: to base an argument, action, or belief on a particular foundation (usually 'predicate on')
x: Our weekend plans were predicated on good weather, so the storm forced us to stay home.
The entire business plan is predicated on the assumption that interest rates will stay low.
The researcher predicated her hypothesis on earlier studies of sleep and memory.
Critics say the policy is predicated on outdated data about population growth.
Their friendship was predicated on honesty, which made his lie all the more painful.
tc: It is unwise to ______ an entire investment strategy on a single year of unusually high returns.
The structure '______ a strategy on' a single year of data shows the blank means to base one thing on another.
se: The lawyer chose to ______ her defence on the unreliability of the only witness.
base
Both 'predicate' and 'base' mean to build an argument on a foundation, so the sentence means the same.

m: serving as an introduction; preliminary
x: After a few prefatory remarks about the weather, my father got to the point: he was selling the house.
In a short prefatory note, the CEO explained why the annual report would look different this year.
Readers who skip the prefatory chapter will miss the author's explanation of her methods.
The treaty's prefatory clauses set out the shared goals of the signatory nations.
She skipped any prefatory small talk and told him directly that she was moving to Canada.
tc: Before presenting her main argument, the author offers several ______ remarks explaining how the book came to be written.
'Before presenting her main argument' shows the remarks come first, as an introduction.
se: The speaker kept his ______ comments brief and moved quickly to the main topic.
introductory
Both 'prefatory' and 'introductory' describe comments made before the main topic.

m: giving a warning in advance of something about to happen
x: The dark clouds gathering over the river were premonitory signs of a monsoon storm.
Engineers ignored the premonitory creaks in the old bridge until a crack appeared in its main beam.
Medical students learn to recognise premonitory symptoms, such as sudden numbness, that may precede a stroke.
Some seismologists study premonitory tremors in the hope of predicting larger earthquakes.
She had a premonitory feeling of dread the morning before she received the bad news.
tc: The patient ignored the ______ headaches that warned of the illness to come, and only saw a doctor after he collapsed.
The restatement 'that warned of the illness to come' defines the blank as giving advance warning.
se: The small tremors proved to be ______ signals of the major earthquake that struck a week later.
ominous
Both 'premonitory' and 'ominous' describe signals warning of a coming disaster.

m: attractive or appealing in appearance or manner; making a good first impression
x: The flat was hardly prepossessing from the outside, but inside it was bright and spacious.
The candidate's prepossessing manner made an excellent impression on the interview panel.
Though the library building is not prepossessing, its collection of rare manuscripts is world-class.
The party chose a young and prepossessing candidate, hoping her charm would win over undecided voters.
He was not a prepossessing man, yet she found his gentle humour impossible to resist.
tc: The restaurant's shabby entrance was far from ______, yet the food inside was the best in town.
'Shabby' and the contrast with 'yet the food ... was the best' show the entrance was unattractive, so the blank means attractive.
se: With her ______ smile and easy confidence, she quickly won over the hiring committee.
engaging
Both 'prepossessing' and 'engaging' mean pleasing and attractive, explaining how she won people over.

m: the state of being first or most important
x: In our house, my grandmother's opinion has always held primacy over everyone else's.
The new strategy gives primacy to customer satisfaction rather than short-term profits.
The debate over the primacy of nature or nurture has occupied psychologists for over a century.
The court reaffirmed the primacy of the constitution over ordinary legislation.
For him, the primacy of his career meant that friends and family always came second.
tc: Although several factors contributed to the crisis, the report gives clear ______ to poor management, calling it the most important cause.
The restatement 'calling it the most important cause' defines the blank as first place in importance.
se: The company's founders insisted on the ______ of product quality over rapid growth.
precedence
Both 'primacy' and 'precedence' mean being ranked above something else in importance.

m: having value in proving something; serving as evidence
x: My sister's photo of the broken vase had real probative value when we argued over who was to blame.
The compliance team must decide whether the emails have any probative value before handing them to regulators.
Historians debate the probative weight of private diaries, which may reflect personal bias rather than fact.
The judge excluded the photograph because its probative value was outweighed by the risk of prejudice.
He kept her old letters as probative evidence that she had once loved him.
tc: Because the fingerprint was too smudged to be identified, the court ruled that it had no ______ value in the trial.
A fingerprint too smudged to identify cannot prove anything, so the blank means serving as proof.
se: The defence argued that the anonymous letter had little ______ weight and should be excluded.
evidentiary
Both 'probative' and 'evidentiary' describe the value of something as evidence.

m: indiscriminate; made up of many different things mixed without careful selection
x: My brother is a promiscuous reader, finishing a thriller one day and a book on astrophysics the next.
The consultant warned against the promiscuous use of jargon in reports meant for customers.
Her essay is a promiscuous mixture of history, gossip and philosophy that somehow works.
Doctors blame the promiscuous prescribing of antibiotics for the rise of drug-resistant bacteria.
He is so promiscuous with praise that his compliments have come to mean very little to her.
tc: Rather than choosing his sources carefully, the student made ______ use of anything he found online, reliable or not.
'Rather than choosing his sources carefully' and 'reliable or not' point to indiscriminate use.
se: The ______ use of pesticides has harmed bees as well as the pests that farmers wanted to kill.
indiscriminate
Both 'promiscuous' and 'indiscriminate' mean used without careful selection, so the sentence means the same.

m: the patterns of rhythm, stress, and intonation in poetry or speech, or the study of them
x: Even my toddler responds to the prosody of a lullaby long before she understands the words.
Voice-assistant engineers work hard to make the software's prosody sound less robotic.
Her dissertation analyses the prosody of Tagore's songs and how their rhythms shape meaning.
Neuroscientists have found that patients with certain brain injuries struggle to interpret the prosody of speech.
He could tell she was upset from the prosody of her voice, even though her words were polite.
tc: Although the poem's vocabulary is simple, its ______ is complex, with shifting rhythms and stresses that reward reading aloud.
'Shifting rhythms and stresses' restates what the blank refers to: the poem's patterns of rhythm and sound.
se: Students of classical poetry must master the rules of ______ before they can scan a line correctly.
versification
Both 'prosody' and 'versification' refer to the principles of metre and rhythm in verse.

m: playful in a mischievous way
x: My little nephew gave me a puckish grin just before hiding my phone in the rice jar.
In a puckish mood, the manager replaced everyone's chairs with exercise balls for April Fool's Day.
The professor's puckish asides kept even the dullest lecture on tax law entertaining.
The artist, known for his puckish sense of humour, hid a tiny cartoon mouse in every mural.
She loved his puckish way of teasing her, which never crossed the line into cruelty.
tc: Though the old judge appeared stern in court, friends knew him for his ______ sense of humour and love of practical jokes.
'Though ... stern' sets up a contrast, and 'love of practical jokes' points to mischievous playfulness.
se: The boy flashed a ______ smile that told his mother he had been up to something.
mischievous
Both 'puckish' and 'mischievous' describe a playful look that hints at harmless trouble.

m: lack of courage or determination; timidity
x: My pusillanimity about spiders means I still call my roommate whenever one appears in the bathroom.
The board's pusillanimity in the face of the scandal allowed the problem to grow for years.
The historian blames the war partly on the pusillanimity of leaders who failed to confront aggression early.
Editorials condemned the council's pusillanimity in refusing to stand up to powerful developers.
She regretted her pusillanimity in never telling him how she felt before he moved abroad.
tc: Rather than showing the courage the crisis demanded, the government displayed shameful ______, backing down at the first sign of opposition.
'Rather than showing the courage' and 'backing down at the first sign of opposition' point to cowardice.
se: Historians have criticized the general's ______ in retreating before the battle had even begun.
cowardice
Both 'pusillanimity' and 'cowardice' mean lack of courage, shown by retreating without a fight.

m: to decay or rot and give off a foul smell
x: We forgot the fish in the car during the heatwave, and by evening it had begun to putrefy.
When the refrigeration system failed, tonnes of meat putrefied in the warehouse before anyone noticed.
In the lab, students recorded how quickly the samples putrefied at different temperatures.
After the floods, health officials warned that animal carcasses left to putrefy could spread disease.
She felt that resentments left unspoken would only putrefy, slowly poisoning their friendship.
tc: Without refrigeration in the tropical heat, fresh fish will ______ within hours, giving off an unbearable smell.
Heat without refrigeration and 'an unbearable smell' point to rotting.
se: If the fruit is left in a damp, warm room, it will quickly ______.
rot
Both 'putrefy' and 'rot' mean to decay, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: (of a victory) won at such great cost that it is hardly better than a defeat
x: Our cricket team won the final, but it was a pyrrhic victory: three of our best players were injured.
The company won the lawsuit, but the enormous legal fees made it a pyrrhic victory.
Historians describe the battle as a pyrrhic triumph that left the army too weak to continue the campaign.
Economists warned that a budget surplus achieved by closing hospitals would be pyrrhic at best.
Winning the argument with my sister proved pyrrhic, since she refused to speak to me for a month.
tc: The general won the battle, but he lost so many soldiers that the triumph was ______ and the war was soon lost.
A win that cost so many soldiers that the war was lost describes a victory not worth its price.
se: The union won its strike, but with the factory now closed, the victory seemed ______.
hollow
Both 'pyrrhic' and 'hollow' describe a victory that brings no real benefit because of what it cost.

m: feeling uneasy or doubtful, especially about whether something is right; also slightly sick
x: The rickshaw ride over bumpy roads left me feeling qualmish by the time we reached the market.
He felt qualmish about signing a contract he had not fully read.
Some researchers were qualmish about publishing results that had not yet been replicated.
Many voters seemed qualmish about granting the government sweeping new surveillance powers.
She grew qualmish as the wedding day approached, wondering whether she was truly ready.
tc: Although the deal was perfectly legal, she felt ______ about it, unable to shake the sense that it was unfair to the workers.
'Although ... legal' and her lingering sense of unfairness show she felt morally uneasy.
se: Many parents were ______ about letting their children travel alone on the train.
uneasy
Both 'qualmish' and 'uneasy' mean anxious and doubtful about whether something is wise.

m: habitually complaining in a whining or irritable way (a variant of querulous)
x: Our querulent neighbour complains about the noise every time we have guests, even at six in the evening.
A querulent customer kept the help desk on the phone for an hour over a two-dollar fee.
The lecturer had little patience for querulent students who disputed every mark.
Online forums are full of querulent posts blaming the government for everything from rain to traffic.
As he aged, my grandfather became querulent, though we knew his complaints hid his loneliness.
tc: Unlike his cheerful brother, who never complained about anything, Tom was ______, grumbling about the food, the weather and the service.
The contrast with a brother 'who never complained' and Tom's constant grumbling point to a complaining nature.
se: After hours of waiting at the airport, the passengers grew increasingly ______.
peevish
Both 'querulent' and 'peevish' mean irritable and complaining, as long waits tend to make people.

m: uncontrollably energetic, noisy, and boisterous
x: Our rambunctious puppy knocked over a vase and two chairs in his first hour at home.
The office party became rather rambunctious after the director left early.
The teacher struggled to keep a class of thirty rambunctious ten-year-olds focused on fractions.
The parliamentary session turned rambunctious as members shouted and banged on their desks.
Even after fifty years of marriage, my grandparents still have rambunctious arguments over card games.
tc: The normally quiet children became ______ once the birthday cake arrived, running and shrieking around the garden.
The contrast with 'normally quiet' and the 'running and shrieking' show the blank means noisy and wild.
se: The fans grew so ______ that security guards had to calm them down.
rowdy
Both 'rambunctious' and 'rowdy' mean noisy and hard to control.

m: to branch out or spread into many parts, often creating complications or consequences
x: What started as a small disagreement over the electricity bill began to ramify into a quarrel about every shared expense.
As the company's operations ramified across twelve countries, coordinating them became a full-time job.
Under the microscope, students watched the fungus ramify through the bread in delicate white threads.
The effects of the new policy ramified far beyond farming, touching banks, schools and transport.
Their small lie ramified over the years until neither of them could remember where the truth ended.
tc: Like the roots of a banyan tree, the scandal continued to ______, reaching into ministries and banks that at first seemed unconnected.
The comparison with spreading roots and 'reaching into' many institutions point to branching out.
se: Once the river reaches the delta, it begins to ______ into dozens of smaller channels.
branch
Both 'ramify' and 'branch' mean to split into many parts, as a river does in a delta.

m: the re-establishment of friendly relations, especially between countries or groups
x: A shared love of gardening led to an unexpected rapprochement between the feuding neighbours.
The merger required a rapprochement between two departments that had long competed for the same budget.
Scholars have traced the gradual rapprochement between Darwinian biology and genetics in the early twentieth century.
The trade agreement marked a cautious rapprochement between the two countries after decades of hostility.
Her letter of apology opened the way to a rapprochement with her oldest friend.
tc: After decades of bitter rivalry, the two nations achieved the kind of ______ that few diplomats had thought possible, reopening embassies and trade routes.
Moving from 'bitter rivalry' to reopening embassies and trade shows a restoration of friendly relations.
se: The mediator worked for months to achieve ______ between the two estranged families.
reconciliation
Both 'rapprochement' and 'reconciliation' mean restoring friendly relations after a rift.

m: opposing political or social change and wanting to return to earlier conditions
x: My uncle's reactionary views on women working outside the home lead to heated arguments at every family dinner.
Younger employees found the firm's reactionary dress code, which banned trousers for women, simply absurd.
The historian traces how reactionary movements arose in Europe after the revolutions of 1848.
Critics described the new law as reactionary, saying it reversed decades of progress on workers' rights.
She worried that marrying into such a reactionary family would limit her freedom to pursue a career.
tc: While the young reformers pushed for change, the ______ old guard fought to restore the customs of the previous century.
The contrast with reformers and the wish to 'restore the customs of the previous century' point to opposition to change.
se: The party's ______ wing opposed every reform and longed for the policies of fifty years ago.
ultraconservative
Both 'reactionary' and 'ultraconservative' describe people who resist change and want to go back to the past.

m: unattractive and objectionable; tending to irritate or repel
x: The flat's rebarbative wallpaper, orange with brown swirls, was the first thing we replaced.
His rebarbative manner in meetings made colleagues reluctant to share their ideas with him.
The theory is sound, but the textbook's rebarbative prose discourages most students from reading past chapter one.
Critics called the new concrete tower rebarbative, a grey block that overshadows the old market square.
She found his constant boasting rebarbative and soon stopped answering his messages.
tc: Far from being charming, the new manager's personality was so ______ that half the team requested transfers within a month.
'Far from being charming' and staff fleeing to other teams point to a repellent personality.
se: Many readers find the novelist's style ______, full of ugly words and deliberately awkward sentences.
repellent
Both 'rebarbative' and 'repellent' mean unpleasant enough to drive people away.

m: rare, exotic, or obscure; sometimes overly refined or far-fetched
x: My friend only drinks recherché teas from tiny estates that most shops have never heard of.
The restaurant's menu is so recherché that the waiters have to explain nearly every dish.
His dissertation explores a recherché corner of medieval law that only a handful of scholars study.
The exhibition gathers recherché objects from private collections, many never shown in public before.
She found his recherché compliments, which quoted obscure French poets, more puzzling than flattering.
tc: Instead of choosing familiar pop songs, the DJ played ______ recordings that even the music critics in the room had never heard.
'Instead of ... familiar' and recordings even critics had never heard point to something rare and obscure.
se: The novel is full of ______ allusions that only specialists in Renaissance philosophy will recognise.
esoteric
Both 'recherché' and 'esoteric' mean obscure and known only to a few specialists.

m: cowardly, or disloyal to a cause, duty, or belief
x: My brother was too recreant to tell our parents he had dented the car, so he let me take the blame.
The union denounced the recreant members who crossed the picket line during the strike.
In medieval romances, a recreant knight who fled from battle lost both his honour and his title.
Activists accused the recreant politicians of abandoning the promises that had won them their seats.
She could never forgive the recreant friend who stayed silent while others spread lies about her.
tc: Instead of defending the colleague who had always supported him, the ______ manager joined the others in blaming her.
Turning on someone who 'had always supported him' shows disloyal, cowardly behaviour.
se: The soldier was branded ______ after he abandoned his post and fled at the first sound of gunfire.
craven
Both 'recreant' and 'craven' mean shamefully cowardly, as fleeing one's post shows.

m: a recurrence or fresh outbreak of something undesirable after a period of quiet
x: After a calm year, the neighbours' quarrel over the shared driveway saw an unwelcome recrudescence last spring.
Managers feared a recrudescence of old rivalries once the popular mediator retired.
The historian links the recrudescence of nationalist sentiment in the 1930s to the economic depression.
Experts warned of a recrudescence of dengue in Dhaka once the monsoon rains returned.
Each anniversary brought a painful recrudescence of the grief she thought she had overcome.
tc: Just when officials believed the epidemic was over, the sudden ______ of cases in the capital forced schools to close again.
'Just when officials believed the epidemic was over' and 'close again' show the problem has broken out anew.
se: Police were deployed to prevent any ______ of the rioting that had shaken the city last summer.
resurgence
Both 'recrudescence' and 'resurgence' mean a fresh outbreak of something that had died down.

m: to edit a text for publication, especially by removing confidential or sensitive information
x: Before posting the screenshot online, I redacted my friend's phone number and address.
The legal team spent the weekend redacting client names from the documents before the audit.
Scholars believe later scribes redacted the ancient text, combining several older versions into one.
The government released the report, but large sections had been redacted for reasons of national security.
She showed me his letter but redacted the most personal lines, saying some things were only for her.
tc: To protect the witnesses, the court ordered the lawyers to ______ every name and address in the transcript before it was made public.
'To protect the witnesses' before publication shows the blank means to remove sensitive details.
se: Officials will ______ any passages that might reveal the identity of undercover agents.
censor
Both 'redact' and 'censor' mean to remove sensitive material before release.

m: shining very brightly; radiant
x: The lake looked refulgent in the late-afternoon sun as we walked home from the market.
The newly polished trophies stood refulgent in the glass case outside the chairman's office.
The poet describes the moon as refulgent, flooding the silent valley with silver light.
Astronomers recorded a refulgent burst of light as the distant star exploded.
On her wedding day she looked refulgent, her face glowing with happiness.
tc: Unlike the dim, flickering candles in the hall, the chandelier was ______, filling the ballroom with dazzling light.
'Unlike the dim, flickering candles' and 'dazzling light' point to something shining brilliantly.
se: The cathedral's golden dome looked ______ in the morning sunshine.
radiant
Both 'refulgent' and 'radiant' mean shining brightly.

m: becoming active, popular, or vigorous again after a period of decline
x: There is a renascent interest in handloom saris among young women in Dhaka.
The renascent shipbuilding industry has brought hundreds of jobs back to the old port town.
Scholars have noted a renascent enthusiasm for Latin in some secondary schools.
Officials are worried about renascent nationalism in several European countries.
After her divorce, she felt a renascent confidence, as if she had rediscovered who she was.
tc: After decades of decline, the city's jazz scene is now ______, with new clubs opening every month.
'After decades of decline' and new clubs opening show the scene is coming back to life.
se: Analysts were surprised by the ______ demand for typewriters among young writers.
resurgent
Both 'renascent' and 'resurgent' mean rising again after a decline.

m: the act of making amends for a wrong, often by paying money or helping those wronged
x: As reparation for breaking our neighbour's window, my son spent two Saturdays weeding her garden.
The airline offered free flights as reparation to passengers whose luggage had been lost.
Her research examines how post-war reparations shaped the economies of both the victors and the defeated.
Survivors are demanding reparations from the company whose factory poisoned the river.
He knew no apology could make full reparation for the years of neglect his daughter had suffered.
tc: Admitting that its negligence had caused the flooding, the company agreed to make full ______ to every family whose home had been damaged.
Admitting fault for the damage leads to making amends to the victims, which is what the blank means.
se: The government promised ______ to the farmers whose land had been seized without fair payment.
compensation
Both 'reparation' and 'compensation' mean making up for a loss or wrong, here to the farmers.

m: to feel or express discontent, especially by complaining about one's situation or longing for what is lost
x: Rather than repine over the lost scholarship, she applied to three other universities the following week.
My grandmother never repined at the hardships of village life; she simply got on with the work.
There is little point repining about a project the board has already cancelled.
After the election defeat, party members spent months repining instead of rebuilding their organisation.
He repined for the friends he had left behind when the family moved abroad.
tc: Instead of accepting her modest circumstances with grace, she continued to ______ about the wealth she had never had.
'Instead of accepting ... with grace' signals the opposite attitude, so the blank must mean complain or fret.
se: It is useless to ______ over opportunities that are already gone; better to look for new ones.
fret
Both 'repine' and 'fret' mean to brood or complain unhappily, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: to criticize or correct someone, usually gently, for a fault
x: The teacher reproved the boy quietly for talking during the exam rather than shaming him in front of the class.
My manager reproved me for missing the deadline, but she also offered to help me plan better.
Professor Rahman gently reproved his students for relying on summaries instead of reading the original papers.
In its ruling, the court reproved the government for failing to consult local communities before approving the dam.
She reproved her younger brother with a look rather than words when he interrupted their parents.
tc: Rather than harshly punishing the intern for his mistake, the editor chose to ______ him mildly and explain what had gone wrong.
'Rather than harshly punishing' and 'mildly' point to a gentle form of criticism.
se: The coach was quick to ______ any player who showed up late to training.
chide
Both 'reprove' and 'chide' mean to scold mildly, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: boastful, inflated talk or behaviour
x: After all his rodomontade about winning the tournament, my cousin was knocked out in the first round.
Investors were tired of the chief executive's rodomontade and wanted to see actual profits.
The reviewer complained that the thesis contained more rodomontade than evidence.
Critics dismissed the candidate's campaign rally as an hour of empty rodomontade.
Her friends had learned to ignore his rodomontade about his business, knowing how little money he actually had.
tc: For all his ______ about single-handedly saving the company, the records showed he had contributed very little.
The contrast between his claims and his tiny contribution shows the blank means boastful talk.
se: Voters had grown weary of the politician's ______ and wanted concrete policies instead.
bluster
Both 'rodomontade' and 'bluster' mean loud, boastful talk, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: calmness and composure, especially in dangerous or difficult situations
x: The pilot's sangfroid during the emergency landing reassured the terrified passengers.
She handled the hostile questions at the press conference with remarkable sangfroid.
Even when his laptop crashed the night before his thesis defence, Arif kept his sangfroid and rebuilt the slides.
Surgeons need great sangfroid to stay focused when an operation suddenly goes wrong.
I envy my sister's sangfroid; nothing seems to rattle her, not even a family argument at dinner.
tc: While everyone else in the control room panicked, the chief engineer displayed extraordinary ______, calmly working through the checklist.
The contrast with 'panicked' and the word 'calmly' show the blank means composure.
se: The negotiator's ______ in the face of angry threats impressed even her opponents.
composure
Both 'sangfroid' and 'composure' mean calmness under pressure, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: wise and showing deep understanding or good judgement
x: My grandfather was a sapient man whose advice the whole village sought before any major decision.
Her sapient comments in the meeting steered the team away from a costly mistake.
The professor's sapient analysis of the data revealed a pattern no one else had noticed.
Societies need sapient leaders who think about the long-term consequences of their policies.

She felt there was something untoward about his sudden interest in her finances.
tc: The trip went perfectly smoothly; apart from a slight delay at the airport, nothing ______ happened.

se: The hospital reported that the operation went ahead without any ______ complications.
unexpected
Both 'untoward' and 'unexpected' describe unforeseen problems, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: unusual or not habitual; out of character

Dhaka's streets fell into an unwonted calm during the nationwide strike.
She blushed at his unwonted compliment, unsure how to respond.
tc: Normally reserved and formal, the judge spoke with ______ emotion as she sentenced the man.
'Normally reserved and formal' signals that the emotion was unusual for her.
se: The normally grumpy clerk greeted us with ______ cheerfulness.
uncharacteristic
Both 'unwonted' and 'uncharacteristic' mean unusual for that person, so the meaning holds.

m: erratic and unpredictable; marked by sudden, whimsical changes
x: Our vagarious spring weather means you should carry an umbrella even on sunny mornings.

The contrast with 'steady and predictable' and constant changes show the blank means erratic.
se: The ______ policies of the new administration left businesses unable to plan ahead.
erratic
Both 'vagarious' and 'erratic' mean unpredictable and changeable, so the sentence means the same.

m: lack of interest, liveliness or intellectual substance; dullness

The vapidity of the corporate mission statement made employees roll their eyes.
Examiners complained about the vapidity of essays that repeated clichés without real argument.
Critics lamented the vapidity of political debates focused on slogans instead of policies.
She grew tired of the vapidity of their conversations, which never went beyond gossip and shopping.
tc: Expecting a thoughtful lecture, the audience was disappointed by the ______ of the speech, which offered nothing but empty platitudes.
'Expecting a thoughtful lecture' and 'empty platitudes' show the blank means lack of substance.
se: The ______ of the dialogue made the film's two hours feel endless.
insipidity
Both 'vapidity' and 'insipidity' mean dull emptiness, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: boastful; excessively proud of oneself or one's achievements
x: His vaunting claims about his cooking skills collapsed when he burned the rice.
The startup's vaunting press releases promised far more than its product could deliver.
The scholar's vaunting tone in the introduction irritated reviewers before they even reached the evidence.
Vaunting ambition has brought down many leaders who believed they could not fail.
I grew tired of his vaunting talk about his wealthy friends and expensive holidays.
tc: Far from being modest about her success, she was ______, telling everyone who would listen how brilliant she was.
'Far from being modest' and telling everyone how brilliant she was show the blank means boastful.
se: The general's ______ speech promised a swift victory that never came.
boastful
Both 'vaunting' and 'boastful' describe proud, bragging talk, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: too many words, especially unnecessary or overly technical ones

My supervisor returned my thesis chapter with a note: too much verbiage, not enough analysis.
Political manifestos are often padded with verbiage that commits the party to nothing.
Beneath all the flowery verbiage of his apology, I could find no real admission of fault.

Halving the article while keeping every fact means the removed material was needless words.
se: Readers lose patience with reports full of ______ that take three pages to make a simple point.
wordiness
Both 'verbiage' and 'wordiness' mean using too many words, so the sentence means the same.

m: harsh, abusive criticism meant to damage someone's reputation
x: The vilification of the referee on social media after the match was shocking.
Whistle-blowers often face vilification from colleagues who see them as traitors.
Historians have documented the vilification of early women scientists by their male peers.

tc: Instead of praise for exposing the fraud, the journalist received a storm of ______, with critics calling her a liar and a traitor.
'Instead of praise' and being called a liar and traitor show the blank means abusive attack on her reputation.
se: The actor sued the tabloid over its relentless ______ of his character.
defamation
Both 'vilification' and 'defamation' mean attacking someone's reputation, so the meaning holds.

m: a domineering, violent or bad-tempered woman (an old-fashioned, often unfair label)
x: In the novel, the innkeeper's wife is a virago who terrorises guests and servants alike.

Scholars of Victorian literature note how often strong-willed women were portrayed as viragos.
Old cartoons depicted female reformers as screaming viragos to discredit their cause.

'Formidable' and screaming over the slightest noise point to a domineering, bad-tempered woman.
se: The play's heroine is no gentle maiden but a fierce ______ who bullies everyone around her.
harridan
Both 'virago' and 'harridan' mean a domineering, bad-tempered woman, so the sentence means the same.

m: having strength, energy and vigour, traditionally associated with men; forceful
x: Her grandfather, still virile and energetic at seventy, insisted on carrying the luggage himself.
Our new chief executive promised a virile, aggressive strategy to win back market share.
Students analysed how wartime posters portrayed soldiers as virile defenders of the nation.
Farmers select the most virile bulls for breeding to strengthen their herds.
The advertisement relied on a tired image of a virile cowboy riding into the sunset.
tc: Once frail and sickly, the athlete had become strong and ______ after years of hard training.
The contrast with 'frail and sickly' and the pairing with 'strong' show the blank means vigorous.
se: The film's hero is an adventurer so ______ that he wrestles crocodiles and climbs cliffs with ease.
vigorous
Both 'virile' and 'vigorous' describe someone full of strength and energy, so the meaning holds.

m: to give life, energy, or vividness to; to enliven
x: A few bright cushions and a new rug vivified our dull living room almost overnight.
Our manager hoped the team retreat would vivify a department worn down by months of layoffs.
Good teachers vivify history by connecting ancient events to the everyday lives of their students.
Researchers found that small parks and gardens can vivify neglected urban neighbourhoods and lift residents' moods.
Her letters, full of jokes and family gossip, always vivified him during the long winter abroad.
tc: The novelist's vivid descriptions do more than decorate the story; they ______ characters who might otherwise feel flat and lifeless.
'Who might otherwise feel flat and lifeless' shows the blank must mean bring to life.
se: The festival organisers hoped that music and street food would ______ the sleepy old market district.
enliven
Both 'vivify' and 'enliven' mean to fill with life and energy, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: to shout or cry out loudly and insistently, especially in complaint or protest
x: Street vendors in Old Dhaka vociferate their prices over the constant din of rickshaw bells.

Protesters vociferated outside parliament for hours, demanding that the controversial bill be withdrawn.

tc: Rather than quietly submitting a written complaint, the angry tenant chose to ______ in the hallway until the landlord appeared.
'Rather than quietly' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean shout loudly.
se: Whenever the umpire made a doubtful call, a few spectators would ______ angrily from the stands.
shout
Both 'vociferate' and 'shout' describe crying out loudly, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: the quality of talking fluently, readily, and at great length
x: His volubility at dinner parties means that quieter guests rarely get a word in.

Voters seemed charmed by the mayor's volubility, even when his long answers avoided the question entirely.
After years of her husband's volubility, she found the silence of the empty house unsettling.
tc: Known for his ______, the usually chatty host surprised everyone by saying almost nothing all evening.
'Usually chatty' restates the blank, so it must mean talkativeness.
se: The interviewer found the young graduate's ______ refreshing after a morning of nervous, one-word answers.
talkativeness
Both 'volubility' and 'talkativeness' mean a readiness to talk at length, contrasting with one-word answers.

m: a large, confused mass or jumble of things

Managers struggled to make decisions amid a welter of conflicting reports from different departments.

She tried to sort through the welter of emotions she felt on the morning of her sister's wedding.

'Far from being orderly' and 'confused' show the blank means a disordered jumble.
se: Investors had to make sense of the ______ of rumours that followed the company's sudden announcement.
jumble
Both 'welter' and 'jumble' mean a confused mass, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: foolish; lacking intelligence or good sense
x: Leaving the front door unlocked all weekend was a witless thing to do, and I paid for it.
Our team wasted a month on a witless marketing plan that nobody had bothered to test.

Critics dismissed the new reality show as witless entertainment aimed at the lowest common denominator.
He felt witless and clumsy whenever he tried to talk to her, though she found him charming.
tc: Far from being clever, the comedian's jokes were so ______ that even his loyal fans stopped laughing.
'Far from being clever' tells us the blank must mean foolish.
se: Trying to overtake a bus on that narrow mountain road during a storm was utterly ______.
foolish
Both 'witless' and 'foolish' mean showing no sense, so the sentence means the same.

m: in the habit of doing something; accustomed or inclined
x: As my grandfather was wont to say, a cup of tea solves most problems before lunch.

'Although' and 'normally punctual' show that arriving early is his habit, so the blank means accustomed.
se: When anxious, she is ______ to talk too much and too quickly.
apt
Both 'wont to' and 'apt to' describe a habitual tendency, so the sentence means the same.

m: wildly unreasonable, illogical, or inappropriate; ridiculous

'Not just ambitious but downright' intensifies toward something wildly unreasonable.
se: Expecting a newly hired intern to fix the company's finances alone is completely ______.
ridiculous
Both 'absurd' and 'ridiculous' mean wildly unreasonable, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to adapt to a new climate, environment, or situation

'Giving their bodies time' to deal with the altitude indicates the blank means adapt.
se: It can take months for a family that moves abroad to fully ______ to a new culture.
adjust
Both 'acclimate' and 'adjust' mean to adapt to new surroundings, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to make something worse or more bitter; to irritate or embitter

'Instead of calming' signals the opposite, so the blank means make worse.

worsen
Both 'acerbate' and 'worsen' mean to make a bad feeling more severe, so the sentence means the same.

acceptable

worsen

defense

antiquary

The contrast with 'forgettable' and the phrase 'stop in their tracks' show the blank means striking.

striking
Both 'arresting' and 'striking' mean attention-grabbing, so the sentence means the same.

The essay was an artful blend of personal memoir and serious historical research.

She was artful enough to hide her disappointment behind polite congratulations.

'Far from being naive' and 'subtle tricks' show the blank means crafty.
se: The con man's ______ scheme fooled even experienced bankers.
cunning
Both 'artful' and 'cunning' mean cleverly deceptive, so the sentence means the same.

m: causing great surprise or wonder; astonishing

astonishing

m: to make aware of or responsive to something; to bring into harmony

se: A good teacher tries to ______ her lessons to the needs of each class.
adapt

m: genuine and real; not fake, copied, or pretended

genuine
Both 'authentic' and 'genuine' mean real rather than forged, so the sentence means the same.

m: to prevent something bad from happening; also, to turn away one's eyes

prevent
Both 'avert' and 'prevent' mean to stop something bad from happening, so the meaning is the same.

m: to relapse into bad habits or worse behavior after having improved

relapse
Both 'backslide' and 'relapse' mean to fall back into a bad habit, so the sentence means the same.

m: the quality of being dull, unoriginal, and commonplace; a trite remark

Critics praised the film for exposing the banality of everyday corruption in local government.
After the excitement of their honeymoon, they were surprised by the banality of married life.
tc: Hoping for fresh insights, readers were disappointed by the ______ of the author's latest book, which simply repeated familiar cliches.
'Hoping for fresh insights' contrasts with 'repeated familiar cliches', so the blank means unoriginality.
se: The ______ of the politician's slogans made it hard to believe he had any new ideas.
triteness
Both 'banality' and 'triteness' mean dull unoriginality, so the sentence means the same.

m: a pointed, hurtful remark; also, a sharp backward-pointing spike

The reviewer's barb that the thesis was long on words but short on ideas stung the young scholar.
Rival candidates traded barbs throughout the televised debate, but neither offered a clear plan for jobs.
He laughed off her barb, but later admitted that it had hurt more than he showed.
tc: Instead of offering praise, the critic directed one sharp ______ after another at the inexperienced director.
'Instead of offering praise' and 'sharp' show the blank means a hurtful remark.
se: The comedian's ______ about the mayor's haircut drew loud laughter from the audience.
jibe
Both 'barb' and 'jibe' mean a mocking remark, so the sentence means the same.

m: to exchange goods or services for other goods or services without using money
x: At the village market, my grandmother still barters rice for fresh fish from the river.
Two freelancers bartered services: one designed a logo while the other wrote the website copy.
Anthropologists study how communities bartered long before coins and paper money existed.
After the currency collapsed, many families bartered jewellery and clothing for food.
As children, my sister and I would barter chores, trading washing-up for laundry duty.
tc: In the remote island community, where cash was scarce, residents had to ______ fish and vegetables for tools and cloth.
'Cash was scarce' and swapping fish for tools show the blank means exchange goods without money.
se: During the war, families had to ______ their furniture for bread and fuel.
trade
Both 'barter' and 'trade' mean to exchange one thing for another, so the sentence means the same.

m: morally low; lacking honor, dignity, or principle
x: Stealing from a charity collection box is about as base as behaviour gets.
The manager's base decision to take credit for his intern's work cost him the team's respect.
In the novel, the villain is driven by base motives such as greed and envy rather than ideals.
Commentators condemned the campaign's base appeal to fear and prejudice.
She was ashamed of the base jealousy she felt when her best friend got engaged.
tc: Unlike his noble brother, who gave away his fortune to help others, Edmund was driven only by ______ greed.
'Unlike his noble brother' signals a contrast, so the blank means morally low.
se: The scheme appealed to the voters' most ______ instincts, encouraging selfishness and spite.
ignoble
Both 'base' and 'ignoble' mean morally low, so the sentence means the same.

m: a source of guidance, hope, or inspiration; originally a signal light or fire
x: For fishing boats returning after dark, the lighthouse served as a beacon guiding them home.
During the chaotic restructuring, our small office became a beacon of calm and good sense.
The university library has long been a beacon for scholars seeking rare manuscripts.
For many refugees, the country stood as a beacon of hope and freedom.
During her darkest months, her mother's letters were a beacon that kept her going.
tc: In a region torn apart by war, the small hospital became the only ______ of hope, guiding the injured toward safety.
'Of hope' and 'guiding the injured toward safety' show the blank means a source of guidance.
se: On stormy nights, the lighthouse was the only ______ that the sailors could trust.
guide
Both 'beacon' and 'guide' mean something that shows the way, so the sentence means the same.

m: flattering to one's appearance; suitable or appropriate
x: That shade of green is very becoming on you; you should wear it more often.
Shouting at junior staff is hardly becoming behaviour for a senior manager.
Our professor reminded us that such sloppy citations were hardly becoming in a doctoral thesis.
Critics said that such gloating after an election victory was not becoming in a public servant.
She wore a modest, becoming dress to meet her fiancé's parents for the first time.
tc: Her new hairstyle was so ______ that several friends said she looked years younger.
Looking years younger shows the hairstyle was flattering.
se: Everyone agreed that the soft blue dress was very ______ on her.
flattering
Both 'becoming' and 'flattering' mean making someone look attractive, so the sentence means the same.

m: wet, dirty, and untidy in appearance
x: We arrived at the hotel bedraggled after walking through the monsoon rain without umbrellas.
A bedraggled courier delivered the package, dripping water all over the office carpet.
By the end of exam week, the students looked bedraggled and exhausted.
Rescuers pulled several bedraggled survivors from the floodwaters early on Tuesday morning.
She hugged the bedraggled puppy her son had found shivering under a parked car.
tc: After hours of hiking through mud and rain, the once-neat scouts returned to camp looking thoroughly ______.
'Once-neat' contrasted with 'mud and rain' shows the blank means wet and untidy.
se: The kitten crawled out of the drain, ______ and shivering.
disheveled
Both 'bedraggled' and 'disheveled' describe a messy, untidy appearance, so the sentence means the same.

m: appropriate or suitable for a particular person, status, or occasion
x: We gave my grandfather a gift befitting his eightieth birthday: a beautifully bound family album.
The firm gave its retiring founder a send-off befitting someone who had built the company from scratch.
The graduate's thesis was praised as work befitting a far more experienced researcher.
The fallen firefighters were given a funeral befitting their courage, with thousands lining the streets.
She spoke with a dignity befitting the occasion, even though her heart was breaking.
tc: Rather than gloating, the champion warmly congratulated his opponent in a manner ______ a true sportsman.
'Rather than gloating' shows his behaviour was suitable for a true sportsman.
se: The palace hosted a banquet ______ the visiting queen's royal status.
fitting
Both 'befitting' and 'fitting' mean appropriate to her status, so the sentence means the same.

m: to rouse oneself to action; to make an effort after being idle
x: On Sunday mornings, I can barely bestir myself to make breakfast.
Only after the deadline had passed did the team bestir themselves to finish the report.
Our lecturer urged us to bestir ourselves and start our research projects before the holidays.
Officials finally bestirred themselves to repair the bridge after a bus nearly fell into the river.
When her friend fell ill, she bestirred herself from her own gloom to help.
tc: After weeks of lying on the sofa, he finally managed to ______ himself and start looking for a job.
'After weeks of lying on the sofa' and 'finally' show the blank means rouse to action.
se: The alarm rang three times before she could ______ herself and get out of bed.
rouse
Both 'bestir' and 'rouse' mean to wake oneself into action, so the sentence means the same.

m: to confuse or puzzle someone completely
x: The new self-checkout machines at the supermarket bewilder my grandparents every time.
Constantly changing instructions from head office bewildered even our most experienced staff.
The professor's dense notation tends to bewilder first-year students who are new to the subject.
Voters were bewildered by the complicated ballot paper, which listed more than forty candidates.
His sudden coldness bewildered her, since they had parted on such good terms the night before.
tc: The magician's tricks were designed to ______ the audience, leaving even sharp-eyed adults unable to explain what they had seen.
'Unable to explain what they had seen' shows the blank means confuse completely.
se: The maze of one-way streets is bound to ______ any visitor who arrives without a map.
confuse
Both 'bewilder' and 'confuse' mean to leave someone puzzled, so the sentence means the same.

m: (of the eyes) dim, unfocused, or watery, especially from tiredness
x: I stumbled into the kitchen with bleary eyes, searching for the coffee.
After a night of preparing slides, she presented to the board with bleary eyes and a hoarse voice.
Students spilled out of the library at dawn, bleary from a night of last-minute revision.
Commuters stood bleary-eyed on the platform as the delayed train finally pulled in.
He gazed at her with bleary eyes, too tired to argue any longer.
tc: After driving through the night without rest, his eyes were red and ______, and he could hardly read the road signs.
No rest and being unable to read signs show the blank means dim and unfocused.
se: She stared at the screen with ______ eyes, struggling to stay awake.
blurry
Both 'bleary' and 'blurry' describe tired eyes that cannot focus, so the sentence means the same.

m: swollen; excessively large or inflated, bigger than is necessary
x: I felt bloated after eating three plates of biryani at my cousin's wedding.
The new chief executive promised to cut the bloated management structure by half.
My supervisor said my bloated literature review needed trimming by at least five thousand words.
Taxpayers are tired of funding a bloated bureaucracy that delivers very few services.
His ego became so bloated after the promotion that old friends stopped calling him.
tc: The new mayor promised to trim the city's ______ payroll, which had grown far beyond what its services required.
'Grown far beyond what its services required' shows the blank means excessively large.
se: Critics argued that the defence budget had become ______ and wasteful.
inflated
Both 'bloated' and 'inflated' mean grown larger than necessary, so the sentence means the same.

m: a loud, boastful person who talks too much about himself
x: The blowhard at the next table spent the whole dinner bragging about his new car.
Every office seems to have one blowhard who claims credit for everyone else's ideas.
In seminars, he came across as a blowhard who talked endlessly but rarely cited any evidence.
Columnists dismissed the radio host as a blowhard whose outrage was mostly for ratings.
She found him charming at first, but soon realised he was a blowhard with little substance.
tc: Everyone at the club knew that the man who bragged about climbing Everest and founding three companies was the biggest ______ in town.
Constant bragging identifies him as a boastful person.
se: The party's founder was an arrogant ______ who never stopped boasting about his own achievements.
braggart
Both 'blowhard' and 'braggart' mean a boastful person, so the sentence means the same.

m: very direct and frank in speech, without trying to be tactful
x: My grandmother is famously blunt and will tell you straight away if she doesn't like your cooking.
In my performance review, the manager was blunt: my reports were consistently late.
My supervisor's blunt feedback on the draft stung, but it made the final thesis much stronger.
Health officials issued a blunt warning that hospitals could soon run out of beds.
Let me be blunt with you: I don't think this relationship is working anymore.
tc: Unlike her tactful colleagues, who softened every criticism, Maria was so ______ that she sometimes hurt people's feelings.
'Unlike her tactful colleagues' signals a contrast, so the blank means bluntly direct.
se: The doctor was refreshingly ______ about the risks of the surgery.
frank
Both 'blunt' and 'frank' mean speaking directly and honestly, so the sentence means the same.

m: a wasteful, pointless project that squanders time and money, often public funds
x: Our neighbourhood's new fountain, which has never worked, is a costly boondoggle.
Staff joked that the five-day leadership retreat at a beach resort was a boondoggle disguised as training.
Some economists call the research centre an academic boondoggle that has produced nothing useful.
Opposition lawmakers denounced the half-finished stadium as a billion-dollar boondoggle.
He suspected that his brother's latest business scheme was another boondoggle that would drain the family's savings.
tc: The high-speed rail line, which cost billions yet carried almost no passengers, became the city's most notorious ______.
Costing billions while carrying almost no one shows the blank means a wasteful project.
se: The auditors concluded that the expensive new software system was a complete ______.
waste
Both 'boondoggle' and 'waste' describe a pointless use of money, so the sentence means the same.

m: to carry out a task badly or carelessly; to bungle
x: I botched the recipe by adding salt instead of sugar to the cake batter.
The contractor botched the bathroom renovation, and water now leaks into the flat below.
Nervous and unprepared, he botched his thesis defence and had to resubmit.
Officials admitted they had botched the vaccine rollout, leaving rural clinics without supplies.
She was afraid she would botch the proposal, so she rehearsed her speech for days.
tc: The surgeon was so careless that hospital managers feared he would ______ even the simplest procedure.
'So careless' implies he would perform the procedure badly.
se: If you rush the final coat of paint, you'll ______ the whole job.
bungle
Both 'botch' and 'bungle' mean to do something clumsily and badly, so the sentence means the same.

m: to arrange or negotiate an agreement between other parties
x: My aunt brokered a truce between my cousins after their argument over the family car.
Our team leader brokered a compromise between engineering and marketing on the launch date.
The dean helped broker an agreement that lets students take courses at a partner university.
Neighbouring countries offered to broker peace talks between the warring factions.
Friends tried to broker a reconciliation, but the couple had already decided to separate.
tc: Because neither side trusted the other, a neutral diplomat was invited to ______ a ceasefire between the two armies.
A neutral party brought in because the sides distrust each other is there to negotiate an agreement.
se: The United Nations tried to ______ an agreement between the rival groups.
negotiate
Both 'broker' and 'negotiate' mean to arrange a deal between parties, so the sentence means the same.

m: acting in a confused, clumsy, or incompetent way
x: A bumbling waiter spilled soup on two guests before we had even ordered our main course.
Our bumbling new manager kept forgetting meetings and misplacing important files.
The novel's hero is a bumbling professor who solves crimes almost entirely by accident.
Critics blamed bumbling officials for the chaotic evacuation during the floods.
Her friends found his bumbling attempts at romance oddly endearing.
tc: Far from being efficient, the ______ clerk lost three passports and misspelled half the names on the forms.
'Far from being efficient' and the list of mistakes show the blank means clumsy and incompetent.
se: The film's ______ detective keeps tripping over clues that he never actually understands.
blundering
Both 'bumbling' and 'blundering' mean clumsily incompetent, so the sentence means the same.

m: excited, busy, and often noisy activity
x: I love the bustle of the market on Friday mornings, when everyone is shopping for the weekend.
Amid the bustle of the newsroom, she somehow managed to finish her article on time.
The campus library offered a quiet escape from the bustle of student life.
The constant bustle of Dhaka's streets, crowded with rickshaws, buses and vendors, can overwhelm first-time visitors.
After the bustle of the wedding, the family enjoyed a quiet evening together at home.
tc: After weeks in the noisy ______ of the capital, the travellers welcomed the silence of the mountain village.
'Noisy' and the contrast with 'silence' show the blank means busy activity.
se: Now retired, he misses the ______ of the busy hospital where he worked for thirty years.
hustle
Both 'bustle' and 'hustle' mean lively, busy activity, so the sentence means the same.

m: a person or thing widely seen as the perfect example of a particular quality
x: In our family, Uncle Karim's fruitcake is a byword for something nobody wants to eat.
The company's customer service has become a byword for efficiency across the industry.
Among young scientists, her lab is a byword for rigorous, careful research.
Once a byword for corruption, the agency has spent a decade rebuilding public trust.
To his friends, he was a byword for loyalty; he never let anyone down.
tc: Thanks to decades of consistently excellent service, the hotel's name is now the region's ______ for luxury.
Decades of excellent service have made the name stand for luxury, which is what a byword is.
se: In its day, the old bridge was considered a true ______ for engineering excellence.
synonym
Both 'byword for' and 'synonym for' mean a name that stands for a quality, so the sentence means the same.

m: to ask for or get something free by imposing on other people's generosity
x: My flatmate is always trying to cadge a cup of milk or a few teabags from me.
A colleague cadged a lift home from me every evening for a month without offering petrol money.
Graduate students often cadge free meals by attending departmental seminars with catering.
Reports revealed that several officials had cadged luxury holidays from companies seeking contracts.
Even as a child, he could cadge sweets from relatives with a single charming smile.
tc: Never willing to pay for anything himself, Tom would always ______ drinks from whoever was sitting next to him.
'Never willing to pay' shows the blank means get things free from others.
se: He tried to ______ a few dollars from his friends to pay for the cinema ticket.
scrounge
Both 'cadge' and 'scrounge' mean to get something by begging from others, so the sentence means the same.

m: causing great damage, suffering, or disaster; catastrophic
x: Forgetting my passport on the morning of the flight could have been calamitous.
The merger proved calamitous, wiping out half the company's value within a year.
Historians describe the Bengal famine of 1943 as one of the most calamitous events of the century.
Scientists warn that unchecked warming could have calamitous consequences for coastal cities.
Their calamitous holiday, with lost luggage and a week of storms, somehow brought the couple closer together.
tc: The decision to build on the floodplain proved ______: within ten years, repeated floods had destroyed hundreds of homes.
The colon introduces the destruction of hundreds of homes, showing the blank means disastrous.
se: The sudden drought had ______ effects on the region's harvest.
disastrous
Both 'calamitous' and 'disastrous' mean causing great damage, so the sentence means the same.

m: (of a boat) to overturn in the water; figuratively, to upset or ruin
x: Our little rowing boat nearly capsized when my cousin stood up to take a photo.
One bad quarter threatened to capsize the startup, which had very little cash in reserve.
Engineers tested scale models to find the angle at which the new ferry design would capsize.
An overloaded ferry capsized in the river during a storm, prompting a large rescue operation.
His affair nearly capsized their marriage, but counselling helped them start again.
tc: The fishing boat was so badly overloaded that a single large wave caused it to ______.
An overloaded boat hit by a big wave would overturn, which is what the blank means.
se: If too many people lean over the same side, the canoe may ______.
overturn
Both 'capsize' and 'overturn' mean to turn upside down in the water, so the sentence means the same.
